topics.title: Logic and The Language of Proof

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a **mathematical proof**?
options: A sequence of logical deductions from given assumptions that establishes the truth of a statement
A numerical example that demonstrates a pattern
A diagram showing a geometric relationship
A hypothesis that has been tested many times
questions.solution: A mathematical proof is a rigorous logical argument that establishes the truth of a statement from axioms and previously proven results.

steps.explain: Identify what distinguishes a proof from other mathematical reasoning.
steps.work: A proof must logically deduce the conclusion from accepted assumptions using valid inference rules.

steps.explain: Eliminate the other options.
steps.work: Numerical examples (option B) are not proofs — they may show a pattern but cannot establish universal truth. Diagrams (option C) can illustrate but not prove. A hypothesis (option D) is unproven conjecture.

steps.explain: State the correct definition.
steps.work: Option A correctly defines a proof as a sequence of logical deductions from given assumptions.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following best describes a **mathematical proof**?
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information and connect it to the relevant mathematical method.

questions.stem: In a proof by **direct method**, we:
options: Assume the conclusion is false and derive a contradiction
Assume the negation of the hypothesis and prove the negation of the conclusion
Start from the hypothesis and use logical steps to reach the conclusion
Test specific numerical examples to confirm the result
questions.solution: In a direct proof, we start from the hypothesis (given conditions) and use logical steps to arrive at the conclusion.

steps.explain: Recall the definition of a direct proof.
steps.work: A direct proof starts with the hypothesis \(P\) and uses axioms, definitions, and previously established results to prove the conclusion \(Q\), establishing \(P \Rightarrow Q\).

steps.explain: Distinguish from other proof types.
steps.work: Option A is proof by contradiction. Option B is proof by contrapositive. Option D is not a proof method at all.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is a counter-example to the following statement?

All people who get ATARS over 99 do Extension 2 Mathematics.
questions.hint: A counter-example to 'if P then Q' is a case where P is true and Q is false.

steps.explain: Write the statement as an implication: for every person, ATAR over 99 \(\Rightarrow\) does Extension 2.
A counter-example is one person for whom \(P\) is true but \(Q\) is false.
Polly got over 99 (\(P\) true) and did not do Extension 2 (\(Q\) false), so she is a counter-example: option D.
A is a different general statement, not one example. Jesse might also have done Extension 2, so B is not certain. Sam has \(P\) false, so says nothing about the statement.

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: No people who get ATARS over 99 do Extension 2 Mathematics.
Jesse did History and got an ATAR over 99.
Sam did Extension 2 Mathematics and got an ATAR under 99.
Polly did not do Extension 2 Mathematics and got an ATAR over 99.

keyPoints.text: All people who get ATARS over 99 do Extension 2 Mathematics
keyPoints.note: Find one person with an ATAR over 99 who definitely did NOT do Extension 2.

questions.stem:
Consider the statement for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\):

If \(n\) is prime then \(n\) has exactly two factors.

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.hint: Converse of P ⇒ Q is Q ⇒ P.

steps.explain: Label the parts of the statement \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
steps.work: \(P:\ n\text{ is prime},\qquad Q:\ n\text{ has exactly two factors}\)

steps.explain: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion: \(Q\Rightarrow P\).

So the converse is: if \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime. (Option 'if not prime then not two factors' is the inverse \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\); 'if not two factors then not prime' is the contrapositive.)

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: If \(n\) is not prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime.

keyPoints.note: The converse swaps the 'if' part and the 'then' part.

parts.hint: Contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is (not Q) ⇒ (not P).

steps.explain: With \(P:\ n\) is prime and \(Q:\ n\) has exactly two factors, the contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): swap and negate both parts.
So: if \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime. A statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent.

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: If \(n\) is not prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) is prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime.

keyPoints.note: Swap the two parts AND negate both.

parts.stem: Determine whether or not the statement is an equivalence. Give reasons.
parts.hint: An equivalence needs the statement AND its converse to be true.

steps.explain: \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\) (an equivalence) means both \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and its converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\) are true.
\(P\Rightarrow Q\) is true: a prime has exactly the two factors 1 and itself.

\(Q\Rightarrow P\) is also true: if \(n\) has exactly two factors, they must be 1 and \(n\) (with \(n\neq1\)), which is the definition of a prime. (1 has only one factor, so it is not a counter-example.)
Both directions hold, so the statement is an equivalence. Note the contrapositive is always equivalent to the statement, so it cannot be used as the reason.

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: It is an equivalence, because the statement and its contrapositive are both true.
It is an equivalence: the statement is true and its converse (if \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime) is also true.
It is not an equivalence, because the converse is false for \(n=1\).
It is not an equivalence, because a statement and its contrapositive are never both true.

keyPoints.text: whether or not the statement is an equivalence
keyPoints.note: Check whether the converse (from (i)) is also true.

parts.stem:
Georg said that:

If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is composite.

Determine whether or not this statement is true. If not, give a counter-example.
parts.hint: Natural numbers are prime, composite, or … one more case.

steps.explain: A composite number has more than two factors. So the statement says: if \(n\) does not have exactly two factors, it has more than two.
Look for an \(n\) without exactly two factors that is not composite. \(n=1\) has exactly one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
So the statement is false, with counter-example \(n=1\). (\(n=4\) is composite, so it agrees with the statement; \(n=2\) does not satisfy the hypothesis.)

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: It is true, because every number that is not prime is composite.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=4\) does not have exactly two factors.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=2\) has exactly two factors.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=1\) has only one factor but is not composite.

keyPoints.text: If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is composite
keyPoints.note: Think about n = 1: how many factors does it have, and is it composite?

questions.stem:
Write the negation of the statement:

All meerkats eat grubs.
questions.hint: The negation of 'all … do' is 'at least one … does not'.

steps.explain: The statement is 'for all meerkats, it eats grubs'.
The negation of 'for all' is 'there exists one that does not'.
So the negation is: at least one meerkat does not eat grubs. 'No meerkats eat grubs' is too strong — it is not the negation.

meta.source: Ascham 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: Some meerkats eat grubs.
All animals that eat grubs are meerkats.
At least one meerkat does not eat grubs.
No meerkats eat grubs.

keyPoints.note: Negating 'all' gives 'there exists at least one that does not'.

questions.stem:
Consider the following proposition.
“If a positive integer is not a perfect square, then it is not prime.”
If a number was found which had the following properties, which would be a counterexample to the proposition?
questions.hint: A counterexample to 'if P then Q' has P true and Q false.

steps.explain: The proposition has the form \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
A counterexample makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false: \(P\) true and \(Q\) false.
\(Q\) false means the number IS prime. So we need a number that is not a perfect square and is prime (e.g. 7): option A.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

options: A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is not prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is not prime.

keyPoints.note: Make the 'if' part true and the 'then' part false.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is the contrapositive of the statement
“if \(x\gt y\gt 0\) then \(0\lt\frac{1}{x}\lt\frac{1}{y}\)” ?
questions.hint: Contrapositive: not Q ⇒ not P. A squeezed inequality is an 'and', so its negation is an 'or'.

steps.explain: The contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).
A chain like \(0\lt\frac1x\lt\frac1y\) means two conditions joined by 'and': \(0\lt\frac1x\) together with \(\frac1x\lt\frac1y\). Negating an 'and' gives an 'or' of the negations.
Similarly \(\neg P\) is: \(x\le y\) or \(y\le 0\).
So the contrapositive is option A. Options C and D keep a squeezed chain, which wrongly stays an 'and'.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

options: If \(0\ge\frac1x\) or \(\frac1x\ge\frac1y\) then \(x\le y\) or \(y\le0\).
If \(0\ge\frac1x\) and \(\frac1x\ge\frac1y\) then \(x\le y\) and \(y\le0\).
If \(0\ge\frac1x\ge\frac1y\) then \(x\le y\le0\).
If \(x\le y\le0\) then \(0\ge\frac1x\ge\frac1y\).

keyPoints.note: Negate both parts and swap them. 'a < b < c' means a < b AND b < c, whose negation is an OR.

questions.stem:
The following slogan is used at a particular swimming centre.
“If you are a strong swimmer, then you are unlikely to drown.”
Which of the following statements is logically equivalent to the above slogan?
questions.hint: Logically equivalent = contrapositive.

steps.explain: Label the slogan \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
Only the contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) is always logically equivalent to \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
\(\neg Q\): likely to drown. \(\neg P\): not a strong swimmer. So: if you are likely to drown, then you are not a strong swimmer — D.
A is the converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\), C is the inverse \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\); neither is equivalent. B contradicts the slogan.

meta.source: Blacktown Boys 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

options: If you are unlikely to drown, then you are a strong swimmer.
If you are a strong swimmer, then you are likely to drown.
If you are not a strong swimmer, then you are likely to drown.
If you are likely to drown, then you are not a strong swimmer.

keyPoints.note: Swap and negate both parts of the slogan.

questions.stem: Given that x and y are real numbers, which of the following statements is true?
questions.hint: For each statement, ask whether you can choose a real x for every possible real y, including very large positive and negative values.
questions.solution: \(\forall y(\exists x:x>y)\)

steps.explain: The statement in option C says: for every real \(y\), there exists a real \(x\) such that \(x>y\).
For any chosen real y, choose \(x=y+1\). Since 1 is positive, this x is real and strictly greater than y.
The same construction works for every real y, so C is true. The other choices fail for some y: for example, no absolute value is negative, and equality to y is not possible when y<0.

questions.stem: It is given that \(a>0\) and \(b>0\) are real numbers. Consider the statement \(\forall a\,\left(\forall b,\;\log_{\frac{1}{a}}\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)=\log_a b\right)\). Prove that the statement is true.
questions.hint: Rewrite each logarithm using natural logarithms. Track the negative signs from \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)=-\ln a\) and \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)=-\ln b\).
questions.solution: For a positive base different from 1, \(\log_{\frac{1}{a}}\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)=\frac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)}=\frac{-\ln b}{-\ln a}=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}=\log_a b\). The source statement omits the necessary restriction \(a\ne1\); at \(a=1\), both sides are undefined.

steps.explain: Use the change-of-base formula. The logarithms are defined only when their bases are positive and not equal to 1, so the stated identity is understood for \(a>0, a\ne1\) and \(b>0\).
Use \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{u}\right)=-\ln u\) for positive \(u\) in both numerator and denominator. The two negative signs cancel.
Apply change of base again to recognise the final expression. Note that \(a=1\) is excluded because both logarithms with base 1 are undefined.

meta.source: Caringbah 2020 4U Trials & Solutions
meta.paper: Mathematics Extension 2 HSC Course Assessment Task 4

keyPoints.note: Rewrite each logarithm using natural logarithms. Track the negative signs from \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)=-\ln a\) and \(\ln\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)=-\ln b\).

The source statement omits the necessary restriction \(a\ne1\); at \(a=1\), both sides are undefined.

questions.stem: The converse of the statement “If \(x\) is odd, then \(y\) is even” is:
options: “If \(y\) is odd, then \(x\) is even”.
“If \(y\) is even, then \(x\) is odd”.
“If \(y\) is even, then \(x\) is even”.
“If \(y\) is odd, then \(x\) is odd”.
questions.hint: The converse swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion: \(P \Rightarrow Q\) becomes \(Q \Rightarrow P\).

steps.explain: Name the parts. P: “\(x\) is odd”. Q: “\(y\) is even”. The statement is \(P \Rightarrow Q\).
The converse is \(Q \Rightarrow P\): swap the two parts.
Write it in words: “If \(y\) is even, then \(x\) is odd.”
Do not confuse the converse with the contrapositive (\(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\)), which would be “If \(y\) is odd, then \(x\) is even”.
steps.work: Option A negates both parts, so it is not the converse.

keyPoints.note: Swap the 'if' part and the 'then' part.

questions.stem: Consider the statements \(P\): \(\underset{\sim}{a}=\lambda\underset{\sim}{b}\), and \(Q\): the vectors are parallel. Determine if \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\).
options: Yes, \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\) because both implications are true.
No, \(Q\Rightarrow P\) is false.
No, \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is false.
Yes, but only \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is true.
questions.hint: An equivalence needs both \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\Rightarrow P\) to be true.

steps.explain: \(P\Rightarrow Q\): if one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, they point in the same or opposite direction, so they are parallel. True.
\(Q\Rightarrow P\): if the vectors are parallel, one is a scalar multiple of the other (provided the second is non-zero). True.
Both directions hold, so \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\).

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?
options: \(\forall a\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\ \exists b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}:\ b=a^{3}\)
\(\forall a\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\ \exists b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}:\ b=\sqrt[3]{a}\)
\(\forall a\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\ \exists b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}:\ a=b^{3}\)
\(\forall a\ \exists b\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}:\ b=a^{3}\)
questions.hint: Read each statement in words and test it with a small number such as \(a=2\).

steps.explain: Read option A in words: \(\text{"for every positive integer }a\text{ there is a positive integer }b\text{ with }b=a^{3}.\text{"}\) Take \(b=a^{3}\): the cube of a positive integer is always a positive integer.
Test option B: \(b=\sqrt[3]{a}\). For \(a=2\), \(b=\sqrt[3]{2}\approx1.26\) is not an integer, so B is false.
Option C says every positive integer is a perfect cube \(a=b^{3}\). For \(a=2\) no integer \(b\) works, so C is false.
Option D does not say what kind of number \(a\) is. If \(a=-1\) then \(b=a^{3}=-1\), which is not positive, so D is false.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Write the following mathematical statement in words. \(\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\ \exists x\in\mathbb{Z}\) such that \(x^{2}+x-k=0\)
options: For all positive integers \(k\), there exists some integer \(x\) such that \(x^{2}+x-k=0\).
There exists a positive integer \(k\) such that, for all integers \(x\), \(x^{2}+x-k=0\).
For some positive integers \(k\), there is an integer \(x\) with \(x^{2}+x-k=0\).
For all integers \(x\), there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that \(x^{2}+x-k=0\).
questions.hint: Read the symbols in order: \(\forall\) means \"for all\", \(\exists\) means \"there exists\", \(\mathbb{Z}^{+}\) is the positive integers, \(\mathbb{Z}\) the integers. The ORDER of the quantifiers matters.

steps.explain: \(\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\) reads \"for all positive integers \(k\)\".
\(\exists x\in\mathbb{Z}\) reads \"there exists an integer \(x\)\" (\"some\" integer, at least one).
\"such that \(x^{2}+x-k=0\)\" is the condition. Keeping the order (first \(k\), then \(x\)): \"For all positive integers \(k\), there exists some integer \(x\) such that \(x^{2}+x-k=0\).\"
Why not the others: B swaps the order (one \(x\) that works for every \(k\)); C weakens \"for all\" to \"for some\"; D swaps the roles of \(k\) and \(x\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}\). Which of the following statements is false?
options: \(n\) is even if and only if \(n+1\) is odd.
\(m+n\) is odd if and only if \(m-n\) is odd.
\(m+n\) is even if and only if \(m\) and \(n\) are even.
\(m\) and \(n\) are odd if and only if \(mn\) is odd.
questions.hint: \"If and only if\" statements must be true in BOTH directions. Look for ONE counterexample (a pair of numbers where one direction fails) to prove a statement false. Test small numbers such as 1 and 3.

steps.explain: Statement A: if \(n\) is even then \(n+1\) is odd, and if \(n+1\) is odd then \(n\) is even. Both directions are true.
Statement B: \(m+n\) and \(m-n\) always have the same parity, because their difference \((m+n)-(m-n)=2n\) is even. So one is odd exactly when the other is odd. True.

Statement C: \(m+n\) even does NOT force both to be even. Counterexample: take \(m=1\) and \(n=3\), both odd. Then \(m+n=4\), which is even, but \(m\) and \(n\) are not even. The direction \(m+n\) even \(\Rightarrow\) both even FAILS.
Statement D: odd \(\times\) odd \(=\) odd, and if either factor is even the product is even. So \(mn\) is odd exactly when both are odd. True.
Only statement C is false.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following statements is false
keyPoints.note: One counterexample is enough to show an 'if and only if' false.

questions.stem: Write down the contrapositive for the statement ‘If I like walking, then I do not like cycling’
options: If I dislike cycling, then I do not like walking.
If I like cycling, then I like walking.
If I dislike cycling, then I like walking.
If I like cycling, then I do not like walking.
questions.hint: For \(P\Rightarrow Q\) the contrapositive is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): swap the two parts AND negate each. Here \(Q\) is already a negative (“do not like cycling”), so negating it gives “like cycling”.

steps.explain: Name the parts: \(P\): “I like walking”; \(Q\): “I do not like cycling”.
steps.work: \(P\Rightarrow Q\ \ \text{ where }P=\text{like walking},\ Q=\text{do not like cycling}\)

steps.explain: The contrapositive is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) (it always has the same truth value as the original).
Negate \(Q\): not (do not like cycling) \(=\) “I like cycling” (two negatives cancel).
Negate \(P\): not (like walking) \(=\) “I do not like walking”.
Assemble: swap the order.
steps.work: \(\text{If I like cycling, then I do not like walking.}\)

steps.explain: Why not the others: A negates \(P\) but leaves \(Q\) un-negated; B negates \(Q\) but leaves \(P\) un-negated; C is the CONVERSE \(Q\Rightarrow P\) (swapped but not negated).
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Swap AND negate: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).

questions.stem: Given that \(x\) and \(y\) are natural numbers, which of the following is a FALSE statement?
options: \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x-y=0)\)
\(\forall x\,\exists y\,(3x-y=0)\)
\(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x-3y=0)\)
\(\exists x\,\exists y\,(x+y=8)\)
questions.hint: Read each statement aloud: \(\forall x\,\exists y\) means “for EVERY natural \(x\) there is at least one natural \(y\) that works”. Solve for \(y\) and ask whether it is always a natural number.

steps.explain: \(\forall\) = “for all”, \(\exists\) = “there exists”. Natural numbers are \(1,2,3,\dots\).
steps.work: \(\forall x\ \exists y:\ \text{every }x\text{ needs a natural partner }y\)

steps.explain: A: \(x-y=0\Rightarrow y=x\). Take \(y=x\) — always a natural number. TRUE.
B: \(3x-y=0\Rightarrow y=3x\). A natural number times 3 is natural. TRUE.

C: \(x-3y=0\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x}{3}\). This is natural only when \(3\mid x\). For \(x=1\) we would need \(y=\dfrac{1}{3}\), which is NOT natural, so “for every \(x\)” fails. FALSE (counterexample \(x=1\)).
D: \(\exists x\,\exists y\,(x+y=8)\) only needs ONE pair, e.g. \(x=3,\ y=5\). TRUE.
So the only FALSE statement is C.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.text: which of the following is a FALSE statement
keyPoints.note: \(\forall x\exists y\): solve for \(y\) — is it natural for EVERY \(x\)?

questions.stem: For the conditional statement ‘If \(n\) is divisible by 16 then \(n\) is divisible by 4’, write the converse statement.
options: If \(n\) is divisible by 4 then \(n\) is divisible by 16.
If \(n\) is not divisible by 16 then \(n\) is not divisible by 4.
If \(n\) is not divisible by 4 then \(n\) is not divisible by 16.
\(n\) is divisible by 16 and \(n\) is not divisible by 4.
questions.hint: For \(P\Rightarrow Q\): the CONVERSE is \(Q\Rightarrow P\) — just swap the two parts (no negating).

steps.explain: Identify the parts.
steps.work: \(P:\ n\text{ is divisible by }16;\qquad Q:\ n\text{ is divisible by }4\)

steps.explain: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion: \(Q\Rightarrow P\).
steps.work: \(Q\Rightarrow P:\ \text{If }n\text{ is divisible by }4\text{ then }n\text{ is divisible by }16\)

steps.explain: Note the converse is FALSE here (\(n=4\) is divisible by 4 but not by 16) — a converse need not have the same truth value as the original statement.

Why not the others: B is the INVERSE \(
eg P\Rightarrow
eg Q\); C is the CONTRAPOSITIVE \(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\); D is the NEGATION \(P\wedge
eg Q\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Converse: swap \(P\) and \(Q\).

meta.source: Hornsby Girls High School 2021 Year 12 Trial Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: For the conditional statement ‘If \(n\) is divisible by 16 then \(n\) is divisible by 4’, write the negation statement.
options: \(n\) is divisible by 16 and \(n\) is not divisible by 4.
\(n\) is not divisible by 16 and \(n\) is divisible by 4.
If \(n\) is not divisible by 16 then \(n\) is not divisible by 4.
If \(n\) is not divisible by 4 then \(n\) is not divisible by 16.
questions.hint: The negation of an “if … then …” statement is the situation where it FAILS: the “if” part is TRUE but the “then” part is FALSE. So \(\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q\).

steps.explain: \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is false only when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false.
Keep \(P\) as it is and negate \(Q\).
steps.work: \(P:\ n\text{ divisible by }16;\qquad\neg Q:\ n\text{ NOT divisible by }4\)

steps.explain: Join with “and” (the negation is NOT an “if … then” statement).
steps.work: \(n\text{ is divisible by 16 and }n\text{ is not divisible by 4}\)

steps.explain: Why not the others: B negates the wrong part; C is the inverse (still an implication); D is the contrapositive (logically EQUIVALENT to the original, not its negation).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\) is \(P\) AND \(\neg Q\).

questions.stem: Consider the statement: ‘If an animal can fly then it is a bird.’ Which of the following is the contrapositive of this statement?
options: If an animal is not a bird then it cannot fly.
If an animal is a bird then it can fly.
If an animal can fly then it is not a bird.
If an animal cannot fly then it is not a bird.
questions.hint: For \(P\Rightarrow Q\) the contrapositive is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): REVERSE the two parts and NEGATE each.

steps.explain: Name the parts: \(P\): “an animal can fly”; \(Q\): “it is a bird”.
Reverse the order and negate both: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).
Write it out: “If an animal is not a bird then it cannot fly.”
Why not the others: B is the CONVERSE \(Q\Rightarrow P\); C negates only the conclusion; D is the INVERSE \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Reverse AND negate: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).

questions.stem: Consider the following proposition. ‘If a positive integer is not a perfect square, then it is not prime.’ If a number was found which had the following properties, which would be a counterexample to the proposition?
options: A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is not prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is not prime.
questions.hint: A counterexample to “\(P\Rightarrow Q\)” is a case where \(P\) is TRUE but \(Q\) is FALSE. So it must satisfy the “if” part and BREAK the “then” part.

steps.explain: Parts: \(P\): “not a perfect square”; \(Q\): “not prime”.
\(P\Rightarrow Q\) fails exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false: \(P\wedge\neg Q\).
\(P\): not a perfect square. \(\neg Q\): NOT “not prime” \(=\) prime.
Example: \(2\) is prime and is not a perfect square, so \(2\) is a counterexample ✓.
Why not the others: B satisfies both parts (no contradiction); C and D have a perfect square, so the “if” part is false and the statement says nothing about them.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Counterexample to \(P\Rightarrow Q\): \(P\) true AND \(Q\) false.

questions.stem: What is the contrapositive of \(\neg A\Rightarrow B\)?
options: \(\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A\)
\(B\Rightarrow\neg A\)
\(\neg B\Rightarrow A\)
\(B\Rightarrow A\)
questions.hint:
The CONTRAPOSITIVE of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\): swap the two statements AND negate both. A double negation cancels: \(
eg(
eg A)=A\).

steps.explain: Here \(P=\neg A\) and \(Q=B\).

Contrapositive: \(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\), i.e. \(
eg B\Rightarrow
eg(
eg A)\).
Double negative: \(\neg(\neg A)=A\).
Why not the others: A forgets that \(P\) is already negated; B is the CONVERSE-type (not swapped correctly); D is the converse of the contrapositive.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Contrapositive: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).

questions.stem: Consider the following statement, “If you have no treasure, I have no kingdom.” Which of the following is logically equivalent to this statement?
options: If I have no kingdom then you have no treasure.
If you have treasure then I have a kingdom.
If you have no kingdom then I have no treasure.
If I have a kingdom then you have treasure.
questions.hint: A statement “If \(P\) then \(Q\)” is logically equivalent ONLY to its CONTRAPOSITIVE “If not \(Q\) then not \(P\)”. Identify \(P\) and \(Q\) first, negate both and swap them.

steps.explain: Identify the parts: \(P\): “you have no treasure”; \(Q\): “I have no kingdom”. The statement is \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
Contrapositive: negate BOTH parts and swap them. \(\neg Q\): “I have a kingdom”; \(\neg P\): “you have treasure”.
steps.work: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P:\ \text{“If I have a kingdom then you have treasure.”}\)

steps.explain: This is option D. A statement and its contrapositive always have the same truth value.

Why not the others: A is the CONVERSE (\(Q\Rightarrow P\)); B is the INVERSE (\(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\)); the converse and the inverse are NOT equivalent to the original. C mixes up the roles (it is about “you” and “I” in the wrong places).
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Equivalent = contrapositive: \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the negation of the statement “\(\forall p\in P\) (\(p\) is of the form \(4m+1\Longrightarrow p\) can be written as a sum of two squares)”?
options: \(\forall p\in P\) (\(p\) is of the form \(4m+1\) and \(p\) cannot be written as a sum of two squares)
\(\exists p\in P\) (\(p\) is not of the form \(4m+1\) and \(p\) can be written as a sum of two squares)
\(\forall p\in P\) (\(p\) is not of the form \(4m+1\) or \(p\) cannot be written as a sum of two squares)
\(\exists p\in P\) (\(p\) is of the form \(4m+1\) and \(p\) cannot be written as a sum of two squares)
questions.hint: Negating “for all” gives “there exists”. Negating an implication \(A\Rightarrow B\) gives “\(A\) AND NOT \(B\)” (the implication fails only when \(A\) is true and \(B\) is false).

steps.explain: Structure: \(\forall p\ (A\Rightarrow B)\) where \(A\): “\(p\) is of the form \(4m+1\)” and \(B\): “\(p\) is a sum of two squares”.
Negate the quantifier: \(\neg\forall\equiv\exists\neg\).
Negate the implication: \(A\Rightarrow B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is TRUE and \(B\) is FALSE.
Combine: there exists a prime of the form \(4m+1\) that cannot be written as a sum of two squares.

Why not the others: A and C keep the quantifier \(\forall\) (it must become \(\exists\)); B negates the wrong part (“\(p\) is not of the form …”) and keeps \(B\) true, which does not contradict the implication.
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: Of the following, select the statement that is TRUE for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\):
options: If \(x>y\), then \(\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac{1}{y}\)
If \(|x|>|y|\), then \(x>y\)
questions.hint: A statement is TRUE for ALL real numbers only if it can never fail. Test each option with a counterexample using NEGATIVE numbers (squares, absolute values and reciprocals can behave differently for negatives).

steps.explain: (A) The function \(f(x)=x^{3}\) is strictly increasing for ALL real \(x\), so it preserves order in both directions: \(x^{3}>y^{3}\iff x>y\). Test: \(x=-1,y=-2\): \((-1)^{3}=-1>-8=(-2)^{3}\) and indeed \(-1>-2\) ✓.
(C) Counterexample: \(x=1\), \(y=-1\). Then \(x>y\) but \(\dfrac{1}{x}=1\) is NOT less than \(\dfrac{1}{y}=-1\).
(D) Counterexample: \(x=-3\), \(y=1\). Then \(|x|=3>1=|y|\) but \(x<y\).
Only (A) has no counterexample, so (A) is the TRUE statement.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: select the statement that is TRUE for all real numbers
keyPoints.note: Find a counterexample for each wrong option (try negatives).

questions.stem: Consider the statement: For any function \(f(x)\), \(f(x)\) is not continuous at \(x=c\ \Rightarrow\ f(x)\) is not differentiable at \(x=c\). Which of the following is correct?
options: The contrapositive statement is false and the converse statement is false.
The contrapositive statement is false and the converse statement is true.
The contrapositive statement is true and the converse statement is false.
The contrapositive statement is true and the converse statement is true.
questions.hint: For \(P\Rightarrow Q\): contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) (always has the SAME truth value as the original); converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\) (may differ). Use the known fact: differentiable \(\Rightarrow\) continuous.

steps.explain: \(P\): “\(f\) is not continuous at \(c\)”; \(Q\): “\(f\) is not differentiable at \(c\)”. The original statement \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is TRUE (if a function is not continuous it cannot be differentiable).

Contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): “if \(f\) is differentiable at \(c\) then \(f\) is continuous at \(c\)”. This is TRUE (a standard theorem), as it must be since it is equivalent to the original.
Converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\): “if \(f\) is not differentiable at \(c\) then \(f\) is not continuous at \(c\)”. This is FALSE: \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at \(0\) but not differentiable at \(0\).
So the contrapositive is true and the converse is false.
Why not the others: A and B call the contrapositive false (it is always equivalent to the original, which is true); D says the converse is true, but \(|x|\) is a counterexample.
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following is correct

questions.stem: Consider the statement: “If an animal is a bird, then it can fly or swim.” What is the contrapositive statement?
options: If an animal cannot fly or cannot swim, then it is a bird.
If an animal cannot fly or cannot swim, then it is not a bird.
If an animal cannot fly and cannot swim, then it is a bird.
If an animal cannot fly and cannot swim, then it is not a bird.
questions.hint: For “If \(P\) then \(Q\)” the contrapositive is “If NOT \(Q\) then NOT \(P\)”. Negate \(Q\) carefully: the negation of “\(A\) or \(B\)” is “NOT \(A\) AND NOT \(B\)” (De Morgan).

steps.explain: \(P\): “the animal is a bird”; \(Q\): “it can fly OR swim”.
\(\neg Q\): the negation of “can fly or can swim” is “cannot fly AND cannot swim” (both must fail). \(\neg P\): “is not a bird”.
Contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): “If an animal cannot fly and cannot swim, then it is not a bird.”
Why not the others: A and C do not negate \(P\) (they conclude “it IS a bird”); B uses “or” (the negation of “or” is “and”).
So the correct choice is option D.

eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\); \(

eg A\wedge
eg B\).

questions.stem: For all non-zero integers \(x\) and \(y\), if \(x>y\) then \(\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac{1}{y}\). What is a counter-example to the above statement?
questions.hint: A COUNTER-EXAMPLE must satisfy the HYPOTHESIS (\(x>y\), both non-zero integers) but make the CONCLUSION (\(\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac{1}{y}\)) FALSE. Test each option for both.

steps.explain: (A) \(x=2\), \(y=-1\): \(x>y\) ✓ (hypothesis true). \(\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{y}=-1\). Is \(\dfrac{1}{2}<-1\)? NO, conclusion false. This is a counter-example.
(B) \(x=0,y=0\): not allowed (non-zero integers), and \(x>y\) is false.
(C) \(x=4\), \(y=3\): \(4>3\) ✓ and \(\dfrac{1}{4}<\dfrac{1}{3}\) ✓ — the statement holds, so it is NOT a counter-example.
(D) \(x=-2\), \(y=1\): the hypothesis \(x>y\) is FALSE (\(-2<1\)), so this cannot be a counter-example.
So (A) is the counter-example: the rule \(x>y\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac{1}{y}\) only works when \(x\) and \(y\) have the SAME sign.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: What is a counter-example to the above statement
keyPoints.note: Counter-example: hypothesis TRUE, conclusion FALSE.

questions.stem: For positive integers \(m\) and \(n\), consider the propositions: \(p\): \(m+n\) is even; \(q\): \(m\) and \(n\) are both even; \(r\): \(m\) and \(n\) are both odd. Write in symbolic form the compound proposition \(P\) where \(P\): If \(m+n\) is even, then \(m\) and \(n\) are both even or \(m\) and \(n\) are both odd. You may use \(\vee\) for ‘or’ and \(\wedge\) for ‘and’ where appropriate.
options: \(p\Rightarrow(q\vee r)\)
\(p\Rightarrow(q\wedge r)\)
\((q\vee r)\Rightarrow p\)
\(p\vee(q\Rightarrow r)\)
questions.hint: “If … then …” is the implication \(\Rightarrow\): the “if” part comes FIRST. Translate the two parts, then connect with \(\Rightarrow\). “both even or both odd” is \(q\vee r\).

steps.explain: The “if” part: “\(m+n\) is even” is \(p\).
The “then” part: “\(m\) and \(n\) are both even OR \(m\) and \(n\) are both odd” is \(q\vee r\). (Each of \(q\) and \(r\) already contains the “both … and”.)
Combine with \(\Rightarrow\).
Why not the others: B uses “and” (a pair cannot be both all-even and all-odd); C reverses the implication (that is the converse); D is not an if-then.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Write in symbolic form the compound proposition
keyPoints.note: if \(p\) then \(q\vee r\): \(p\Rightarrow(q\vee r)\).

So the correct choice is option A.

topics.title: Further Logic and Language of Proof

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is the negation of the statement
“\(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^+,\ \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^+\) such that \(xy=1\)” ?
questions.hint: Negating swaps ∀ and ∃, and negates the final condition.

steps.explain: To negate, swap each quantifier (\(\forall\leftrightarrow\exists\)) and negate the final statement.
steps.work: \(\neg\left(\forall x\ \exists y:\ xy=1\right)\ \equiv\ \exists x\ \forall y:\ xy\neq1\)

steps.explain: So the negation is: there is a positive real \(x\) such that for every positive real \(y\), \(xy\neq1\) — option B.
Sense check: the original says every positive real has a positive reciprocal (true), so the negation must be false — and B says some positive real has no reciprocal, which is false ✓.

\(\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^+\) such that \(\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^+,\ xy\neq1\)
\(\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^+,\ xy\neq1\)
\(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^+\), there exists a positive real number \(y\) such that \(xy\neq1\)

steps.explain: The statement is 'for every day, at least one problem'. Its negation is 'there exists a day without at least one problem'.
'Fewer than one problem' means no problems. So some day next week Max does no maths problems: A.
D is too strong (it claims every day), and B, C don't follow.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is true?
questions.hint: Test each statement with a counterexample; watch the order of ∀ and ∃.

steps.explain: A says every real \(x\) has a \(y\) with \(xy=10\). Test \(x=0\): \(0\cdot y=0\neq10\) for every \(y\). So A is false (one counterexample is enough).
B says every real \(x\) has a real \(y\) equal to \(x^2\). That is always possible: just choose \(y=x^2\), which is a real number. So B is true.
C says one fixed \(x\) makes \(xy=10\) for EVERY \(y\). Impossible: \(y=0\) gives \(xy=0\).
D says one fixed \(x\) has every real \(y\) equal to \(x^2\) — but \(x^2\) is a single number, so it cannot equal every \(y\). False.
Only B is true. Notice how the ORDER of \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) changes the meaning: in B, \(y\) may depend on \(x\).

questions.stem: What is the contrapositive of the following statement? “If you’re happy and you know it, then you will clap your hands.”
options: If you clap your hands, then you’re happy and you know it.
If you clap your hands, then you’re either not happy or you don’t know it.
If you don’t clap your hands, then you’re not happy and you don’t know it.
If you don’t clap your hands, then you’re either not happy or you don’t know it.
questions.hint: The contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): swap the two parts AND negate both. Remember De Morgan's law when negating \"and\".

steps.explain: Identify the two parts. \(P\): \"you’re happy AND you know it\". \(Q\): \"you will clap your hands\".
The contrapositive is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\). Negate \(Q\): \"you don’t clap your hands\".
Negate \(P\) using De Morgan's law: the negation of \"A and B\" is \"not A OR not B\", so \(\neg P\): \"you’re not happy OR you don’t know it\".
Put them together: \"If you don’t clap your hands, then you’re either not happy or you don’t know it.\"
A is the converse (swap only); B swaps but does not negate \(Q\); C negates \(P\) as \"not happy AND don't know it\" (wrong De Morgan).
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: Prove that the sum of two odd integers is even. Which of the following is the correct setup for a direct proof?
options: Let \(m = 2a\) and \(n = 2b\) for integers \(a, b\)
Let \(m = 2a + 1\) and \(n = 2b + 1\) for integers \(a, b\)
Let \(m = 2a + 1\) and \(n = 2b\) for integers \(a, b\)
Assume \(m + n\) is odd and derive a contradiction
questions.solution: Since \(m\) and \(n\) are odd, we write \(m = 2a+1\) and \(n = 2b+1\). Then \(m+n = 2a+2b+2 = 2(a+b+1)\), which is even.

steps.explain: Write odd integers in general form.
steps.work: Any odd integer can be written as \(2k+1\) for some integer \(k\). So let \(m = 2a+1\) and \(n = 2b+1\) for integers \(a, b\).

steps.explain: Add the two integers.
Conclude.
steps.work: Since \(a+b+1\) is an integer, \(m+n = 2(a+b+1)\) is divisible by 2, hence even. \(\square\)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly proves that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational?
options: Direct proof: show \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) for integers \(p, q\)
Proof by contradiction: assume \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) in lowest terms and derive that both \(p\) and \(q\) are even
Proof by induction: show \(\sqrt{n}\) is irrational for all \(n \geq 2\)
Proof by contrapositive: if \(n\) is not a perfect square then \(\sqrt{n}\) is rational
questions.solution: The classic proof is by contradiction: assume \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) in lowest terms, then \(2q^2 = p^2\), so \(p\) is even. Write \(p = 2k\), then \(q^2 = 2k^2\), so \(q\) is also even — contradicting \(p/q\) being in lowest terms.

steps.explain: Assume for contradiction that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational.
steps.work: Suppose \(\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}\) where \(p, q \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(q \neq 0\), and \(\gcd(p,q) = 1\) (in lowest terms).

steps.explain: Square both sides and rearrange.
steps.work: \(2 = \dfrac{p^2}{q^2} \Rightarrow p^2 = 2q^2\). So \(p^2\) is even, which means \(p\) is even. Write \(p = 2k\).

steps.explain: Show \(q\) is also even — contradiction.
steps.work: \((2k)^2 = 2q^2 \Rightarrow 4k^2 = 2q^2 \Rightarrow q^2 = 2k^2\). So \(q\) is even. But then \(\gcd(p,q) \geq 2\), contradicting our assumption. Therefore \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational. \(\square\)

questions.stem: Prove if \(x,y\in\mathbb{Z}\), then \(x^2-4y\neq2\).
questions.hint: Assume x² − 4y = 2 and show x must be even; then reach a non-integer.

steps.explain: Use proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of what is to be proved.
Rearrange to see that \(x^2\) is even.
steps.work: \(x^2=4y+2=2(2y+1)\ \Rightarrow\ x^2\text{ is even}\ \Rightarrow\ x\text{ is even}\)

steps.explain: (If \(x\) were odd, \(x^2\) would be odd.) So write \(x=2c\) for some integer \(c\) and substitute.
\(c\) and \(y\) are integers, so \(c^2-y\) is an integer and cannot equal \(\frac12\). This contradiction shows the assumption is false.

questions.answer: Proof by contradiction. Suppose there are integers \(x,y\) with \(x^2-4y=2\). Then \(x^2=4y+2=2(2y+1)\) is even, so \(x\) is even; write \(x=2c\) with \(c\in\mathbb Z\). Then \(4c^2-4y=2\), so \(c^2-y=\frac12\). But \(c^2-y\) is an integer, which is a contradiction. Hence \(x^2-4y\neq2\) for all integers \(x,y\).

keyPoints.note: Assume x² − 4y = 2. Then x² is even, so x = 2c, which leads to c² − y = ½.

questions.stem: Prove, using contradiction, that \(\sqrt{4n-2}\) is irrational for all positive integers \(n\).
questions.answer: Assume \(\sqrt{4n-2}=\dfrac{p}{q}\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are positive integers with no common factor. Then \(p^2=(4n-2)q^2=2(2n-1)q^2\), so \(p\) is even. Let \(p=2k\). Then \(2k^2=(2n-1)q^2\). Since \(p\) is even, \(q\) is odd, so the right side is odd while the left side is even. This is a contradiction, so \(\sqrt{4n-2}\) is irrational.
questions.hint: Assume the number is rational and write it as \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) in lowest terms. Compare the factors of 2 on both sides.

steps.explain: Assume the opposite: the number is rational. Write it as a fraction in lowest terms, where \(p\) and \(q\) are positive integers with no common factor.
Square both sides and multiply by \(q^2\).
The right side has a factor of 2, so \(p^2\) is even, and therefore \(p\) is even. Write \(p=2k\) for some integer \(k\).
Substitute and divide both sides by 2.
Since \(p\) is even and \(p\), \(q\) have no common factor, \(q\) is odd. Also \(2n-1\) is odd, so the right side is odd (odd times odd), but the left side \(2k^2\) is even.
The assumption leads to a contradiction, so it is false.
steps.work: \(\sqrt{4n-2}\text{ is irrational for all positive integers } n\)

questions.stem: Prove for all integers \(x,y\) that if \(10x+y\) is divisible by 17, \(3y-4x\) is also divisible by 17. If \(10x+y=17k\), what is \(3y-4x\) in terms of \(k\) and \(x\)?
questions.hint: Make \(y\) the subject of \(10x+y=17k\), substitute into \(3y-4x\) and take out a factor of 17.

steps.explain: Let \(10x+y=17k\) where \(k\) is an integer (divisible by 17).
Make \(y\) the subject.
Substitute into \(3y-4x\).
Factorise out 17: \(51=17\times3\) and \(34=17\times2\).
Since \(k\) and \(x\) are integers, \(3k-2x\) is an integer, so \(3y-4x\) is a multiple of 17. (Notice the factor is \(3k-2x\), not \(3-2x\): the \(k\) from \(17k\) must stay.)
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: It is given that \(a,b,c\) and \(d\) are consecutive integers. Which of the following statements may be false?
options: \(abcd\) is divisible by 3
\(abcd\) is divisible by 8
\(a+b+c+d\) is divisible by 2
\(a+b+c+d\) is divisible by 4
questions.hint: Write the four integers as \(k,\ k+1,\ k+2,\ k+3\). Test the sum algebraically, and for the product think about multiples of 2, 3 and 4 among four consecutive numbers.

steps.explain: Let the integers be \(k,\ k+1,\ k+2,\ k+3\). Their sum is
\(4k+6=2(2k+3)\) is always even, so statement C is always true.

Statements A and B are always true: among 4 consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3, and there are two even numbers, one of which is a multiple of 4, so the product has a factor \(2\times4=8\).
Answer: D is the statement that may be false.

questions.stem: Use proof by contradiction to prove the following statement: “If \(p\) is odd, then \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) has no integer solution.” Which proof is correct?
options: Assume \(p\) is odd and \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) has an integer solution. Let \(p=2k+1\), so \(p^{2}=4k^{2}+4k+1\) is odd. If \(x=2m\): \(x^{2}+x=4m^{2}+2m\) is even, so \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}\) is even \(-\) odd \(=\) odd \(\ne0\). If \(x=2n+1\): \(x^{2}+x=4n^{2}+6n+2\) is even, so again the expression is odd \(\ne0\). So \(x\) is neither even nor odd, a contradiction.

Assume \(p\) is even and \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) has an integer solution. Let \(p=2k\), so \(p^{2}\) is even. Then \(x^{2}+x\) is even, which is possible for any integer \(x\), so there is no contradiction and the statement is true.
Assume \(p\) is odd and \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) has an integer solution. If \(x=2m\) then \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}\) is odd \(\ne0\). So \(x\) cannot be even, which is a contradiction.
Assume \(p\) is odd and \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) has an integer solution. For \(x=2n+1\): \(x^{2}+x\) is odd, and odd \(-\) odd \(=0\), so a solution exists, which contradicts the statement.
questions.hint: Contradiction: assume the statement is FALSE, i.e. \(p\) odd AND an integer \(x\) solves the equation. Split into cases (\(x\) even, \(x\) odd), show the left side is odd in both, so it can never equal 0.

steps.explain: Negate the statement. \"If \(P\) then \(Q\)\" is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false: assume \(p\) is odd AND \(x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\) HAS an integer solution \(x\).
Case I: \(x\) even, \(x=2m\). Then \(x^{2}+x=4m^{2}+2m=2(2m^{2}+m)\) is even, so even \(-\) odd \(=\) odd.
Case II: \(x\) odd, \(x=2n+1\). Then \(x^{2}+x=4n^{2}+4n+1+2n+1=2(2n^{2}+3n+1)\) is even (note \(x(x+1)\) is always even), so again even \(-\) odd \(=\) odd.
Every integer is even or odd, and both cases give a nonzero value, so no integer \(x\) satisfies the equation. This contradicts our assumption, so the original statement is true.
steps.work: \(\therefore\ p\text{ odd}\Rightarrow x^{2}+x-p^{2}=0\text{ has no integer solution}\)

steps.explain: Why not the others: B assumes the wrong thing (\(p\) even); C checks only the case \(x\) even; D wrongly claims \(x^{2}+x\) is odd (it is always even).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Show that \(k^{2}+k\) is always even. Which proof is correct?
options: If \(k=2x\): \(k^{2}+k=4x^{2}+2x=2(2x^{2}+x)\), even. If \(k=2x+1\): \(k^{2}+k=4x^{2}+4x+1+2x+1=2(2x^{2}+3x+1)\), even. Every integer is even or odd, so \(k^{2}+k\) is always even.
If \(k=2x\): \(k^{2}+k=4x^{2}+2x=2(2x^{2}+x)\), even. Hence \(k^{2}+k\) is always even.
Test \(k=1\): \(2\); \(k=2\): \(6\); \(k=3\): \(12\). All are even, so it is always even.
Let \(k^{2}+k=2y\). Then \(k^{2}+k\) is even, because it equals \(2y\).
questions.hint: Every integer is EVEN or ODD. Treat the two cases separately: write an even \(k\) as \(2x\) and an odd \(k\) as \(2x+1\), then show each time that \(k^{2}+k\) is a multiple of 2.

steps.explain: Case 1: \(k\) even, \(k=2x\) for some integer \(x\). Substitute.
Factor out 2: the result is 2 times an integer.
Case 2: \(k\) odd, \(k=2x+1\). Expand \((2x+1)^{2}\) and add \(k\).
Factor out 2.
Both cases give an even number, and every integer is in one of the two cases, so \(k^{2}+k\) is always even.
Why not the others: B covers only the even case; C tests three values (not a proof); D assumes the conclusion (circular).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Split into k even and k odd.

questions.stem: Prove that \(33^{n}-16^{n}-28^{n}+11^{n}\) is divisible by \(85\) for all positive integers \(n\ge2\). Which proof is correct?
options: \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): each bracket is divisible by \(33-16=17\) and \(28-11=17\), so the expression is divisible by 17. Also \(\left(33^{n}-28^{n}\right)-\left(16^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): each bracket is divisible by \(33-28=5\) and \(16-11=5\), so it is divisible by 5. 17 and 5 are different primes, so it is divisible by \(17\times5=85\).
For \(n=2\): \(1089-256-784+121=170=2\times85\). So it is divisible by 85 for all \(n\ge2\).
It is divisible by 17 and by 5, so it is divisible by \(17+5=22\), and hence by 85.
Assume it is divisible by 85 for \(n=k+1\); then it is divisible by 85 for \(n=k\), so it is true for all \(n\).
questions.hint: \(85=17\times5\) where 17 and 5 are DIFFERENT primes. Show it is divisible by 17 and by 5 separately using \(a^{n}-b^{n}\) is divisible by \(a-b\), then combine. Group the four terms in two different ways.

steps.explain: Fact: \(a^{n}-b^{n}\) is divisible by \(a-b\) (because \(a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2}b+\cdots+b^{n-1})\)).
Divisible by 17: group as \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\). The brackets are divisible by \(33-16=17\) and \(28-11=17\).
Divisible by 5: group differently as \(\left(33^{n}-28^{n}\right)-\left(16^{n}-11^{n}\right)\). The brackets are divisible by \(33-28=5\) and \(16-11=5\).
The expression is a multiple of BOTH 17 and 5. Since 17 and 5 are different primes (no common factor), it is a multiple of their product.

Check with \(n=2\): \(1089-256-784+121=170=2\times85\) ✓. Why not the others: B only checks \(n=2\) (an example); C wrongly adds the divisors (it should multiply coprime factors); D uses an invalid form of induction.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: a^n − b^n is divisible by a − b; group two ways.

questions.stem: Prove that \((n+1)^{n}-n^{n+1}\) is odd for all positive integers \(n\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&n\text{ odd}\Rightarrow n+1\text{ even}:\ (n+1)^{n}\text{ even},\ n^{n+1}\text{ odd}\Rightarrow\text{even}-\text{odd}=\text{odd}\\ &n\text{ even}\Rightarrow n+1\text{ odd}:\ (n+1)^{n}\text{ odd},\ n^{n+1}\text{ even}\Rightarrow\text{odd}-\text{even}=\text{odd}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&n\text{ odd}\Rightarrow n+1\text{ even}:\ (n+1)^{n}\text{ even},\ n^{n+1}\text{ odd}\Rightarrow\text{even}-\text{odd}=\text{even}\\ &n\text{ even}\Rightarrow n+1\text{ odd}:\ (n+1)^{n}\text{ odd},\ n^{n+1}\text{ even}\Rightarrow\text{odd}-\text{even}=\text{even}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&n\text{ odd}:\ n+1\text{ even and }n\text{ odd, so both terms are odd}\\ &\text{odd}-\text{odd}=\text{odd}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Test }n=1:\ 2^{1}-1^{2}=1\text{ (odd)}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{true for all }n\\ &\text{(a single example is a proof)}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Split into TWO cases by parity of \(n\). Use: an even number to any positive power is even; an odd number to any power is odd; even \(-\) odd \(=\) odd and odd \(-\) even \(=\) odd.

steps.explain: One of \(n\) and \(n+1\) is even and the other is odd. Treat the two cases separately (they cover every positive integer \(n\)).
Case 1: \(n=2k+1\) (odd). Then \(n+1=2k+2=2(k+1)\) is EVEN, so \((n+1)^{n}\) is even (even to a positive power). And \(n^{n+1}\) is odd (odd to any power).
Case 2: \(n=2k\) (even). Then \(n+1=2k+1\) is ODD, so \((n+1)^{n}\) is odd; and \(n^{n+1}\) is even (even to a positive power).
In both cases the difference is odd. Since every positive integer is odd or even, \((n+1)^{n}-n^{n+1}\) is odd for all positive integers \(n\). ∎

Why not the others: B concludes “even” (wrong parity rule: even \(-\) odd is odd); C wrongly says \(n+1\) is odd when \(n\) is odd; D tests one value only, which is NOT a proof (it proves nothing for other \(n\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Cases: \(n\) odd / \(n\) even; even\(-\)odd \(=\) odd.

questions.stem: Prove that the product of two consecutive even counting numbers is a multiple of 4. Which proof is correct?
options: Let the numbers be \(2n\) and \(2n+2\) (\(n\) a counting number). Product \(=2n(2n+2)=4n(n+1)\), which is \(4\times\) an integer, so a multiple of 4
Let the numbers be \(n\) and \(n+2\). Product \(=n(n+2)\), which is even, so a multiple of 4
Take \(2\times4=8\), which is a multiple of 4, so it is always true
Let the numbers be \(2n\) and \(2n+1\). Product \(=2n(2n+1)=2\left(2n^{2}+n\right)\), a multiple of 2
questions.hint: A PROOF must work for ALL cases (an example is not a proof). Represent an EVEN number as \(2n\); the NEXT even number is \(2n+2\) (not \(2n+1\)). Multiply and FACTORISE to show a factor of 4.

steps.explain: Two consecutive even counting numbers: \(2n\) and \(2n+2\), where \(n\) is a counting number.
Multiply, then factor out 2 from the second bracket.
\(n(n+1)\) is an INTEGER, so the product is 4 times an integer: a multiple of 4. ∎
Why not the others: B uses \(n\) and \(n+2\) without making them even; C is one example (not a proof); D uses \(2n+1\) (odd, not the next even number).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Prove that the product of two consecutive even counting numbers is a multiple of 4.
keyPoints.note: Even: \(2n\); next even: \(2n+2\).

questions.stem: By considering the cases where a positive integer \(k\) is even (\(k=2x\)) and odd (\(k=2x+1\)), show that \(k^{2}+k\) is always even. Which working is correct?
options: Even: \(4x^{2}+2x=2\left(2x^{2}+x\right)\). Odd: \(4x^{2}+6x+2=2\left(2x^{2}+3x+1\right)\). Both are \(2\times\)integer.
Even: \(4x^{2}+2x=2\left(2x^{2}+x\right)\). Odd: \(4x^{2}+4x+2=2\left(2x^{2}+2x+1\right)\). Both are \(2\times\)integer.
Even: \(2x^{2}+2x=2\left(x^{2}+x\right)\). Odd: \(4x^{2}+6x+2=2\left(2x^{2}+3x+1\right)\). Both are \(2\times\)integer.
Even: \(4x^{2}+2x=2\left(2x^{2}+x\right)\). Odd: \(4x^{2}+6x+1\), which is odd, so the result is not always even.
questions.hint: Substitute \(k=2x\) and \(k=2x+1\) in turn into \(k^{2}+k\), expand carefully (remember \((2x+1)^{2}=4x^{2}+4x+1\)), and factor out 2 to show each result is \(2\times\)an integer.

steps.explain: Case 1: \(k\) even, \(k=2x\). Substitute and factor out 2.
Case 1 conclusion: \(2x^{2}+x\) is an integer, so \(k^{2}+k\) is \(2\times\)integer, i.e. EVEN.
Case 2: \(k\) odd, \(k=2x+1\). Expand the square first: \((2x+1)^{2}=4x^{2}+4x+1\). Then add \(k=2x+1\).
Factor out 2.
Case 2 conclusion: again \(2\times\)integer, EVEN. Both cases are even, so \(k^{2}+k\) is always even.

Why not the others: B has \(4x\) instead of \(6x\) in the odd case (the two \(x\) terms are \(4x\) and \(2x\)); C has a wrong even case (\((2x)^{2}\) is \(4x^{2}\), not \(2x^{2}\)); D drops the \(+1\) from \(k\) in the odd case.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Expand \((2x+1)^2\) first; factor out 2.

questions.stem: Show that \(\dfrac{n}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge1\). Which working is correct?
options: \({}^{2n}C_{n-1}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{(n-1)!\,n!}\) (the factorial lower indices add to \(2n-1\)), and dividing by \(\dfrac{n+1}{n}\) gives \({}^{2n}C_{n}\).
questions.hint: Use \({}^{N}C_{k}=\dfrac{N!}{k!\,(N-k)!}\) with \(N=2n\). Write both sides in factorials and use \(n!=n\cdot(n-1)!\) and \((n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n!\).

steps.explain: Left side: \(^{2n}C_{n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}\).
Use \(n!=n\,(n-1)!\) in ONE of the \(n!\) to cancel the factor \(n\) in the numerator.
Use \((n+1)!=(n+1)\,n!\) to combine \((n+1)\cdot n!\) into \((n+1)!\).
Right side: \(^{2n}C_{n-1}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{(n-1)!\,(2n-(n-1))!}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{(n-1)!\,(n+1)!}\). Same as the left side.
Why not the others: B uses \((n+1)n!=(n+2)!\) (it equals \((n+1)!\)); C has wrong factorials for \({}^{2n}C_{n-1}\); D replaces \({}^{2n}C_{n}\) by a wrong number.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Using \(\dfrac{n}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n-1}\), show that \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}\) is an integer for \(n\ge1\). Which argument is correct?
options: \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n}-\dfrac{n}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n}-{}^{2n}C_{n-1}\), because \(1-\dfrac{n}{n+1}=\dfrac1{n+1}\). A difference of two binomial coefficients (integers) is an integer.
\(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n}+{}^{2n}C_{n-1}\), a sum of two integers, so it is an integer.
\(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n-1}\) directly (the factor \(n\) can be ignored), which is an integer.
Since \(n+1\) divides \(2n\) for all \(n\), \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}\) is an integer.
questions.hint: Write \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}=1-\dfrac{n}{n+1}\). Then \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}={}^{2n}C_{n}-\dfrac{n}{n+1}\,{}^{2n}C_{n}\) and use part (i) on the second term.

steps.explain: Split \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}=1-\dfrac{n}{n+1}\) (check: \(\dfrac{n+1-n}{n+1}=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\)).
Substitute part (i) into the second term.
Binomial coefficients are integers, and a difference of integers is an integer.
Why not the others: B has a plus sign; C drops the factor \(\dfrac{n}{n+1}\) (it is not 1); D is false (e.g. \(n=2\): \(n+1=3\) does not divide \(2n=4\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\dfrac1{n+1}=1-\dfrac n{n+1}\); use part (i).

questions.stem: Recall that \({}^{n}C_{r}\) is defined for non-negative integers \(r\) and \(n\) where \(0\le r\le n\). Consider the equation \(\dfrac{100\,{}^{x}C_{100}}{{}^{x-1}C_{99}}=\dfrac{1}{x^{99}}\). How many real solutions in \(x\) does this equation possess?
options: infinite
questions.hint: Simplify the left side with factorials: \({}^{x}C_{100}=\dfrac{x!}{100!\,(x-100)!}\) and \({}^{x-1}C_{99}=\dfrac{(x-1)!}{99!\,(x-100)!}\). Then solve the resulting equation and CHECK that each answer makes the combinations defined (\(x\ge100\)).

steps.explain: Write the ratio with factorials. The \((x-100)!\) cancels.
So the left side is \(100\times\dfrac{x}{100}=x\). The equation becomes \(x=\dfrac{1}{x^{99}}\).

Real solutions of \(x^{100}=1\): \(x=1\) or \(x=-1\). BUT \({}^{x}C_{100}\) is only defined for integers \(x\ge100\), and \({}^{x-1}C_{99}\) needs \(x-1\ge99\). Neither \(x=1\) nor \(x=-1\) satisfies \(x\ge100\).
So the equation has NO solutions.
Why not the others: 1 and 2 count \(x=1\) and \(x=\pm1\) without checking the domain; “infinite” would need the equation to be an identity.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: How many real solutions in \(x\) does this equation possess
keyPoints.note: LHS simplifies to \(x\); then check the domain \(x\ge100\).

questions.stem: Suppose \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers, where \(a\) is even and \(b\) is odd. Show that the sum of \(a\) and \(b\) is odd. Which proof is correct?
options: Write \(a=2k\) and \(b=2m+1\) for integers \(k,m\) (any even number is \(2\times\)integer; any odd number is \(2\times\)integer \(+1\)). Then \(a+b=2k+2m+1=2(k+m)+1\), which is of the form \(2\times\)integer \(+1\), so it is odd.
Write \(a=2k\) and \(b=2k+1\) (using the SAME \(k\)). Then \(a+b=4k+1\), which is odd.
Take \(a=2\), \(b=3\): \(a+b=5\), which is odd. Hence the sum is always odd.
Even \(+\) odd \(=\) even, because even numbers dominate.
questions.hint: Use the definitions: even \(=2k\); odd \(=2m+1\) with DIFFERENT integers \(k\) and \(m\) (two unrelated numbers need two different letters). Add and factor out 2.

steps.explain: Definitions. \(a\) even: \(a=2k\) for some integer \(k\). \(b\) odd: \(b=2m+1\) for some integer \(m\).
Add.
Factor 2 from the first two terms: \(2(k+m)+1\), and \(k+m\) is an integer. A number of the form \(2n+1\) is odd.
Why not the others: B uses the same \(k\) for both (that only covers consecutive numbers); C is one example (not a proof); D is false.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Show that the sum of \(a\) and \(b\) is odd

questions.stem: If \(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers with \(x>y\), prove that \(6(x+y)^{2}-2(x-y)^{2}\) is divisible by four. Which proof is correct?
options: Expand: \(6\left(x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}\right)-2\left(x^{2}-2xy+y^{2}\right)=4x^{2}+16xy+4y^{2}=4\left(x^{2}+4xy+y^{2}\right)\). Since \(x^{2}+4xy+y^{2}\) is an integer, the expression is divisible by 4.
Expand: \(6\left(x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}\right)-2\left(x^{2}-2xy+y^{2}\right)=4x^{2}+8xy+4y^{2}=4\left(x^{2}+2xy+y^{2}\right)\), which is divisible by 4.
Take \(x=2\), \(y=1\): \(6(9)-2(1)=52=4\times13\). Hence it is divisible by 4 for all \(x,y\).
Expand: \(6(x+y)^{2}-2(x-y)^{2}=4(x+y)^{2}-(x-y)^{2}\), which is divisible by 4.
questions.hint: Expand both squares, collect like terms, and FACTOR OUT 4. Be careful with the middle terms: \(6\cdot2xy=12xy\) and \(-2\cdot(-2xy)=+4xy\).

steps.explain: Factor out 4: \(x^{2}+4xy+y^{2}\) is an integer (since \(x,y\) are integers).
Hence the expression is 4 times an integer, divisible by 4.
Why not the others: B has \(8xy\) (it is \(12xy+4xy=16xy\)); C is one example (not a proof); D is not factored correctly.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem:
Prove the following statement for positive \(n\) using a proof by contradiction.
“For each irrational number \(n\), \(\sqrt{n}\) is also irrational.”
questions.hint: Assume √n = a/b and square both sides.

steps.explain: Assume the opposite: \(n\) is irrational but \(\sqrt n\) is rational.
Square both sides.
\(a^2\) and \(b^2\) are integers (and \(b^2\neq0\)), so \(n\) is rational. This contradicts \(n\) being irrational.
Therefore the assumption is false: \(\sqrt n\) is irrational.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

questions.answer: Suppose n > 0 is irrational but \(\sqrt n\) is rational, say \(\sqrt n=\frac ab\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z^+\). Squaring gives \(n=\frac{a^2}{b^2}\), a ratio of integers, so n is rational — contradicting that n is irrational. Hence \(\sqrt n\) is irrational.

keyPoints.note: Assume √n is rational, write it as a/b, square, and see what that says about n.

parts.answer: Prove the contrapositive: let a be even and b odd (WLOG), a = 2m, b = 2n + 1. Then \(a^2+b^2=4m^2+4n^2+4n+1=2(2m^2+2n^2+2n)+1\), which is odd. So if one is even and the other odd, a² + b² is odd; hence by contraposition, if a² + b² is even then a, b are both even or both odd.

questions.stem: Prove \(\textit{by contraposition}\) that if \(n^{2}+6n\) is even, then \(n\) is even. Which statement must be proved, and what does it show?
options: Prove: if \(n\) is odd then \(n^{2}+6n\) is odd; with \(n=2k-1\), \(n^{2}+6n=2\left(2k^{2}+4k-2\right)-1\), which is odd
Prove: if \(n\) is odd then \(n^{2}+6n\) is even; with \(n=2k+1\), \(n^{2}+6n=2\left(2k^{2}+5k+3\right)\), which is even
Prove: if \(n^{2}+6n\) is odd then \(n\) is even, by letting \(n=2k\)
Prove: if \(n\) is even then \(n^{2}+6n\) is even; with \(n=2k\), \(n^{2}+6n=2\left(2k^{2}+6k\right)\)
questions.hint:
The contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\). Here \(
eg Q\) is '\(n\) is odd' and \(
eg P\) is '\(n^{2}+6n\) is odd'.

steps.explain: Write the statement as \(P\Rightarrow Q\): \(P\) is '\(n^{2}+6n\) is even' and \(Q\) is '\(n\) is even'.
The contrapositive is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): 'if \(n\) is odd, then \(n^{2}+6n\) is odd'. Proving this proves the original statement.
Let \(n\) be odd: \(n=2k-1\) for some integer \(k\). Substitute.
Expand and simplify.
Write it as \(2\times(\text{integer})-1\) to show it is odd: \(4k^{2}+8k-5=2\left(2k^{2}+4k-2\right)-1\).
So if \(n\) is odd then \(n^{2}+6n\) is odd. By contraposition, if \(n^{2}+6n\) is even then \(n\) is even.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Prove the contrapositive: not Q implies not P.

questions.stem: Prove \(\textit{by contradiction}\) that \(\log_{3}11\) is irrational. Which is the correct way to start and finish the proof?
options: Assume \(\log_{3}11=\dfrac{p}{q}\). Then \(3^{p}=11^{q}\), which is true when \(p=q\)
Assume \(\log_{3}11=\dfrac{p}{q}\) with \(p,q\) integers. Then \(3^{p}=11^{q}\), impossible by unique prime factorisation (3 and 11 are different primes)
Assume \(\log_{3}11\) is irrational. Then \(3^{p}=11^{q}\), which is impossible
Assume \(\log_{3}11=\dfrac{p}{q}\). Then \(3^{q}=11^{p}\), which is always true
questions.hint: Assume the OPPOSITE of what you want to prove (that it is rational), write it as \(\dfrac{p}{q}\), convert the logarithm to an index equation and find a contradiction.

steps.explain: A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite. Assume \(\log_{3}11\) is RATIONAL.
Convert the logarithm to index form: \(\log_{3}11=\dfrac{p}{q}\) means \(3^{\frac{p}{q}}=11\).
Raise both sides to the power \(q\) (so that there are no fractional powers).

The left side is a power of 3 and the right side is a power of 11. By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, every whole number has exactly ONE prime factorisation, but \(3^{p}\) has only the prime 3 and \(11^{q}\) only the prime 11 (with \(p,q>0\)).
The assumption led to a contradiction, so \(\log_{3}11\) is irrational.
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: Assume rational p over q, rewrite as 3 to the p equals 11 to the q, use prime factorisation.

If \(m\) and \(n\) are even, then \(mn\) and \(m+n\) are even.
If \(m\) is odd or \(n\) is odd, then \(mn\) is odd and \(m+n\) is odd.
questions.hint: The contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): swap the two parts AND negate each. Negating \"and\" gives \"or\" (De Morgan), and negating \"even\" gives \"odd\" (for integers).

steps.explain: Identify \(P\) and \(Q\). \(P\): \(mn\) is even AND \(m+n\) is even. \(Q\): \(m\) is even AND \(n\) is even.
Negate \(Q\): \"\(m\) and \(n\) are both even\" is false when AT LEAST ONE is odd. So \(\neg Q\): \"\(m\) is odd OR \(n\) is odd\".
Negate \(P\): \"\(mn\) even AND \(m+n\) even\" is false when \(mn\) is odd OR \(m+n\) is odd.
Contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).
Why not the others: B and D use \"and\" where De Morgan gives \"or\"; C is neither swapped nor negated properly (it is a different statement).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Swap and negate both; and ↔ or.

questions.stem: Consider this statement: If \(mn\) and \(m+n\) are even, then \(m\) and \(n\) are even, for \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}\). Prove the contrapositive. Which proof is correct?
options: Case 1: \(m\) odd, \(n\) even: \(m=2j+1,\ n=2k\), so \(m+n=2(j+k)+1\) is odd. Case 2: \(m\) even, \(n\) odd: same by symmetry. Case 3: both odd: \(m=2j+1,\ n=2k+1\), so \(mn=2(2jk+j+k)+1\) is odd. In every case \(mn\) or \(m+n\) is odd.
Test \(m=1,\ n=2\): \(m+n=3\) is odd. Test \(m=3,\ n=5\): \(mn=15\) is odd. So it is always true.
Assume \(mn\) and \(m+n\) are even. Then \(m\) and \(n\) must both be even, which is what we wanted.
Let \(m=2j+1\) be odd and \(n=2k\) be even. Then \(m+n=2(j+k)+1\) is odd. Hence the statement is proved.
questions.hint: To prove \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) assume \(m\) or \(n\) is odd and split into ALL the possible cases: (odd, even), (even, odd), (odd, odd). Write odd as \(2j+1\) and even as \(2k\).

steps.explain: Case 1: \(m\) odd and \(n\) even. Write \(m=2j+1\) and \(n=2k\) for integers \(j,k\) and add.
Case 2: \(m\) even and \(n\) odd: the same as Case 1 with the roles of \(m\) and \(n\) swapped (addition is commutative), so \(m+n\) is odd.
Case 3: \(m\) and \(n\) both odd. Write \(m=2j+1\) and \(n=2k+1\) and multiply.
These cases cover every situation where at least one of \(m,n\) is odd, and in each case \(mn\) is odd or \(m+n\) is odd. So the contrapositive is proved (and so is the original statement).
Why not the others: B only tests examples (examples are not a proof); C assumes the ORIGINAL statement instead of proving the contrapositive (circular); D covers only one of the three cases.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Cover every case: (odd, even), (even, odd), (odd, odd).

questions.stem: Suppose \(c^{2}-b^{2}=4\). Prove that \(b\) and \(c\) cannot both be positive integers. Which proof is correct?
options: Suppose \(b,c\) are positive integers. \((c-b)(c+b)=4\), and \(c-b\), \(c+b\) are positive integer factors of 4 with \(c-b<c+b\) or equal: \((1,4)\) or \((2,2)\). If \(c-b=1,\ c+b=4\) then \(c=\dfrac{5}{2}\), not an integer. If \(c-b=2,\ c+b=2\) then \(b=0\), not positive. Contradiction.
Suppose \(b,c\) are positive integers. \((c-b)(c+b)=4\), so \(c-b=1\) and \(c+b=4\). Then \(c=\dfrac{5}{2}\), not an integer. Contradiction.
Suppose \(b,c\) are positive integers. \((c-b)(c+b)=4\), so \(c-b=2\) and \(c+b=2\). Then \(b=0\), not positive. Contradiction.
Try \(b=1\): \(c^{2}=5\); try \(b=2\): \(c^{2}=8\). Neither \(c\) is an integer, so \(b\) and \(c\) cannot both be positive integers.
questions.hint: PROOF BY CONTRADICTION: assume \(b\) and \(c\) ARE both positive integers. Factorise \(c^{2}-b^{2}=(c-b)(c+b)\) and list ALL the ways to write 4 as a product of two positive integers.

steps.explain: Assume \(b\) and \(c\) are both positive integers. Factorise the difference of two squares.
\(c+b\) and \(c-b\) are integers with product 4, and \(c+b>c-b>0\) when \(b>0\) (here \(c-b>0\) because the product is positive and \(c+b>0\)). The factor pairs of 4 are \((1,4)\) and \((2,2)\).
Pair \((1,4)\): add the equations \(c-b=1\) and \(c+b=4\).
Pair \((2,2)\): subtract to find \(b\): \(c+b=2\) and \(c-b=2\) give \(2b=0\).

Both cases contradict the assumption, so \(b\) and \(c\) cannot both be positive integers. Why not the others: B and C check only ONE factor pair (they miss the other); D tests only two values of \(b\), which is not a proof.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Prove that \(b\) and \(c\) cannot both be positive integers
keyPoints.note: Factorise, list all factor pairs of 4.

questions.stem: For the positive real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), with \(a\ne2b\), prove that \(\dfrac{1}{a-2b}\ne\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&\text{Suppose }\dfrac{1}{a-2b}=\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}=\dfrac{2b-a}{2ab}=-\dfrac{a-2b}{2ab}\\ &\Rightarrow-2ab=(a-2b)^{2}\ \text{: LHS}<0\ (a,b>0),\ \text{RHS}>0\ \text{: contradiction}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Suppose }\dfrac{1}{a-2b}=\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}=\dfrac{2b-a}{2ab}=-\dfrac{a-2b}{2ab}\\ &\Rightarrow2ab=(a-2b)^{2}\ \text{, which can be solved, so the statement is true}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Suppose }\dfrac{1}{a-2b}=\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}=\dfrac{a-2b}{2ab}\\ &\Rightarrow2ab=(a-2b)^{2}\ \text{(no contradiction)}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Test }a=1,\ b=1:\ \dfrac{1}{-1}\ne\dfrac{1}{1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &\text{so the statement holds for all }a,b\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Proof by CONTRADICTION: assume the two sides ARE equal, simplify, and reach something impossible. Combine \(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac1{2b}\) over the common denominator \(2ab\). Look at the SIGN of each side: \(a,b>0\) makes \(-2ab\) negative, but a square is never negative.

steps.explain: Assume the opposite: suppose \(\dfrac{1}{a-2b}=\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}\).
Common denominator on the right: \(\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}=\dfrac{2b-a}{2ab}=-\dfrac{a-2b}{2ab}\).
Cross-multiply (allowed since \(a\ne2b\), \(a,b\ne0\)): \(2ab=-(a-2b)^{2}\), i.e. \(-2ab=(a-2b)^{2}\).
LEFT side: \(a>0\) and \(b>0\) so \(-2ab<0\). RIGHT side: a real square is \(\ge0\) (and \(>0\) here because \(a\ne2b\)). A negative number cannot equal a positive one.
So the assumption is false: \(\dfrac{1}{a-2b}\ne\dfrac{1}{a}-\dfrac{1}{2b}\). ∎
Why not the others: B drops the minus sign and finds no contradiction; C makes a sign slip so no contradiction appears; D checks one example (that is not a proof for ALL \(a,b\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Assume equal; common denominator \(2ab\); \(-2ab<0\le(a-2b)^{2}\).

questions.stem: Prove by contradiction that \(\log_{3}4\) is irrational. Which proof is correct?
options: Assume \(\log_{3}4=\dfrac{p}{q}\) with integers \(p,q>0\). Then \(3^{\frac{p}{q}}=4\), so \(3^{p}=4^{q}\). The left side is ODD and the right side is EVEN: a contradiction, so \(\log_{3}4\) is irrational
Assume \(\log_{3}4\) is irrational and show it equals a fraction
\(\log_{3}4=1.26\ldots\) never repeats, so it is irrational
questions.hint: PROOF BY CONTRADICTION: ASSUME the OPPOSITE (that \(\log_{3}4\) IS rational, \(=\dfrac{p}{q}\)), then DERIVE something impossible. Convert the log to an exponential equation and compare PARITY (odd/even).

steps.explain: Assume \(\log_{3}4=\dfrac{p}{q}\) where \(p,q\) are positive integers (\(\log_{3}4>0\)).
Convert to exponential form, then raise both sides to the power \(q\).
\(3^{p}\) is a power of 3 (ODD, with no factor 2). \(4^{q}=2^{2q}\) is EVEN (\(q\ge1\)). An odd number cannot equal an even number: CONTRADICTION.
So the assumption is false: \(\log_{3}4\) is irrational. ∎ Why not the others: B assumes the wrong thing; C is not a proof (decimals do not show irrationality); D only locates the number.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Prove by contradiction that \(\log_{3}4\) is irrational.
keyPoints.note: Assume \(\dfrac{p}{q}\): \(3^p=4^q\): odd = even.

questions.stem: A student wants to prove that there is an infinite number of prime numbers. To prove this statement by contradiction, what assumption would the student start their proof with?
options: There is only one prime number that is even.
There is an infinite number of primes.
There is a finite number of primes.
All prime numbers are less than 100.
questions.hint: Proof by contradiction: assume the OPPOSITE (the negation) of what you want to prove, then show that this assumption leads to something impossible. What is the opposite of “infinite”?

steps.explain: Write down the statement to be proved.
Proof by contradiction starts by assuming the NEGATION of P: the opposite of “infinitely many” is “only finitely many”.
steps.work: \(\neg P:\ \text{“There are only finitely many primes.”}\)

steps.explain: Then the proof continues: list all the primes \(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n}\), form \(N=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{n}+1\), and show \(N\) has a prime factor not in the list, which contradicts the assumption.

Why not the others: A is a true fact (2 is the only even prime), not the negation; B assumes the statement itself, which proves nothing; D is not the negation either (the negation of “infinite” is “finite”, not “all below 100”).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Assume the negation: “finitely many”.

questions.stem: Assuming \(n>0\), prove using the contrapositive that if \(4^{n}-1\) is prime, then \(n\) is odd. Which proof is correct?
options: Contrapositive: “If \(n\) is even, then \(4^{n}-1\) is NOT prime.” Let \(n=2k\), \(k\ge1\). Then \(4^{n}-1=4^{2k}-1=\left(4^{k}-1\right)\left(4^{k}+1\right)\). Since \(k\ge1\), both factors are greater than 1 (\(4^{k}-1\ge3\)), so \(4^{n}-1\) is composite.
Contrapositive: “If \(n\) is odd, then \(4^{n}-1\) is NOT prime.” Test \(n=3\): \(4^{3}-1=63=7\times9\), which is not prime. Hence the statement is true.
Contrapositive: “If \(n\) is odd, then \(4^{n}-1\) is prime.” Test \(n=1\): \(4-1=3\), which is prime, and \(n=3\): \(63\)...
Contrapositive: “If \(n\) is even, then \(4^{n}-1\) is prime.” Let \(n=2k\): \(4^{2k}-1=\left(4^{k}-1\right)\left(4^{k}+1\right)\), which is a product of two primes.
questions.hint:
The contrapositive of “\(P\Rightarrow Q\)” is “\(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\)”. Here \(P\): “\(4^{n}-1\) is prime”; \(Q\): “\(n\) is odd”. So \(
eg Q\): “\(n\) is even” and \(
eg P\): “\(4^{n}-1\) is not prime (composite)”. For \(n=2k\) use the DIFFERENCE OF TWO SQUARES.

steps.explain: Statement: if \(4^{n}-1\) is prime then \(n\) is odd. Contrapositive: negate and swap: “if \(n\) is not odd (even) then \(4^{n}-1\) is not prime”.
Assume \(n\) is even and \(n>0\): \(n=2k\) with \(k\ge1\) an integer.
Difference of two squares \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\).
Neither factor is 1: since \(k\ge1\), \(4^{k}-1\ge3\) and \(4^{k}+1\ge5\). A number that is a product of two factors both greater than 1 is composite (not prime).
The contrapositive is true, so the original statement is true.

Why not the others: B proves a different statement with one example (an example is not a proof, and “odd \(\Rightarrow\) not prime” is not the contrapositive); C writes the converse/inverse; D states the wrong conclusion (composite, not prime).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Contrapositive: even \(\Rightarrow\) composite; \(4^{2k}-1\) = difference of squares.

questions.stem: Prove by contradiction that \(\log_{5}7\) is irrational. Which proof is correct?
options: Assume \(\log_{5}7\) is rational: \(\log_{5}7=\dfrac{a}{b}\) with \(a,b\) positive integers. Then \(5^{\frac ab}=7\), so \(5^{a}=7^{b}\). The left side is divisible by 5 but the right side is not (7 and 5 are distinct primes, and by unique factorisation \(7^{b}\) has no factor 5). This is a contradiction, so \(\log_{5}7\) is irrational.
Assume \(\log_{5}7\) is irrational. Then \(5^{a}=7^{b}\) for integers \(a,b\), a contradiction, so it is rational.
\(\log_{5}7\approx1.209\), which does not terminate or repeat in a calculator, so it is irrational.
Assume \(\log_{5}7=\dfrac{a}{b}\) in lowest terms. Then \(5^{a}=7^{b}\), so both \(a\) and \(b\) are even, contradicting lowest terms.
questions.hint: Proof by contradiction: assume the OPPOSITE (that \(\log_{5}7\) is rational, \(=\dfrac{a}{b}\)), convert the logarithm to an index equation \(5^{a}=7^{b}\) and find a statement that cannot be true (divisibility by 5).

steps.explain: ASSUME the opposite: \(\log_{5}7=\dfrac{a}{b}\) for positive integers \(a,b\) (positive since \(\log_{5}7>0\)).
Convert to index form: \(\log_{5}7=\dfrac{a}{b}\iff5^{\frac ab}=7\). Raise both sides to the power \(b\).
The left side \(5^{a}\) (with \(a\ge1\)) is DIVISIBLE by 5. The right side \(7^{b}\) is a power of the prime 7: its only prime factor is 7, so it is NOT divisible by 5.
A number cannot be both divisible and not divisible by 5, so we have a CONTRADICTION. Hence the assumption is false and \(\log_{5}7\) is irrational.
Why not the others: B assumes the wrong thing (irrational); C uses a calculator decimal (not a proof); D invents an “even” argument (5 and 7 are odd).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Prove by contradiction that \(\log_{5}7\) is irrational
keyPoints.note: Assume \(\dfrac{a}{b}\); \(5^a=7^b\); divisibility by 5.
