questions.stem: Prove the following statement using a proof by contradiction. “For each irrational number \(s\), the number \(2s+1\) is also irrational”. Which proof is correct?
options: Assume the statement is false: there is an irrational \(s\) with \(2s+1\) RATIONAL, say \(2s+1=\dfrac{p}{q}\) (\(p,q\) integers, \(q\ne0\)). Then \(s=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{p}{q}-1\right)=\dfrac{p-q}{2q}\), a ratio of integers, so \(s\) is rational. This contradicts \(s\) irrational, so \(2s+1\) must be irrational.
Assume \(s\) is RATIONAL, \(s=\dfrac{p}{q}\). Then \(2s+1=\dfrac{2p+q}{q}\) is rational. This contradicts the statement, so the statement is false.
Assume \(2s+1\) is IRRATIONAL. Then \(s=\dfrac{(2s+1)-1}{2}\) is irrational, which is what we wanted to prove. Hence the statement is true.
Take \(s=\sqrt2\). Then \(2\sqrt2+1\) is irrational. Hence the statement is true for all irrational \(s\).
questions.hint: Proof by contradiction: assume the NEGATION of the statement. The statement is “for all irrational \(s\), \(2s+1\) is irrational”, so its negation is “there EXISTS an irrational \(s\) such that \(2s+1\) is RATIONAL”. Write \(2s+1=\dfrac{p}{q}\) and solve for \(s\) to show \(s\) would be rational: a contradiction.

steps.explain: ASSUME the opposite: for some irrational \(s\), \(2s+1\) is rational. A rational number is a ratio of integers.
Solve for \(s\): subtract 1 (write \(1=\dfrac{q}{q}\)) and divide by 2.
\(p-q\) and \(2q\) are integers and \(2q\ne0\), so \(s\) is RATIONAL. But \(s\) was assumed IRRATIONAL: CONTRADICTION.
Hence the assumption is false, and for every irrational \(s\), \(2s+1\) is irrational.
Why not the others: B assumes \(s\) rational (not the negation); C assumes the conclusion is false but then derives something that is not a contradiction; D checks one example (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The contrapositive of \(P\) is: if \(m\) and \(n\) are not both even and not both odd, then \(m+n\) is odd. Hence explain why the proposition \(P\) is true. Which explanation is correct?
options: If \(m\) and \(n\) are not both even and not both odd, then one is even and the other is odd. By part (i), the sum of an even and an odd number is odd. So the contrapositive is TRUE. A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, so \(P\) is true.
The contrapositive is true for the example \(m=2,n=3\), so \(P\) is true.
The contrapositive is true because \(m+n\) is odd, so its converse \(P\) is also true.
The contrapositive is the same as \(P\), so no explanation is needed.
questions.hint: A statement and its contrapositive are LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT (always the same truth value). So prove the contrapositive (easier here) using part (i).

steps.explain: Hypothesis of the contrapositive: \(m,n\) are not both even and not both odd. Then one of them is even and the other is odd.
By part (i) (even \(+\) odd), \(m+n\) is odd. So the contrapositive conclusion (\(m+n\) is not even) holds. The contrapositive is TRUE.
Equivalence: \(P\Leftrightarrow\) contrapositive. Since the contrapositive is true, \(P\) is true.
Why not the others: B uses one example (not a proof); C confuses contrapositive with converse; D is false (they are different statements, though equivalent).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: explain why the proposition \(P\) is true
keyPoints.note: Contrapositive true by (i); equivalent to \(P\).

Assume \(\log_{3}7\) is irrational. Then \(3^{a}=7^{b}\) for some integers, which is a contradiction, so it is rational.
\(\log_{3}7\approx1.77124\ldots\), a non-terminating decimal, so it is irrational.

parts.answer: For \(k \gt 0\), \(\sqrt k \lt \sqrt{k+1}\). Adding \(\sqrt k\): \(2\sqrt k \lt \sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k\). parts.answer: Rationalising, \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k}=2(\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k)\), so by (i) \(\frac1{\sqrt k} \gt 2(\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k)\). Summing for \(k=1\) to \(80\) (telescoping): \(\sum\frac1{\sqrt k} \gt 2(\sqrt{81}-\sqrt1)=16\). Similarly, from \(\sqrt{k-1} \lt \sqrt k\) we get \(\frac{2}{\sqrt k+\sqrt{k-1}} \gt \frac1{\sqrt k}\), i.e. \(\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 2(\sqrt k-\sqrt{k-1})\). Summing for \(k=2\) to \(80\): \(\sum_{k=2}^{80}\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 2(\sqrt{80}-1)\), so \(\sum_{k=1}^{80}\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 1+2\sqrt{80}-2=2\sqrt{80}-1\approx16.89 \lt 17\).

questions.stem:
Heron’s formula states that the area of a triangle is given by

\(A=\sqrt{s(s-x)(s-y)(s-z)}\)

where \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are the lengths of the sides of the triangle and \(s\) is the semi-perimeter.

steps.explain: Apply AM–GM to the three positive numbers \(s-x\), \(s-y\), \(s-z\).

Multiply by \(s\) and take the square root.
With constant perimeter this bound is a constant, reached exactly when AM = GM, i.e. \(s-x=s-y=s-z\), so \(x=y=z\): the triangle is equilateral.

questions.stem: Given that \(a>0,\ b>0\), prove that \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\). Which proof is correct?
options: \(\left(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}\right)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a-2\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}+b\ge0\Rightarrow a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\).
\((a-b)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\), so \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\).
The arithmetic mean \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\) is always at least the geometric mean \(\sqrt{ab}\) (AM-GM inequality), so \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\).
Try \(a=4,\ b=1\): \(4+1=5\ge2\sqrt{4}=4\). It works, so it is always true.
questions.hint: Start from something that is always true, a square is never negative: \(\left(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}\right)^{2}\ge0\). Expand and rearrange.

steps.explain: Because \(a>0\) and \(b>0\), \(\sqrt{a}\) and \(\sqrt{b}\) are real, and the square of any real number is \(\ge0\).
Expand: \(\left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2}=a\), \(\left(\sqrt{b}\right)^{2}=b\) and the middle term is \(-2\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}=-2\sqrt{ab}\).
Add \(2\sqrt{ab}\) to both sides.
Why not the others: B proves a different inequality (\(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\)); C quotes the very statement we have to prove (circular); D tests one example, which is not a proof.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Start with a square that is at least zero: root a minus root b, squared.

questions.stem: Hence, show that \(\sec^{2}x\ge2\tan x\). Which working is correct?

Let \(a=\sec^{2}x\) and \(b=1\) in part (i): \(\sec^{2}x+1\ge2\sqrt{\sec^{2}x}=2\sec x\).
Let \(a=\tan x\) and \(b=1\) in part (i): \(\tan x+1\ge2\sqrt{\tan x}\), so \(\sec^{2}x\ge2\tan x\).
Let \(a=\sin^{2}x\) and \(b=\cos^{2}x\) in part (i): \(\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x\ge2\sin x\cos x\), so \(\sec^{2}x\ge2\tan x\).
questions.hint: Choose \(a\) and \(b\) in part (i) so that \(a+b\) becomes \(\sec^{2}x\). The identity \(\tan^{2}x+1=\sec^{2}x\) suggests \(a=\tan^{2}x\), \(b=1\). Remember \(\sqrt{\tan^{2}x}=|\tan x|\).

steps.explain: We want \(a+b=\sec^{2}x\). Use \(\sec^{2}x=\tan^{2}x+1\), so take \(a=\tan^{2}x\) and \(b=1\) (both positive or non-negative; \(\tan^{2}x>0\) when \(\tan x\ne0\)).
Apply \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\).
Replace the left side by \(\sec^{2}x\). Finally \(|\tan x|\ge\tan x\) (the absolute value is never smaller), so \(2|\tan x|\ge2\tan x\).
Why not the others: B gives \(\sec^{2}x+1\), not \(\sec^{2}x\); C does not produce \(\sec^{2}x\) on the left; D produces \(1\ge\sin2x\), a different inequality.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Prove that, for all integers \(n\ge0\) and \(x\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(\sec^{2n}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge2^{n+1}\). Which proof is correct?
options: From (ii): \(\sec^{2}x\ge2\tan x\) and (by the same working with \(\cot x\)) \(\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\ge2\cot x\). All terms are positive for \(x\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so raise to the power \(n\): \(\sec^{2n}x\ge2^{n}\tan^{n}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge2^{n}\cot^{n}x\). Add: \(\sec^{2n}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge2^{n}\left(\tan^{n}x+\cot^{n}x\right)\ge2^{n}\cdot2\sqrt{\tan^{n}x\cot^{n}x}=2^{n}\cdot2=2^{n+1}\).

Since \(\sec x\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}x\ge1\), we get \(\sec^{2n}x\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge1\). Adding, \(\sec^{2n}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge2\), which is at least \(2^{n+1}\) for all \(n\).
By part (ii) with \(n=1\): \(\sec^{2}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\ge2\tan x+2\cot x\ge4=2^{2}\). So the statement is true for all \(n\).
Using AM-GM only: \(\sec^{2n}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x\ge2\sqrt{\sec^{2n}x\operatorname{cosec}^{2n}x}\). This is always at least \(2^{n+1}\).
questions.hint: Use part (ii) twice (once for \(\sec^{2}x\) and once for \(\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\) with \(\cot x\)), raise the inequalities to the power \(n\), add them, and use part (i) (AM-GM) on \(\tan^{n}x+\cot^{n}x\). Note \(\tan x\cot x=1\).

steps.explain: Part (ii) gives \(\sec^{2}x\ge2\tan x\). Similarly with \(a=\cot^{2}x,\ b=1\): \(\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x\ge2\cot x\). For \(x\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) all these quantities are POSITIVE.
Both sides are positive, so we can raise both sides to the power \(n\) (the inequality is preserved).
Add the two inequalities and take out the common factor \(2^{n}\).
Part (i) with \(a=\tan^{n}x,\ b=\cot^{n}x\) (positive): \(\tan^{n}x+\cot^{n}x\ge2\sqrt{\tan^{n}x\cot^{n}x}\). Since \(\tan x\cot x=1\), the product is 1, so the right side is \(2\).
Combine.
Why not the others: B proves only \(\ge2\) (too weak for \(n\ge1\)); C covers only \(n=1\); D does not give the power of 2.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Use part (ii) for sec and cosec, raise to the power n, then AM-GM on tan to the n plus cot to the n.

questions.stem: If \(a,b\) and \(c\) are any real numbers with \(a>b\), which of the following statements must always be true?
options: \(\dfrac{1}{a}>\dfrac{1}{b}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{a}<\dfrac{1}{b}\)
\(ac>bc\)
questions.hint: \"Must ALWAYS be true\" means true for EVERY choice of real numbers. One counterexample (using negative numbers, or \(c=0\) or \(c<0\)) kills a statement.

steps.explain: Option A: try \(a=2,\ b=1\). Then \(a>b\) but \(\dfrac{1}{2}<\dfrac{1}{1}\). A is FALSE for this case.
Option B: try \(a=2,\ b=-1\). Then \(a>b\) but \(\dfrac{1}{2}>-1\), so \(\dfrac{1}{a}<\dfrac{1}{b}\) fails. B is FALSE for this case.
Option C: try \(a=2,\ b=1,\ c=-1\). Then \(ac=-2\) and \(bc=-1\), and \(-2<-1\). C is FALSE (multiplying by a negative reverses the inequality; \(c=0\) also fails).
Option D: adding the same number \(c\) to both sides of an inequality NEVER changes its direction. So \(a>b\Rightarrow a+c>b+c\) always.
Only D must always be true.
So the correct choice is option D.

questions.stem: Deduce that \((a^{2}-b^{2})(a^{4}-b^{4})\le(a^{3}-b^{3})^{2}\). (Use the result \((a^{2}-b^{2})(c^{2}-d^{2})\le(ac-bd)^{2}\) from the previous part.) Which substitution works?
options: Put \(c=a\) and \(d=b\)
questions.hint: Compare the two inequalities. In the target, the second bracket on the left is \(a^{4}-b^{4}\): which \(c,d\) give \(c^{2}-d^{2}=a^{4}-b^{4}\)? Then check that \(ac-bd\) becomes \(a^{3}-b^{3}\).

steps.explain: The first bracket \((a^{2}-b^{2})\) matches \((a^{2}-b^{2})\) already. The second bracket must satisfy \(c^{2}-d^{2}=a^{4}-b^{4}\).
Substitute \(c=a^{2}\) and \(d=b^{2}\) into the left side of the previous result.
Substitute into the right side: \(ac-bd=a\cdot a^{2}-b\cdot b^{2}\).
So the result becomes \((a^{2}-b^{2})(a^{4}-b^{4})\le(a^{3}-b^{3})^{2}\), as required.

Why not the others: \(c=a,d=b\) gives \((a^{2}-b^{2})^{2}\le(a^{2}-b^{2})^{2}\); \(c=a^{3},d=b^{3}\) gives \(a^{6}-b^{6}\) and \((a^{4}-b^{4})^{2}\); \(c=a^{4},d=b^{4}\) gives \(a^{8}-b^{8}\). None of them produce the target.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Choose c and d so that c² − d² = a⁴ − b⁴.

meta.source: Gosford High School 2020 Year 12 Mathematics Extension 2 Trial HSC Examination

questions.stem: If \(a>0\), \(b>0\), \(c>0\) and \(d>0\) show that \(\dfrac{a+b+c+d}{4}\ge\sqrt[4]{abcd}\)
options: \(\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab},\quad\dfrac{c+d}{2}\ge\sqrt{cd}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{a+b+c+d}{4}\ge\dfrac{\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}}{2}\\ &\dfrac{\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}}{2}\ge\sqrt{\sqrt{ab}\sqrt{cd}}=\sqrt[4]{abcd}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab},\quad\dfrac{c+d}{2}\ge\sqrt{cd}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{a+b+c+d}{4}\ge\dfrac{\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}}{2}\\ &\dfrac{\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\sqrt{cd}=\sqrt{abcd}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{a+b}{2}\le\sqrt{ab},\quad\dfrac{c+d}{2}\le\sqrt{cd}\\ &\Rightarrow\dfrac{a+b+c+d}{4}\le\sqrt[4]{abcd}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab},\quad\dfrac{c+d}{2}\ge\sqrt{cd}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{a+b+c+d}{4}\ge\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}\\ &\ge\sqrt[4]{abcd}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Use the TWO-variable AM–GM \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\) (for \(x,y\ge0\)) THREE times: on \((a,b)\), on \((c,d)\), then on the two square roots \(\sqrt{ab}\) and \(\sqrt{cd}\).

steps.explain: Proof of the 2-variable result: \((\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\). Apply to \(a,b\) and to \(c,d\).
Add these and divide by 2 (the inequality direction is preserved when adding \(\ge\)).
Apply AM–GM again to the two positive numbers \(\sqrt{ab}\) and \(\sqrt{cd}\).
Chain the two inequalities.

Why not the others: B applies AM–GM and then gets \(\sqrt{ab}\sqrt{cd}\) (the product, not its square root); C reverses the inequality; D loses the factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and so would give a false inequality.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: AM–GM on \((a,b)\), \((c,d)\), then on \(\sqrt{ab},\sqrt{cd}\).

questions.stem: It is known that for all positive real numbers \(x,\ y\), \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\). Using this result, or otherwise, show that for all real \(a\), \(|a|\le\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&\text{Let }x=a^{2},\ y=1:\quad a^{2}+1\ge2\sqrt{a^{2}\cdot1}=2|a|\\ &\Rightarrow|a|\le\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Let }x=a,\ y=1:\quad a+1\ge2\sqrt{a}\\ &\Rightarrow|a|\le\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}\ \text{(not justified)}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Let }x=a^{2},\ y=1:\quad a^{2}+1\ge2\sqrt{a^{2}}=2a\\ &\Rightarrow a\le\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}\ \text{(only for }a\ge0)\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&\text{Let }x=a^{2},\ y=1:\quad a^{2}+1\le2|a|\\ &\Rightarrow|a|\ge\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Choose \(x\) and \(y\) so that \(2\sqrt{xy}\) becomes \(2|a|\): \(x=a^{2}\) and \(y=1\) are positive for every real \(a\neq0\). Remember \(\sqrt{a^{2}}=|a|\) (NOT just \(a\)), because \(a\) may be negative.

steps.explain: The given result needs positive \(x,y\). Take \(x=a^{2}\) (positive when \(a\ne0\)) and \(y=1\).
\(\sqrt{a^{2}}=|a|\) (the principal square root is never negative, even if \(a<0\)).
Divide both sides by 2.

Case \(a=0\) (not covered by \(x>0\)): \(|0|=0\le\dfrac{0+1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\) ✓. Alternatively: \(\dfrac{a^{2}+1}{2}-|a|=\dfrac{(|a|-1)^{2}}{2}\ge0\). Why not the others: B uses the wrong substitution; C writes \(\sqrt{a^{2}}=a\) (false for \(a<0\)); D reverses the inequality.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: For the positive real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), \(a\ne b\), it is given that \(a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-ab+b^{2}\right)\) and \((a-b)^{2}>0\). Using these facts, or otherwise, prove \(a^{3}+b^{3}>ab(a+b)\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&(a-b)^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-ab+b^{2}>ab\\ &a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)(a^{2}-ab+b^{2})>(a+b)\,ab\quad(a+b>0)\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&(a-b)^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-ab+b^{2}>-ab\\ &a^{3}+b^{3}>-(a+b)\,ab\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&(a-b)^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-ab+b^{2}>ab\\ &a^{3}+b^{3}>ab\ \text{(multiplying by }1\text{)}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&(a-b)^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}>0\\ &\text{so }a^{3}+b^{3}>0\ \text{(this does not give the required result)}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Start from \((a-b)^{2}>0\) and rearrange to \(a^{2}-ab+b^{2}>ab\) (add \(ab\) to both sides). Then multiply BOTH sides by \((a+b)\): you may do this without flipping the inequality because \(a+b>0\) (\(a,b\) are positive).

steps.explain: Expand the square.
Add \(ab\) to both sides to turn \(-2ab\) into \(-ab\).
Multiply (1) by \(a+b\). Since \(a>0\) and \(b>0\), \(a+b>0\), so the inequality sign STAYS the same (multiplying by a positive keeps \(>\)).
The left side is \(a^{3}+b^{3}\) (given factorisation).
Why not the others: B gets \(-ab\) (sign error when rearranging); C multiplies by 1 instead of \(a+b\); D never links to the required result.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \((a-b)^{2}>0\Rightarrow a^{2}-ab+b^{2}>ab\); multiply by \(a+b>0\).

questions.stem: Hence, or otherwise, show that if \(c\) is also a positive real number that is not equal to \(a\) or \(b\), then \(2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)>a^{2}(b+c)+b^{2}(a+c)+c^{2}(a+b)\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&a^{3}+b^{3}>ab(a+b)\ \ \text{(only this one)}\\ &\Rightarrow2(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3})>a^{2}(b+c)+b^{2}(a+c)+c^{2}(a+b)\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Apply part (i) to EACH of the three pairs \((a,b)\), \((a,c)\), \((b,c)\) (all different positive numbers), then ADD the three inequalities. Each cube appears in two of the pairs, which produces the factor 2.

steps.explain: Part (i) applies to any two different positive numbers. Use it three times.
Add the three inequalities (adding inequalities of the same direction keeps the direction). LEFT: each of \(a^{3},b^{3},c^{3}\) appears twice.
Expand the right side: \(a^{2}b+ab^{2}+a^{2}c+ac^{2}+b^{2}c+bc^{2}\), then group by the squared letter.
Why not the others: B multiplies inequalities (not helpful here); C uses only one inequality (it cannot involve \(c\)); D loses the factor 2 on the left (each cube is counted twice).
So the correct choice is option A.

meta.source: Hills Grammar 2025 Trial HSC Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: If \(a>b\) and \(c>0\), which of the following must be true? I. \(a^{2}>b^{2}\) II. \(a-c>b-c\) III. \(\dfrac{a}{c^{2}}>\dfrac{b}{c^{2}}\)
options: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.hint: Test each statement with a COUNTER-EXAMPLE if you suspect it fails. An inequality keeps its direction when you add/subtract a number, or multiply/divide by a POSITIVE number; it can FAIL when squaring negatives.

steps.explain: I: take \(a=1\), \(b=-2\) (\(a>b\) ✓): \(a^{2}=1\) and \(b^{2}=4\), so \(a^{2}>b^{2}\) is FALSE. Statement I does NOT always hold.
II: subtract the same number \(c\) from both sides of \(a>b\): the inequality is unchanged. ALWAYS true.
III: \(c>0\) so \(c^{2}>0\) (positive): dividing both sides of \(a>b\) by \(c^{2}\) keeps the direction. ALWAYS true.
So only II and III must be true. Why not the others: A, C, D include I (false when \(b\) is negative).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.text: If \(a>b\) and \(c>0\), which of the following must be true?
keyPoints.note: Counter-example for squares: \(a=1,b=-2\).

questions.stem: Prove that \(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\). Which proof is correct?
options: \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\)
\((a+b)^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}\ge0\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}\ge-2ab\)
Try \(a=1,\ b=1\): \(2\ge2\), so it is true
questions.hint: Start from something that is ALWAYS true: a SQUARE of a real number is never negative. Choose the square \((a-b)^{2}\) so that expanding gives \(-2ab\); then move \(-2ab\) to the other side.

steps.explain: For all real \(a,b\): \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\).
Expand.
Add \(2ab\) to both sides.
Why not the others: B uses \((a+b)^{2}\) (this gives \(-2ab\)); C is not related; D is a single example (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Start with \((a-b)^2\ge0\).

meta.source: Hunters Hill High School 2020 Trial Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Hence, prove that \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\ge xy+yz+zx\). Which proof is correct?
options: Apply (i) to three pairs: \(x^{2}+y^{2}\ge2xy\), \(y^{2}+z^{2}\ge2yz\), \(z^{2}+x^{2}\ge2zx\); add: \(2\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)\ge2(xy+yz+zx)\); divide by 2
Apply (i) once: \(x^{2}+y^{2}\ge2xy\), so \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\ge xy+yz+zx\)
Multiply the three inequalities instead of adding them
Substitute \(x=y=z\): \(3x^{2}\ge3x^{2}\)
questions.hint: “Hence” means USE part (i). The result is symmetric in \(x,y,z\): apply \(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\) to EACH pair of variables, ADD the three inequalities (inequalities of the same direction can be added), then divide by 2.

steps.explain: Apply part (i) to the pairs \((x,y)\), \((y,z)\), \((z,x)\).
Add the three. Each square appears TWICE on the left.
Divide by 2.
Why not the others: B skips two pairs; C: multiplying inequalities is not valid here; D is one special case (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Apply (i) to three pairs; add.

meta.source: Hunters Hill High School 2020 Trial Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Deduce that if \(x+y+z=1\), then \(xy+yz+zx\le\dfrac{1}{3}\). Which proof is correct?
options: Square \(x+y+z=1\): \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+2(xy+yz+zx)=1\). By (ii) \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\ge xy+yz+zx\), so \(1-2(xy+yz+zx)\ge xy+yz+zx\Rightarrow3(xy+yz+zx)\le1\)
Since \(x+y+z=1\), \(xy+yz+zx=1\)
Cube both sides of \(x+y+z=1\)
questions.hint: Let \(S=xy+yz+zx\). SQUARE the condition \(x+y+z=1\) to bring in \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\) and \(S\); then replace \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\) using the inequality from (ii).

steps.explain: Square both sides of \(x+y+z=1\).
Make the sum of squares the subject: \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1-2S\). Now use (ii): \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\ge S\).
Solve: \(1\ge3S\).
Why not the others: B, C confuse the sum with the sum of products/squares; D doesn’t help.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Square the condition; use (ii).

meta.source: Hunters Hill High School 2020 Trial Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Show that for \(k>0\), \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac{1}{k+1}<0\). Which working is correct?
options: \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}-\left(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac1{k+1}\right)=\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\). Since \(k(k+1)<(k+1)^{2}\), \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}>\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\), so the expression is negative
\(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{k}\), so the expression is positive
\(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac1{k+1}=\dfrac{1}{k+1}\), so it is \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}-\dfrac1{k+1}\)
Substitute \(k=1\): \(\dfrac{1}{4}-1+\dfrac{1}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}<0\), so it is true for all \(k\)
questions.hint: Combine \(-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{k+1}\) into ONE fraction: \(-\left(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac{1}{k+1}\right)=-\dfrac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}=-\dfrac1{k(k+1)}\). Then compare denominators.

steps.explain: Group the last two terms: \(-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{k+1}=-\dfrac{(k+1)-k}{k(k+1)}=-\dfrac1{k(k+1)}\).
For \(k>0\): \(k<k+1\), so \(k(k+1)<(k+1)^{2}\). A SMALLER denominator gives a BIGGER fraction.
So we subtract a bigger number from a smaller one: the result is NEGATIVE. ∎
Why not the others: B has the wrong conclusion; C mis-simplifies \(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac1{k+1}\); D is one example (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac1{k+1}=\dfrac1{k(k+1)}\); compare denominators.

meta.source: Hunters Hill High School 2020 Trial Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: For \(d\), an integer where \(d>1\), show that \(\dfrac{1}{d^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}\). Which argument is correct?
options: Since \(d>d-1>0\), we have \(d^{2}>d(d-1)>0\); taking reciprocals reverses the inequality, so \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}\).
Since \(d>d-1\), we have \(d^{2}<d(d-1)\); taking reciprocals gives \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}\).
Since \(d>d-1>0\), we have \(d^{2}>d(d-1)\); taking reciprocals keeps the same direction, so \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}>\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}\).
Since \(d^{2}=d(d-1)+d\), the two fractions are equal, so \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}\).
questions.hint: Compare the DENOMINATORS: \(d\) versus \(d-1\). The bigger positive denominator gives the smaller fraction. Remember that taking reciprocals of positive numbers REVERSES the inequality.

steps.explain: Since \(d>1\), both \(d\) and \(d-1\) are positive, and \(d>d-1\).
Multiply both sides by the positive number \(d\) (the inequality direction stays).
Take reciprocals of positive numbers: the inequality REVERSES (e.g. \(4>2\) but \(\dfrac{1}{4}<\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
Why not the others: B claims \(d^{2}<d(d-1)\) (false since \(d>d-1\)); C forgets the reversal; D adds \(d\) to the wrong side (\(d^{2}=d(d-1)+d\), so \(d^{2}\) is LARGER, not equal).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Bigger denominator \(\Rightarrow\) smaller fraction.

meta.source: Hurlstone Agricultural High School 2020 Trial Higher School Certificate Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Noting that \(\dfrac{1}{d(d-1)}=\dfrac{1}{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\), show that, for a positive integer \(n\), \(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{2^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{3^{2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{n^{2}}<2\). Which argument is correct?
options: Keep \(\dfrac1{1^{2}}=1\). For \(d=2,\dots,n\) use \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\). The sum telescopes: \(\text{LHS}<1+\left(1-\dfrac{1}{n}\right)=2-\dfrac{1}{n}<2\).
Use \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\) for every \(d\) from 1 to \(n\). The sum telescopes to \(1-\dfrac{1}{n}<2\).
Use \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}>\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\) for \(d=2,\dots,n\). The sum telescopes to \(2-\dfrac{1}{n}<2\).
Use \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\) for \(d=2,\dots,n\), but drop the first term \(\dfrac1{1^{2}}\); the sum telescopes to \(1-\dfrac{1}{n}<2\).
questions.hint: Part (i) is valid only for \(d>1\), so the FIRST term \(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}}\) must be treated separately. For \(d=2,3,\dots,n\) replace each \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}\) by the bigger telescoping term \(\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\) and cancel.

steps.explain: From (i) and the given identity, for every integer \(d>1\): \(\dfrac1{d^{2}}<\dfrac1{d(d-1)}=\dfrac1{d-1}-\dfrac{1}{d}\).
For \(d=1\) the right side is undefined (\(\dfrac{1}{0}\)), so keep \(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}}=1\) as it is. Then apply the inequality to each remaining term.
Add everything: all the middle terms cancel in pairs (\(-\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(-\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{3}\), …), leaving only the first and last.
Simplify. Since \(n\) is a positive integer, \(\dfrac{1}{n}>0\), so \(2-\dfrac{1}{n}<2\).
Why not the others: B applies the identity at \(d=1\), where it is undefined; C reverses the inequality; D drops the first term, which would only prove a smaller sum is less than 2.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: show that, for a positive integer \(n\)
keyPoints.note: Handle \(d=1\) separately; telescoping cancels the middle terms.

questions.stem: For two positive real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), prove that their arithmetic mean \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\) is always greater than or equal to their geometric mean \(\sqrt{ab}\). Which proof is correct?
options: Since \(a,b>0\) we may use \(\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^{2}\ge0\). Expanding: \(a-2\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0\), so \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\), and dividing by 2 gives \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\).
Since \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\): \(a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}\ge0\), so \(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\). Hence \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\).
Assume \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\). Square both sides and rearrange to get \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\), which is true. Hence the result.
Since \(\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^{2}\ge0\): \(a-\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0\), so \(a+b\ge\sqrt{ab}\), hence \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}\).
questions.hint: Start from something you KNOW is true: a square of a real number is never negative. Use the square \(\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^{2}\ge0\) (this needs \(a,b\ge0\)), expand it, and rearrange.

steps.explain: Because \(a>0\) and \(b>0\), \(\sqrt a\) and \(\sqrt b\) are real numbers, and the square of any real number is \(\ge0\).
Expand the square: \(\left(\sqrt a\right)^{2}=a\), \(\left(\sqrt b\right)^{2}=b\) and the middle term is \(-2\sqrt a\sqrt b=-2\sqrt{ab}\).
Move the middle term to the right-hand side.
Divide both sides by 2 (positive, so the inequality direction stays).

Why not the others: B starts from \((a-b)^{2}\), which proves a different inequality (\(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\)); C ASSUMES the result (“working backwards”) which proves nothing unless every step is reversible; D has the wrong middle term (\(-\sqrt{ab}\) instead of \(-2\sqrt{ab}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: is always greater than or equal to their geometric mean
keyPoints.note: Square of a real number \(\ge0\): \((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\ge0\).

meta.source: Hurlstone Agricultural High School 2020 Trial Higher School Certificate Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Given that \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are positive real numbers, prove that \(a^{3}+b^{3}\ge a^{2}b+ab^{2}\). Which proof is correct?
options: \(a^{3}+b^{3}-a^{2}b-ab^{2}=(a-b)^{2}(a-b)\ge0\), because a square is never negative.
Take \(a=b=1\): \(1+1\ge1+1\) is true. Hence \(a^{3}+b^{3}\ge a^{2}b+ab^{2}\) for all positive \(a\) and \(b\).
\(a^{3}+b^{3}-a^{2}b-ab^{2}=(a+b)^{2}(a-b)\), which is \(\ge0\) for all positive \(a,b\).
questions.hint: Move everything to one side, FACTORISE by grouping, and show the result is a product of non-negative factors. Group \(a^{3}-a^{2}b\) and \(b^{3}-ab^{2}\) (or \(a^{2}(a-b)-b^{2}(a-b)\)).

steps.explain: Consider the difference: \(D=a^{3}+b^{3}-a^{2}b-ab^{2}\). Group the terms: \(\left(a^{3}-a^{2}b\right)-\left(ab^{2}-b^{3}\right)\).
Take out the common factor \((a-b)\).
Difference of two squares: \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\).
\((a-b)^{2}\ge0\) (square of a real number) and \(a+b>0\) (a,b positive), so a non-negative number times a positive number is \(\ge0\).

Why not the others: B has the wrong factorisation (\((a-b)^{2}(a-b)\) can be negative); C tests one case only (an example is not a proof); D has the wrong factorisation (\((a+b)^{2}(a-b)\) is negative when \(a<b\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

meta.source: James Ruse Agricultural High School 2020 Trial Higher School Certificate Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Given that \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are positive real numbers, and \(a^{3}+b^{3}\ge a^{2}b+ab^{2}\), prove that \(abc\le\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}\le\dfrac{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}{3}\). You may also assume \(a+b+c\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}\) and \((a+b+c)^{3}=a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3\left(a^{2}b+a^{2}c+b^{2}a+b^{2}c+c^{2}a+c^{2}b\right)+6abc\). Which argument is correct?
options: Left: divide \(a+b+c\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}\) by 3 and cube both sides to get \(\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}\ge abc\). Right: apply part (i) to each pair, so \(3\left(a^{2}b+\cdots+c^{2}b\right)\le6\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\). Also apply the assumed inequality to \(a^{3},b^{3},c^{3}\): \(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\ge3abc\), so \(6abc\le2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\). Then \((a+b+c)^{3}\le9\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\); divide by 27.

Left: divide by 3 and cube to get \(\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}\ge abc\). Right: apply part (i) to each pair to get \(3\left(a^{2}b+\cdots\right)\le6\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\), and replace \(6abc\) by \(0\), so \((a+b+c)^{3}\le7\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\); divide by 27.

Left: cube \(a+b+c\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}\) without dividing by 3 to get \(\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}\ge abc\). Right: part (i) gives \(a^{2}b+ab^{2}\ge a^{3}+b^{3}\), so \((a+b+c)^{3}\ge9\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\), and the result follows.

Left: \(abc\le\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}\) is just the same inequality as the given \(a+b+c\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}\) with no work needed. Right: expand \((a+b+c)^{3}\) and compare term by term with \(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\), then divide by 27.
questions.hint: Two inequalities: LEFT: from \(a+b+c\ge3\sqrt[3]{abc}\): divide by 3 and CUBE (cubing keeps the order for positive numbers). RIGHT: expand \((a+b+c)^{3}\), bound the mixed terms using part (i) (once for each pair) and bound \(6abc\) using AM-GM on \(a^{3},b^{3},c^{3}\).

steps.explain: LEFT inequality: both sides of \(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\ge\sqrt[3]{abc}\) are positive, so cubing keeps the inequality.

RIGHT inequality, step 1: use part (i) for the three pairs \((a,b),(a,c),(b,c)\) and add: \(\left(a^{2}b+ab^{2}\right)+\left(a^{2}c+ac^{2}\right)+\left(b^{2}c+bc^{2}\right)\le2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\) (each cube appears in two pairs).
Step 2: apply the assumed inequality \(x+y+z\ge3\sqrt[3]{xyz}\) to \(x=a^{3}\), \(y=b^{3}\), \(z=c^{3}\): \(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\ge3abc\), so \(6abc\le2\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)\).
Step 3: put the bounds into the expansion of \((a+b+c)^{3}\): \(1+6+2=9\) copies of \(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\).

Divide by 27: \(\left(\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{(a+b+c)^{3}}{27}\le\dfrac{9\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)}{27}=\dfrac{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}{3}\). Combining with the LEFT inequality completes the proof.

Why not the others: B replaces \(6abc\) by 0 (which makes the bound too small: not allowed); C reverses the inequality of part (i); D skips the work for the right-hand inequality and the left one is not identical to the assumption (it needs cubing).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Left: divide by 3 and cube. Right: bound with part (i) and \(\sum a^3\ge3abc\).

questions.stem: Show that, for all positive values of \(x\) and \(y\), \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\). Which proof is correct?
options: Since \(x,y>0\), \(\left(\sqrt x-\sqrt y\right)^{2}\ge0\). Expanding: \(x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0\), so \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\). Dividing by 2: \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\).
Since \((x-y)^{2}\ge0\), \(x^{2}+y^{2}\ge2xy\). Dividing by 2: \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\).
Take \(x=y=1\): \(\dfrac{1+1}{2}=1=\sqrt{1\cdot1}\). Hence true for all positive \(x,y\).
Since \(\left(\sqrt x+\sqrt y\right)^{2}\ge0\): \(x+2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0\), so \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge-\sqrt{xy}\).
questions.hint: Start from a TRUE fact: the square of a real number is never negative. Use \(\left(\sqrt x-\sqrt y\right)^{2}\ge0\) (it needs \(x,y\ge0\)), expand, and rearrange.

steps.explain: \(x,y>0\) so \(\sqrt x,\sqrt y\) are real: \(\left(\sqrt x-\sqrt y\right)^{2}\ge0\).
Expand: \(\left(\sqrt x\right)^{2}-2\sqrt x\sqrt y+\left(\sqrt y\right)^{2}=x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\).
Divide by 2.
Why not the others: B proves a different inequality (\(x^{2}+y^{2}\ge2xy\)); C tests one example only; D uses a plus sign (that gives a weaker statement with \(-\sqrt{xy}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Show that, for all positive values of \(x\) and \(y\)
keyPoints.note: \((\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\ge0\).

questions.stem: Using \(\dfrac{x+y}{2}\ge\sqrt{xy}\) for positive \(x,y\), prove that \((b+c)(c+a)(a+b)\ge8abc\) for positive real numbers \(a,b,c\). Which argument is correct?
options: Apply the result to each factor: \(b+c\ge2\sqrt{bc}\), \(c+a\ge2\sqrt{ca}\), \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\). All sides are positive, so multiply: \((b+c)(c+a)(a+b)\ge8\sqrt{bc\cdot ca\cdot ab}=8\sqrt{a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}}=8abc\).
Apply the result to each factor: \(b+c\ge\sqrt{bc}\), \(c+a\ge\sqrt{ca}\), \(a+b\ge\sqrt{ab}\). Multiply: \((b+c)(c+a)(a+b)\ge\sqrt{a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}}=abc\), and \(abc\ge8abc\).
Add the three inequalities \(b+c\ge2\sqrt{bc}\), \(c+a\ge2\sqrt{ca}\), \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\) to get \(2(a+b+c)\ge2\left(\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{bc}+\sqrt{ca}\right)\), then multiply by \(4abc\).
Apply the result to each factor and SUBTRACT: \((b+c)-(c+a)\ge2\sqrt{bc}-2\sqrt{ca}\), and so on, giving \(8abc\).
questions.hint: Each factor \((b+c)\), \((c+a)\), \((a+b)\) is a sum of two positive numbers, so apply \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\) to each. Because everything is POSITIVE, you may MULTIPLY the three inequalities. Then simplify the product of square roots.

steps.explain: From part (i): \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\) for positive \(x,y\). Apply to each factor.
All six quantities are positive, so we can multiply the three inequalities (multiplying inequalities between positive numbers keeps the direction).
Simplify the product of square roots: \(\sqrt{bc\cdot ca\cdot ab}=\sqrt{a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}}=abc\) (positive).

Why not the others: B uses \(\sqrt{xy}\) without the 2 (its conclusion \(abc\ge8abc\) is false); C ADDS instead of multiplying, which does not give the product; D subtracts inequalities (not allowed).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}\) on each factor; multiply.

questions.stem: If \(p\), \(q\) and \(r\) are positive real numbers and \(p+q\ge r\), prove that \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}+\dfrac{q}{1+q}-\dfrac{r}{1+r}\ge0\). Which proof is correct?
options: \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}\ge\dfrac{p}{1+p+q}\) and \(\dfrac{q}{1+q}\ge\dfrac{q}{1+p+q}\) (the denominators are smaller). Adding: \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}+\dfrac{q}{1+q}\ge\dfrac{p+q}{1+p+q}\). The function \(f(t)=\dfrac{t}{1+t}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+t}\) is increasing and \(p+q\ge r\), so \(\dfrac{p+q}{1+p+q}\ge\dfrac{r}{1+r}\). Combining gives the result.
\(\dfrac{p}{1+p}\le\dfrac{p}{1+p+q}\) and \(\dfrac{q}{1+q}\le\dfrac{q}{1+p+q}\). Adding and using \(f(t)=\dfrac{t}{1+t}\) increasing gives the result.
Since \(p+q\ge r\), \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}+\dfrac{q}{1+q}\ge\dfrac{p+q}{1+p+q}\ge\dfrac{r}{1+p+q}\), and \(\dfrac{r}{1+p+q}\ge\dfrac{r}{1+r}\), which proves it.
Take \(p=q=r=1\): \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ge0\). Hence the inequality is true for all positive \(p,q,r\).
questions.hint: Two steps: (1) \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}\ge\dfrac{p}{1+p+q}\) (a BIGGER denominator makes the fraction smaller), similarly for \(q\); add. (2) The function \(f(t)=\dfrac{t}{1+t}\) is INCREASING, and \(p+q\ge r\).

steps.explain: Compare denominators: \(1+p<1+p+q\), so \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}>\dfrac{p}{1+p+q}\). Similarly \(\dfrac{q}{1+q}>\dfrac{q}{1+p+q}\) (since \(p,q>0\)).
Let \(f(t)=\dfrac{t}{1+t}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+t}\): as \(t\) increases, \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}\) decreases, so \(f(t)\) INCREASES. Because \(p+q\ge r\), \(f(p+q)\ge f(r)\).
Combine the two inequalities (transitivity).
Why not the others: B reverses the first inequality; C changes \(r\)'s denominator without justification; D checks one example only (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Bigger denominator \(\Rightarrow\) smaller; \(\dfrac{t}{1+t}\) is increasing.

questions.stem: Show that \(a^{2}+b^{2}>2ab\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are distinct positive real numbers. Which proof is correct?
options: Since \((a-b)^{2}\ge0\), \(a^{2}+b^{2}\ge2ab\). The inequality is therefore strict.
Take \(a=1\), \(b=2\): \(1+4=5>4=2ab\). Hence \(a^{2}+b^{2}>2ab\) for all distinct positive \(a,b\).
questions.hint: The square of a NON-ZERO real number is strictly positive. \(a\) and \(b\) are DISTINCT, so \(a-b\ne0\). Use \((a-b)^{2}>0\) and expand.

steps.explain: \(a\ne b\Rightarrow a-b\ne0\Rightarrow(a-b)^{2}>0\) (strictly, because the square of a non-zero real number is positive).
Add \(2ab\) to both sides.

Why not the others: B uses \(a+b\) (that gives the weaker \(a^{2}+b^{2}>-2ab\)); C gives only \(\ge\) and then asserts strictness without a reason (the reason is \(a\ne b\)); D checks one example (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Distinct \(\Rightarrow(a-b)^2>0\); expand.

questions.stem: Using \(a^{2}+b^{2}>2ab\) for distinct positive reals, show that \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}>ab+bc+ca\), where \(a,b\) and \(c\) are distinct positive real numbers. Which argument is correct?
options: Apply part (i) to each pair: \(a^{2}+b^{2}>2ab\), \(b^{2}+c^{2}>2bc\), \(c^{2}+a^{2}>2ca\). Add the three: \(2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)>2(ab+bc+ca)\). Divide by 2.
Apply part (i) to each pair and MULTIPLY: \(\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(c^{2}+a^{2}\right)>8abc\cdot abc\). Take the square root.
Apply part (i) to each pair and SUBTRACT: \(\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)-\left(b^{2}+c^{2}\right)>2ab-2bc\), which gives the result.
Put \(a=b=c\): both sides equal \(3a^{2}\). Hence the inequality holds.
questions.hint: Apply part (i) to the THREE pairs \((a,b)\), \((b,c)\), \((c,a)\) and ADD the three inequalities (inequalities in the same direction can be added). Each square appears twice on the left.

steps.explain: Part (i) for each pair of the numbers.
Add the three inequalities (adding inequalities pointing the same way is allowed). Each of \(a^{2},b^{2},c^{2}\) appears twice on the left.
Divide by 2.

Why not the others: B multiplies (that is a different inequality and the conclusion does not follow); C subtracts (not allowed with inequalities); D uses the equal case \(a=b=c\), which is excluded (the numbers are distinct).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Apply (i) to three pairs; ADD.

questions.stem: Using \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}>ab+bc+ca\) for distinct positive reals, prove that \(\dfrac{a^{2}b^{2}+b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}}{a+b+c}>abc\), where \(a,b\) and \(c\) are distinct positive real numbers. Which proof is correct?
options: Apply the previous result to the three numbers \(ab\), \(bc\), \(ca\): \((ab)^{2}+(bc)^{2}+(ca)^{2}>ab\cdot bc+bc\cdot ca+ca\cdot ab=abc(a+b+c)\). Since \(a+b+c>0\), divide both sides by it.
Apply the previous result directly to \(a,b,c\): \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}>ab+bc+ca\). Multiply both sides by \(abc\) and divide by \(a+b+c\).
Apply the previous result to \(ab\), \(bc\), \(ca\): \((ab)^{2}+(bc)^{2}+(ca)^{2}>abc(a+b+c)\). Divide both sides by \(abc\) to get the result.
The previous result with \(a=b=c=1\) gives \(3>3\), hence the statement.
questions.hint: Replace \(a,b,c\) in the result of (ii) by the products \(ab\), \(bc\), \(ca\). Simplify the right side: \(ab\cdot bc+bc\cdot ca+ca\cdot ab=abc(b+c+a)\). Then divide by the POSITIVE number \(a+b+c\).

steps.explain: Let \(x=ab\), \(y=bc\), \(z=ca\) (distinct positive numbers). Part (ii) says \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}>xy+yz+zx\).
Simplify the right side: \((ab)(bc)=ab^{2}c\); \((bc)(ca)=abc^{2}\); \((ca)(ab)=a^{2}bc\). Factor out \(abc\).
So \(a^{2}b^{2}+b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}>abc\,(a+b+c)\). Divide both sides by \(a+b+c>0\) (the direction stays).
Why not the others: B applies the result to \(a,b,c\) (which gives a different inequality); C divides by \(abc\) instead of \(a+b+c\); D uses equal numbers (they must be distinct).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Use (ii) with \(ab,bc,ca\); RHS \(=abc(a+b+c)\).

questions.stem: It is given that \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}=\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac{1}{k+1}\) for \(k\in\mathbb N\). Prove that \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\). Which proof is correct?
options: For \(k\ge1\): \((k+1)^{2}=(k+1)(k+1)>k(k+1)>0\) (since \(k+1>k>0\)). Taking RECIPROCALS of positive numbers reverses the inequality: \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\).
\((k+1)^{2}<k(k+1)\), so taking reciprocals, \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\).
\(\dfrac{1}{k+1}<\dfrac{1}{k}\), so squaring both sides gives \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{k^{2}}\), which is what we want.
\((k+1)^{2}>k(k+1)\), so taking reciprocals keeps the direction: \(\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}>\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\).
questions.hint: Compare the DENOMINATORS: \((k+1)^{2}=(k+1)\cdot(k+1)\) versus \(k(k+1)=k\cdot(k+1)\). They share the factor \(k+1\): compare \(k+1\) with \(k\). A BIGGER positive denominator gives a SMALLER fraction.

steps.explain: Since \(k+1>k>0\), multiply both sides by the positive number \(k+1\).
Reciprocals of positive numbers REVERSE the inequality (e.g. \(4>2\) but \(\dfrac{1}{4}<\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
Test \(k=2\): \(\dfrac{1}{9}\approx0.111<\dfrac{1}{6}\approx0.167\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the false inequality \((k+1)^{2}<k(k+1)\); C proves a different inequality (\(k^{2}\) in the denominator); D forgets to reverse.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \((k+1)^2>k(k+1)\); reciprocals reverse.

questions.stem: If \(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},\dots,x_{n}\) are positive integers, not necessarily consecutive, such that \(1<x_{1}<x_{2}<x_{3}<\cdots<x_{n}\), prove that \(\dfrac{1}{x_{1}^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{x_{2}^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{x_{3}^{2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{x_{n-1}^{2}}<1\). Which proof is correct?
options: Since the \(x_{i}\) are INTEGERS, strictly increasing and \(x_{1}>1\) (so \(x_{1}\ge2\)), we have \(x_{i}\ge i+1\). So \(\dfrac{1}{x_{i}^{2}}\le\dfrac{1}{(i+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{i(i+1)}=\dfrac{1}{i}-\dfrac1{i+1}\) (part (i)). Sum for \(i=1\) to \(n-1\): \(\displaystyle\sum\dfrac{1}{x_{i}^{2}}<\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\cdots+\left(\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac{1}{n}\right)=1-\dfrac{1}{n}<1\).
Since \(x_{1}>1\), \(\dfrac{1}{x_{1}^{2}}<1\). The other terms are smaller, so the total is less than 1.

Since \(x_{i}\ge i+1\), \(\dfrac{1}{x_{i}^{2}}\ge\dfrac{1}{(i+1)^{2}}\). The sum of \(\dfrac{1}{(i+1)^{2}}\) telescopes to \(1-\dfrac{1}{n}\), which is less than 1, so the sum of \(\dfrac{1}{x_{i}^{2}}\) is also less than 1.

Since \(x_{i}\ge i+1\), \(\dfrac{1}{x_{i}^{2}}\le\dfrac{1}{(i+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{i(i+1)}\). The sum of \(\dfrac{1}{i(i+1)}\) from \(i=1\) to \(n-1\) equals \(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\), which is not less than 1.
questions.hint: Because the \(x_{i}\) are strictly increasing INTEGERS starting above 1, \(x_{1}\ge2\), \(x_{2}\ge3\), …, \(x_{i}\ge i+1\). Then bound each \(\dfrac1{x_{i}^{2}}\) using part (i) and the identity \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}=\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac1{k+1}\): the sum TELESCOPES.

steps.explain: Integers: \(x_{1}>1\Rightarrow x_{1}\ge2\). Each next term is at least 1 bigger (strictly increasing integers): \(x_{i}\ge i+1\).
Part (i) with \(k=i\): \(\dfrac{1}{(i+1)^{2}}<\dfrac{1}{i(i+1)}=\dfrac{1}{i}-\dfrac{1}{i+1}\).
Add for \(i=1,2,\dots,n-1\): all the middle terms cancel (telescoping).
\(1-\dfrac{1}{n}<1\) for \(n\ge2\), so the sum is less than 1.
Why not the others: B ignores that MANY terms add up (each is small but the sum needs a bound); C reverses the inequality direction; D mis-sums the telescoping series.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(x_i\ge i+1\); part (i); telescoping to \(1-\dfrac{1}{n}\).

questions.stem: The lengths of the sides of a right triangle are \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\), where \(c\) is the length of the hypotenuse. Prove the Pythagorean Inequality Theorem: \(a^{3}+b^{3}<c^{3}\). Which proof is correct?
options: By Pythagoras, \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\). The hypotenuse is the longest side, so \(a<c\) and \(b<c\). Then \(a^{3}+b^{3}=a\cdot a^{2}+b\cdot b^{2}<c\cdot a^{2}+c\cdot b^{2}=c\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)=c\cdot c^{2}=c^{3}\).
By Pythagoras, \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\). Cubing both sides gives \(a^{6}+b^{6}=c^{6}\), and \(a^{3}+b^{3}<c^{3}\) follows.
By Pythagoras, \(a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}\) (the same rule holds for cubes).
questions.hint: Start from Pythagoras \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\). Write \(a^{3}=a\cdot a^{2}\) and \(b^{3}=b\cdot b^{2}\), and replace the FACTORS \(a\) and \(b\) by the bigger \(c\) (the hypotenuse is the longest side). Then factor and use Pythagoras again.

steps.explain: Pythagoras and the longest side: \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\); \(c\) is the hypotenuse, so \(a<c\) and \(b<c\) (all lengths positive).
Split the cubes: \(a^{3}=a\cdot a^{2}\), \(b^{3}=b\cdot b^{2}\). Since \(a<c\) and \(a^{2}>0\): \(a\cdot a^{2}<c\cdot a^{2}\). Similarly for \(b\).
Factor out \(c\) and use Pythagoras.

Why not the others: B cubes incorrectly (\(\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)^{3}\ne a^{6}+b^{6}\)); C claims equality (false: e.g. \(3^{3}+4^{3}=91<125=5^{3}\)); D proves only the weaker \(a^{3}+b^{3}<2c^{3}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: In a proof by mathematical induction, which is the correct order of steps?
options: Inductive step → Base case → Conclusion
Base case → Inductive step → Conclusion
Conclusion → Base case → Inductive step
Base case → Conclusion → Inductive step
questions.solution: Mathematical induction: (1) Prove the base case, (2) Assume true for \(n = k\) (inductive hypothesis) and prove true for \(n = k+1\), (3) Conclude by induction.

steps.explain: Step 1 — Base case.
steps.work: Verify the statement is true for the initial value (usually \(n = 1\)).

steps.explain: Step 2 — Inductive step.
steps.work: Assume the statement is true for \(n = k\) (inductive hypothesis). Then prove it is true for \(n = k+1\).

steps.explain: Step 3 — Conclusion.
steps.work: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for all integers \(n \geq 1\).

keyPoints.text: In a proof by mathematical induction, which is the correct order of steps?
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information and connect it to the relevant mathematical method.

questions.stem: Prove by induction that \(1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\). In the inductive step, if the result holds for \(n = k\), what do we add to both sides?
questions.solution: Assume \(1+2+\cdots+k = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{2}\). Add \((k+1)\) to both sides to obtain the result for \(n = k+1\).

steps.explain: State the inductive hypothesis.
Add the next term \((k+1)\) to both sides.
Simplify to show the formula holds for \(n = k+1\).
This matches \(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\) with \(n = k+1\). \(\square\)

keyPoints.note: Identify the given information and connect it to the relevant mathematical method.

questions.stem: Prove by induction that if \(S_1=a\) and \(S_n-S_{n-1}=ar^{n-1}\), then \(S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\) for \(r\ne1\).
questions.hint: Verify n=1, then use the recurrence to add the next term to the assumed geometric sum.
questions.solution: Sample answer: The base case is true. Assume the formula holds for n. Then S_(n+1)=S_n+ar^n = a(1−r^n)/(1−r)+ar^n = a(1−r^(n+1))/(1−r). By induction it holds for all n≥1.

steps.explain: Check the base case n=1.
Assume the formula for n.
Use the given recurrence.
Simplify and conclude.
steps.work: Numerator \(=a(1-r^{n+1})\), proving the formula for n+1.

questions.stem: Let \(S_n=\sum_{p=1}^{n}\arctan\left(\frac{1}{2p^2}\right)\). Prove by induction that \(\tan S_n=\frac{n}{n+1}\).
questions.hint: For the induction step, use the tangent addition formula with the new term arctan(1/(2(n+1)²)).
questions.solution: Sample answer: Base case n=1 is immediate. Assume tan(S_n)=n/(n+1). The tangent addition formula gives tan(S_(n+1))=[n/(n+1)+1/(2(n+1)^2)]/[1−n/(2(n+1)^3)]=(n+1)/(n+2). Thus the claim follows by induction.

steps.explain: Check n=1.
Assume the result for n.
Add the next term.
Simplify.
steps.work: Multiply numerator and denominator to obtain \((n+1)/(n+2)\); hence induction completes.

questions.stem:
Mathematical induction is to be used to show \(n(2n-1)(2n+1)\) is divisible by \(3\ \forall\,n\in\mathbb{N}\).
The inductive step that requires proving is:
questions.hint: Substitute n = k + 1 into every factor, including inside 2n − 1 and 2n + 1.

steps.explain: In the inductive step we assume the statement for \(n=k\) and must prove it for \(n=k+1\). So replace every \(n\) by \(k+1\).

questions.stem:
Suppose that \(a_n\ (n\ge1)\) is a sequence defined by:

\(a_1=1,\quad a_2=3\) and \(a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}\ \ \forall\,k\ge3.\)

Prove that \(\forall\,n\ge1\), we have \(a_n\le\left(\frac74\right)^n\).
questions.hint: Check n = 1 and n = 2, assume true for all n ≤ k, then use a_{k+1} = a_k + a_{k−1}.

steps.explain: Each term depends on the two previous terms, so use strong induction with two base cases.
Inductive hypothesis: assume the result holds for every \(n\le k\), where \(k\ge2\). In particular,
Use the recurrence for \(a_{k+1}\), then factor out \(\left(\frac74\right)^{k-1}\).
Compare with \(\left(\frac74\right)^2=\frac{49}{16}\). Write \(\frac{11}{4}=\frac{44}{16} \lt \frac{49}{16}\).
So the result for \(n\le k\) implies it for \(n=k+1\). With the base cases, it holds for all \(n\ge1\) by mathematical induction.

meta.source: Abbotsleigh 2021 4U Trials & Solutions

questions.answer: Strong induction. Base cases: \(a_1=1\le\frac74\) and \(a_2=3\le\frac{49}{16}=3\tfrac1{16}\). Inductive step: assume \(a_n\le\left(\frac74\right)^n\) for all \(n\le k\) (\(k\ge2\)). Then \(a_{k+1}=a_k+a_{k-1}\le\left(\frac74\right)^k+\left(\frac74\right)^{k-1}=\left(\frac74\right)^{k-1}\cdot\frac{11}{4}=\left(\frac74\right)^{k-1}\cdot\frac{44}{16} \lt \left(\frac74\right)^{k-1}\cdot\frac{49}{16}=\left(\frac74\right)^{k+1}\). Hence the result is true for all \(n\ge1\) by induction.

keyPoints.note: Use strong induction: two base cases, then a_{k+1} = a_k + a_{k−1} ≤ (7/4)^{k−1}(11/4) < (7/4)^{k+1}.

questions.stem:
Consider the proposition:

\(P(n):\ \sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k-1)=n^2\)

Which of the following is true for \(P(k+1)\)?
questions.hint: P(k+1) = (sum of first k terms) + (the (k+1)th term).

steps.explain: \(P(k+1)\) is the statement with \(n=k+1\): the sum of the first \(k+1\) terms equals \((k+1)^2\).
Split off the last term: the first \(k\) terms plus the \((k+1)\)th term.
The last term simplifies to \(2k+1\), giving option D.
B and C add \(2k\) or \(2(k+1)\) instead of the actual next term; A drops the first \(k-1\) terms.

questions.stem:
Prove by mathematical induction that \(\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N}\) and odd \(n\):

\(\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}k^3=\frac{(2n-1)(n+1)^2}{4}\)

[Hint: the identity below might be useful:
\(2k^3+15k^2+36k+27=(2k+3)(k+3)^2\).]
questions.hint: Base case n = 1; the next odd case after k is k + 2, which adds −(k+1)³ + (k+2)³.

steps.explain: Base case \(n=1\).
Assume true for some odd \(k\). Because the result is only for odd \(n\), the next case is \(n=k+2\), which adds two terms: \(-(k+1)^3\) (even index) and \(+(k+2)^3\) (odd index).
Target for \(n=k+2\): the RHS becomes
Start from the LHS and use the assumption.
Simplify the bracket and expand.
Use the hint, then conclude by induction.

questions.answer: Step 1 (n = 1): LHS = 1, RHS = (1)(2)²/4 = 1. Step 2: assume true for some odd k: \(1^3-2^3+\dots+k^3=\frac{(2k-1)(k+1)^2}{4}\). Step 3 (next odd number k + 2): LHS \(=\frac{(2k-1)(k+1)^2}{4}-(k+1)^3+(k+2)^3=\frac{(k+1)^2(2k-1-4k-4)+4(k+2)^3}{4}=\frac{-(k+1)^2(2k+5)+4(k^3+6k^2+12k+8)}{4}=\frac{2k^3+15k^2+36k+27}{4}=\frac{(2k+3)(k+3)^2}{4}\), which is the RHS with n = k + 2. Hence true for all odd n by induction.

keyPoints.note: Only odd n: step from k to k + 2, adding the two terms −(k + 1)³ and +(k + 2)³.

questions.stem: Given that \(u_1=1\) and \(u_{n+1}=2u_n+(-1)^{n+1}\), prove that \(u_n=\frac13\left(2^{n+1}+(-1)^n\right)\), where \(n\in\mathbb{Z}^+\), by mathematical induction.

steps.explain: Base case \(n=1\).
Assume true for \(n=k\).
Use the recurrence for \(u_{k+1}\) and substitute.
Write \((-1)^{k+1}=-(-1)^k\) and put everything over 3.
Since \(-(-1)^k=(-1)^{k+1}\), this is the formula for \(n=k+1\). By induction it is true for all \(n\in\mathbb Z^+\).

questions.stem: Given that the product of \(n\) consecutive numbers is divisible by \(n!\), use mathematical induction to prove that \(n^5-n\) is divisible by 2, 3 and 5 for integers \(n\ge2\).
questions.hint: Divisible by 2, 3, 5 means divisible by 30. In the step, create products of consecutive numbers.

steps.explain: 2, 3 and 5 are distinct primes, so it is enough to prove divisibility by \(2\times3\times5=30\). Base case \(n=2\).
Assume \(k^5-k=30l\) for some integer \(l\). Expand \((k+1)^5-(k+1)\).
Use the assumption and factor.
Write \(k^2+k+1=(k-1)(k+2)+3\) to create consecutive numbers.

\((k-1)k(k+1)(k+2)\) is a product of 4 consecutive numbers, so divisible by \(4!=24\), hence by 6; times 5 gives a multiple of 30. Also \(k(k+1)\) is a product of 2 consecutive numbers, divisible by \(2!=2\), so \(15k(k+1)\) is a multiple of 30.
So \((k+1)^5-(k+1)=30(l+p+q)\), and the result follows by induction.

meta.source: Barker 2025 4U Trials & Solutions

questions.answer: Divisible by 2, 3 and 5 ⇔ divisible by 30. n = 2: 32 − 2 = 30 ✓. Assume \(k^5-k=30l\). Then \((k+1)^5-(k+1)=k^5+5k^4+10k^3+10k^2+4k=30l+5k(k^3+2k^2+2k+1)=30l+5k(k+1)(k^2+k+1)\). Write \(k^2+k+1=(k-1)(k+2)+3\): \(5k(k+1)(k-1)(k+2)+15k(k+1)\). The first is 5 × (product of 4 consecutive numbers ⇒ divisible by 4! = 24 ⇒ by 6) ⇒ divisible by 30; the second: k(k+1) is even ⇒ 15k(k+1) divisible by 30. So the sum is divisible by 30. True by induction.

keyPoints.note: Prove divisibility by 30. Rewrite k² + k + 1 = (k − 1)(k + 2) + 3 to get 4 consecutive numbers.

questions.stem:
The real numbers \(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\) are all positive. For each positive \(n\), \(A_n\) and \(G_n\) are defined by
\(A_n=\frac{a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n}{n}\) and \(G_n=(a_1a_2\dots a_n)^{\frac{1}{n}}\)

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.hint: Reduce the difference to a_{k+1} + kG_k − (k+1)G_{k+1}, factor out G_k and write everything with λ_k.

steps.explain: Simplify the difference using \((k+1)A_{k+1}=a_1+\dots+a_{k+1}\) and \(kA_k=a_1+\dots+a_k\).
Factor out \(G_k\gt 0\).
Express both ratios with \(\lambda_k\). Using \(G_{k+1}^{k+1}=G_k^k\,a_{k+1}\):
So the difference is \(G_k\left[\lambda_k^{k+1}-(k+1)\lambda_k+k\right]\), which is \(\ge0\) under the given condition.

meta.source: Baulkham Hills 2020 4U Trials & Solutions

parts.answer: \((k+1)(A_{k+1}-G_{k+1})-k(A_k-G_k)=a_{k+1}+kG_k-(k+1)G_{k+1}=G_k\left[\frac{a_{k+1}}{G_k}+k-(k+1)\frac{G_{k+1}}{G_k}\right]\). Now \(\frac{a_{k+1}}{G_k}=\lambda_k^{k+1}\) and \(\frac{G_{k+1}}{G_k}=\frac{(a_1\cdots a_{k+1})^{\frac{1}{k+1}}}{(a_1\cdots a_k)^{\frac{1}{k}}}=\left(\frac{a_{k+1}}{G_k}\right)^{\frac{1}{k+1}}=\lambda_k\). So the difference is \(G_k[\lambda_k^{k+1}-(k+1)\lambda_k+k]\ge0\) since \(G_k > 0\).

parts.answer: Base case \(n = 1\): \(A_1 = a_1 = G_1\). Assume true for \(n = k\): \(A_k \ge G_k\). By (ii) with \(x = \lambda_k > 0\), we have \(\lambda_k^{k+1} - (k+1)\lambda_k + k = f(\lambda_k) \ge 0\). Thus by (i), \((k+1)(A_{k+1} - G_{k+1}) \ge k(A_k - G_k) \ge 0\), which gives \(A_{k+1} \ge G_{k+1}\). Therefore \(A_n \ge G_n\) holds for all positive integers \(n\) by mathematical induction.

questions.stem:
Prove using mathematical induction for integers \(n\ge2\),

\(n^{n+1}\gt n(n+1)^{n-1}\)
questions.hint: Rewrite the assumption as (k+1)^(k−1)/k^k < 1 and use it to bound (k+1)^(k+1)/(k+2)^k from below.

steps.explain: Base case \(n=2\).
Assume true for \(n=k\ge2\). Divide both sides by \(k\gt0\).
Goal for \(n=k+1\): \((k+1)^{k+2}\gt(k+1)(k+2)^k\). Divide by \(k+1\): we need
Multiply the goal's left side by \(\frac{(k+1)^{k-1}}{k^k}\), which is less than 1 — this makes it SMALLER. So if the smaller quantity is above 1, the original is too.
Simplify using \((k+1)^2=k^2+2k+1\) and \(k(k+2)=k^2+2k\).
So \(\frac{(k+1)^{k+1}}{(k+2)^k}\gt1\), which is the statement for \(n=k+1\). By induction it holds for all integers \(n\ge2\).

questions.stem:
The following induction proof, which aims to show that \(5^n+2\times11^n\) is a multiple of 3 for all positive integers \(n\), contains an algebraic error.

Step 1. When \(n=1\): \(5^1+2\times11^1=27=3\times9\), so the statement is true for \(n=1\).
Step 2. Assume the statement is true for \(n=k\): \(5^k+2\times11^k=3M\) for some integer \(M\).
Step 3. When \(n=k+1\): \(5^{k+1}+2\times11^{k+1}=5\left(5^k+2\times11^k\right)+12\times11^k\)
Step 4. \(=5(3M)+3\left(4\times11^k\right)=3\left(5+4\times11^k\right)\), which is a multiple of 3.

In which step does the error occur?
options: Step 1, showing the statement is true for \(n=1\)
Step 2, the assumption for \(n=k\)
Step 3, rewriting \(5^{k+1}+2\times11^{k+1}\)
Step 4, factorising \(5(3M)+3\left(4\times11^k\right)\)
questions.hint: Check that each line follows from the one before it. Look for a factor that was taken out incorrectly.

steps.explain: Check Step 1 by substituting \(n=1\).
Check Step 2. Writing a multiple of 3 as \(3M\) with \(M\) an integer is a valid assumption.
Check Step 3 by expanding the right-hand side.
Check Step 4. Substituting the assumption gives \(5(3M)+3\left(4\times11^k\right)\), which is correct. Now take out the common factor 3.
The proof wrote \(3\left(5+4\times11^k\right)\), dropping the \(M\). The error is in Step 4.

keyPoints.note: Check that each factor is taken out correctly.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that \(\dfrac{d^ny}{dx^n}=2^{\frac n2}e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right)\) for all positive integers \(n\), where \(y=e^x\sin x\).
questions.answer: Base case n = 1 uses the identity from part (i). Assume true for n = k and differentiate once to get n = k+1, using \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac\pi4\right)\).
questions.hint: Prove the base case first, then assume the result for n = k and differentiate once.

steps.explain: Base case \(n=1\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)=\sqrt2e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), which matches the formula with \(n=1\).
Inductive hypothesis: assume \(\dfrac{d^ky}{dx^k}=2^{\frac{k}{2}}e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{k\pi}{4}\right)\).
Differentiate once: product rule gives \(2^{\frac{k}{2}}e^x\left[\sin\left(x+\dfrac{k\pi}{4}\right)+\cos\left(x+\dfrac{k\pi}{4}\right)\right]\).

Use the identity from part (i): \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac\pi4\right)\). So the derivative is \(2^{\frac{k}{2}}\sqrt2\,e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{(k+1)\pi}{4}\right)=2^{\frac{k+1}{2}}e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{(k+1)\pi}{4}\right)\). Proof complete by induction.

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: Hence, show that \(2^4\times\dfrac{d^ky}{dx^k}=\dfrac{d^{k+8}y}{dx^{k+8}}\), where \(k\) is a positive integer.
questions.answer: Use the formula from part (ii) for \(n=k\) and \(n=k+8\). The phase differs by \(2\pi\) and \(2^{\frac{k+8}{2}}=2^4\cdot2^{\frac{k}{2}}\).
questions.hint: Write both derivatives using the formula, then compare the powers of 2 and the angles.

steps.explain: From part (ii): \(\dfrac{d^ky}{dx^k}=2^{\frac{k}{2}}e^x\sin\left(x+\dfrac{k\pi}{4}\right)\) and \(\dfrac{d^{k+8}y}{dx^{k+8}}=2^{\frac{k+8}{2}}e^x\sin\left(x+(k+8)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\).
Angle: \((k+8)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{k\pi}{4}+2\pi\), and \(\sin\) has period \(2\pi\), so the sine terms are equal.
Power of 2: \(2^{\frac{k+8}{2}}=2^4\cdot2^{\frac{k}{2}}\). So \(\dfrac{d^{k+8}y}{dx^{k+8}}=2^4\dfrac{d^ky}{dx^k}\). Shown.

meta.source: Cheltenham Girls High School 2023 HSC Trial Assessment Task 4 (Mathematics Extension 2)

questions.stem: Prove by induction that \(3^{n}\ge n^{2}\) for all positive integers \(n\ge1\). In the inductive step, assuming \(3^{k}\ge k^{2}\), \(3^{k+1}\ge 3k^{2}\), and which condition on \(k\) makes \(3k^{2}\ge(k+1)^{2}\) true?
options: \(k\ge3\) only
\(k\ge2\) (so check \(n=1\) and \(n=2\) directly)
All \(k\ge1\)
questions.hint: Solve \(3k^{2}\ge(k+1)^{2}\), i.e. \(2k^{2}-2k-1\ge0\), and see which integers \(k\) satisfy it. Check small cases separately.

steps.explain: Step 1: show it is true for \(n=1\).
Step 2: assume true for \(n=k\), \(k\ge1\): \(3^{k}\ge k^{2}\).
Step 3: prove it for \(n=k+1\). Multiply the assumption by 3.

Solve \(2k^{2}-2k-1=0\): \(k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{3}}{2}\approx1.37\) or \(-0.37\). The parabola is \(\ge0\) for \(k\ge\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}\approx1.37\), so for all INTEGERS \(k\ge2\). (For \(k=1\): \(3\ge4\) is false, so \(n=2\) must be checked separately: \(9\ge4\).)
So the statement is true for \(n=1\) and \(n=2\), and if it is true for \(n=k\) (\(k\ge2\)) it is true for \(n=k+1\). By induction it is true for all \(n\ge1\).
So the correct choice is option C.

keyPoints.note: Find when 3 k squared is at least (k + 1) squared; small k need a direct check.

questions.stem: Let \(a_{n}\) be the sequence defined recursively by \(a_{0}=0\) and \(a_{n}=a_{n-1}+3n^{2}\) for all \(n\ge1\). Use mathematical induction to prove that for all integers \(n\ge0\), \(a_{n}=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{2}\). Which proof is correct?
options: Base case \(n=0\): \(a_{0}=0\) and \(\dfrac{0(1)(1)}{2}=0\) ✓. Assume true for \(n=k\): \(a_{k}=\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{2}\). For \(n=k+1\): \(a_{k+1}=a_{k}+3(k+1)^{2}=\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{2}+3(k+1)^{2}=\dfrac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\right]}{2}=\dfrac{(k+1)(2k^{2}+7k+6)}{2}=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{2}\), which is the formula for \(n=k+1\). True for \(n=0\) and \(k\Rightarrow k+1\), so true for all \(n\ge0\) by induction.
Base case \(n=1\): \(a_{1}=0+3=3\) and \(\dfrac{1(2)(3)}{2}=3\) ✓. The inductive step is the same as for the other proof. Hence true for all \(n\ge1\) by induction.

Base case \(n=0\) ✓. Assume true for \(n=k\). For \(n=k+1\): \(a_{k+1}=\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{2}+3(k+1)^{2}=\dfrac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\right]}{2}=\dfrac{(k+1)(2k^{2}+7k+6)}{2}\). This is the same as the formula for \(n=k+1\), so it is true.

Base case \(n=0\) ✓. Assume true for \(n=k+1\): \(a_{k+1}=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{2}\). Then \(a_{k}=a_{k+1}-3(k+1)^{2}=\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{2}\), which is the formula for \(n=k\). So true for all \(n\).
questions.hint: Four parts: (1) BASE CASE \(n=0\) (the statement is for \(n\ge0\)); (2) ASSUME true for \(n=k\); (3) PROVE for \(n=k+1\) using the recursion \(a_{k+1}=a_{k}+3(k+1)^{2}\), factorising \((k+1)\); (4) CONCLUDE.

steps.explain: Base case. The claim is for ALL \(n\ge0\), so the base case is \(n=0\), not \(n=1\).
Inductive hypothesis: assume the formula is true for \(n=k\) (some integer \(k\ge0\)).
Goal: show \(a_{k+1}=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{2}\). Start from the recursive definition and use the hypothesis for \(a_{k}\).
Take out the common factor \((k+1)\) and put over a common denominator (\(3(k+1)^{2}=\dfrac{6(k+1)^{2}}{2}\)).
This is the formula with \(n=k+1\). Conclusion: true for \(n=0\), and if true for \(k\) then true for \(k+1\), so by mathematical induction true for all integers \(n\ge0\).
Why not the others: B uses the wrong base case (\(n=0\) is part of the claim); C never writes the final factorisation, so the result is not shown to match; D assumes the \(k+1\) case (circular).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction, for \(z\ne1\), that \(1+2z+3z^{2}+\cdots+nz^{n-1}=\dfrac{1-(n+1)z^{n}+nz^{n+1}}{(1-z)^{2}}\). Which proof is correct?
options: \(n=0\): LHS \(=0\) and RHS \(=\dfrac{1-z^{0}+0}{(1-z)^{2}}=0\) ✓. The inductive step as in the other proof. True for all \(n\ge0\).

\(n=1\) ✓. Assume true for \(n=k\). For \(n=k+1\): LHS \(=\dfrac{1-(k+1)z^{k}+kz^{k+1}}{(1-z)^{2}}+(k+1)z^{k}=\dfrac{1-(k+1)z^{k}+kz^{k+1}+(k+1)z^{k}(1-z)^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}}\). This is the required result.
\(n=1\) ✓. Assume true for \(n=k+1\): \(1+2z+\cdots+(k+1)z^{k}=\dfrac{1-(k+2)z^{k+1}+(k+1)z^{k+2}}{(1-z)^{2}}\). Remove the last term to get the case \(n=k\). So true for all \(n\).
questions.hint: Base case \(n=1\) (the sum starts at 1 term). Assume for \(n=k\); for \(n=k+1\) ADD the next term \((k+1)z^{k}\) to the left side, put everything over \((1-z)^{2}\), expand \((1-z)^{2}=1-2z+z^{2}\), and simplify to the required form.

steps.explain: Base case \(n=1\) (not \(n=0\)): LHS is the single term 1. RHS: \(\dfrac{1-2z+z^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}}\).
Assume true for \(n=k\).
For \(n=k+1\) add the next term \((k+1)z^{k}\) to the LHS and use \((\ast)\).
Common denominator \((1-z)^{2}\): multiply the extra term by \((1-z)^{2}=1-2z+z^{2}\).
Expand the last product and cancel the \(\pm(k+1)z^{k}\) terms.

Conclusion: true for \(n=1\) and \(k\Rightarrow k+1\), so true for all integers \(n\ge1\) by mathematical induction. Why not the others: B uses the wrong base case; C stops before simplifying; D assumes the \(k+1\) case.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Base n = 1, add the next term to the hypothesis, common denominator, expand and collect.

questions.stem: Hence, or otherwise, prove that \(2+\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{4}{2^{2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{n}{2^{n-2}}=6-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-2}}\). Which working is correct?
options: Put \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(S=1+\dfrac{2}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2^{2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{n}{2^{n-1}}=4\left[1-\dfrac{n+1}{2^{n}}+\dfrac{n}{2^{n+1}}\right]=4-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\). Remove the first term and double: \(2(S-1)=2\left(3-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\right)=6-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-2}}\).
Put \(z=2\): \(1+4+12+\cdots\) does not give the series, so the formula cannot be used.
Put \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(S=4-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\), and this is the required series, so \(2+\dfrac{3}{2}+\cdots+\dfrac{n}{2^{n-2}}=4-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\).
Put \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(S=4-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\). Remove the first term: \(S-1=3-\dfrac{n+2}{2^{n-1}}\), which is the required series.
questions.hint: Use the formula from (i) with \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\) to get \(S=1+\dfrac{2}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2^{2}}+\cdots\). The target series is NOT \(S\): it starts at the second term of \(S\) and every term is doubled.

steps.explain: Substitute \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\) into the left side of (i).
Right side with \(z=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \((1-z)^{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}\), so dividing by it multiplies by 4.
Common denominator \(2^{n+1}\): \(\dfrac{4(n+1)}{2^{n}}=\dfrac{8(n+1)}{2^{n+1}}\).

The target series starts at \(\dfrac{2}{2^{0}}\) which is the SECOND term of \(S\) doubled: each term \(\dfrac{k}{2^{k-2}}=2\cdot\dfrac{k}{2^{k-1}}\). So remove the first term (1) from \(S\) and double.
Compute.

Check \(n=2\): LHS \(=2\); RHS \(=6-\dfrac{4}{1}=2\) ✓. \(n=3\): LHS \(=2+\dfrac{3}{2}=3.5\); RHS \(=6-\dfrac{5}{2}=3.5\) ✓. Option C forgets to remove the first term and double; option D forgets to double.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Put z = 1/2 in the sum formula, then remove the first term and double.

questions.stem: Using the result in the previous part (\(k^{2}+k\) is always even), prove, by mathematical induction, that for all positive integral values of \(n\), \(n^{3}+5n\) is divisible by 6. Which proof is correct?
options: \(n=1\): \(1+5=6\), divisible by 6. Assume \(k^{3}+5k=6p\). Then \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)=k^{3}+5k+3k^{2}+3k+6=6p+6+3(k^{2}+k)=6p+6+3(2y)=6(p+y+1)\), using that \(k^{2}+k=2y\). So true for \(n=k+1\); by induction true for all \(n\ge1\).
Assume \(k^{3}+5k=6p\). Then \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)=6p+6+3(k^{2}+k)\), which is divisible by 6. By induction true for all \(n\).
\(n=1\): \(1+5=6\). Assume true for \(n=k+1\), then show it is true for \(n=k\).
\(n=1\): \(1+5=6\). Assume \(k^{3}+5k=6p\). Then \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)=6p+6+3(k^{2}+k)\), and \(3(k^{2}+k)\) is divisible by 6 because 3 is divisible by 3. So true for all \(n\).
questions.hint: Induction needs 3 parts: (1) BASE CASE \(n=1\); (2) ASSUMPTION for \(n=k\): \(k^{3}+5k=6p\); (3) STEP: expand \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)\), group the part equal to \(6p\), and show the rest is also a multiple of 6 (use \(k^{2}+k\) even).

steps.explain: BASE CASE: test \(n=1\).
ASSUMPTION: assume the result is true for \(n=k\), where \(k\) is a positive integer: \(k^{3}+5k=6p\) for some integer \(p\).
Group the terms into \(k^{3}+5k\) (which is \(6p\)) and the rest.
By the previous part \(k^{2}+k=2y\) for some integer \(y\), so \(3(k^{2}+k)=6y\).

This is a multiple of 6, so the result is true for \(n=k+1\). True for \(n=1\), and true for \(n=k\Rightarrow\) true for \(n=k+1\), so by induction \(n^{3}+5n\) is divisible by 6 for all positive integers \(n\).

Why not the others: B has no base case and does not use the previous part to justify \(3(k^{2}+k)\); C assumes the wrong direction (\(k+1\Rightarrow k\)); D gives a false reason (3 being divisible by 3 does not make \(3(k^{2}+k)\) divisible by 6).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Base case, assumption, step; use k² + k even.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that for \(n\ge1\): \(1\cdot\ln\dfrac{2}{1}+2\cdot\ln\dfrac{3}{2}+\cdots+n\cdot\ln\left(\dfrac{n+1}{n}\right)=\ln\left(\dfrac{(n+1)^{n}}{n!}\right)\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&n=1:\ \text{LHS}=\ln2=\text{RHS}.\quad\text{Assume }S_{k}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}\\ &S_{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}+(k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}=\ln\left[\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}\cdot\dfrac{(k+2)^{k+1}}{(k+1)^{k+1}}\right]=\ln\dfrac{(k+2)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&n=1:\ \text{LHS}=\ln2=\text{RHS}.\quad\text{Assume }S_{k}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}\\ &S_{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}+\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k-1}(k+2)}{k!}\ne\ln\dfrac{(k+2)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&n=1:\ \text{LHS}=\ln2=\text{RHS}.\quad\text{Assume }S_{k}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}\\ &S_{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}+(k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}(k+2)^{k+1}}{k!\,(k+1)^{k}}=\ln\dfrac{(k+2)^{k+1}}{k!}\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}&n=1:\ \text{LHS}=\ln1=0\ne\ln2\ \text{so the statement is false}\\ &\text{(base case fails)}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Three steps: (1) TEST \(n=1\); (2) ASSUME it is true for \(n=k\); (3) PROVE it for \(n=k+1\) by adding the NEXT term \((k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}\) to the assumed sum. Use \(a\ln b=\ln b^{a}\) and \(\ln A+\ln B=\ln AB\).

steps.explain: Base case \(n=1\): LHS \(=1\cdot\ln\dfrac{2}{1}=\ln2\). RHS \(=\ln\dfrac{2^{1}}{1!}=\ln2\). Equal ✓.
Assume \(P(k)\): the sum of the first \(k\) terms is \(\ln\dfrac{(k+1)^{k}}{k!}\).
To prove \(P(k+1)\) we must show \(S_{k+1}=\ln\dfrac{(k+2)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\). The extra term (the \((k+1)\)th) is \((k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}\).
Substitute the assumption and move the multiplier into the log: \((k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}=\ln\left(\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}\right)^{k+1}\).
Add the logs by MULTIPLYING the arguments; then cancel \((k+1)^{k}\) with \((k+1)^{k+1}\) (leaving \(\dfrac{1}{k+1}\)) and use \(k!\,(k+1)=(k+1)!\).
This is \(P(k+1)\). So \(P(1)\) is true and \(P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\), so by mathematical induction \(P(n)\) holds for all \(n\ge1\). ∎

Why not the others: B drops the multiplier \((k+1)\) on the new term; C cancels \((k+1)^{k}\) instead of \((k+1)^{k+1}\), leaving \(k!\) instead of \((k+1)!\); D wrongly evaluates \(\ln\dfrac{2}{1}\) as \(\ln1\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Base \(n=1\); assume \(S_k\); add \((k+1)\ln\dfrac{k+2}{k+1}\).

questions.stem: Given \(a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2a_{n}}\) and \(a_{1}=1\), prove by mathematical induction that for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(a_{n}=2^{\left(1-2^{(1-n)}\right)}\).
options: \(\begin{aligned}&n=1:\ 2^{1-2^{1}}=2^{-1}\ne1\\ &\text{(the base case fails)}\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Base case \(n=1\). Assume \(P(k)\): \(a_{k}=2^{1-2^{1-k}}\). Prove \(P(k+1)\): \(a_{k+1}=2^{1-2^{-k}}\) by substituting \(a_{k}\) into \(a_{k+1}=\sqrt{2a_{k}}\) and using index laws (\(\sqrt{2^{m}}=2^{\frac{m}{2}}\)).

steps.explain: Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some \(k\ge1\).
Use the recurrence and the assumption: \(a_{k+1}=\sqrt{2a_{k}}=\sqrt{2\times2^{1-2^{1-k}}}\). Multiply powers of 2 by ADDING indices: \(2^{1}\times2^{1-2^{1-k}}=2^{2-2^{1-k}}\).
A square root halves the index: \(\dfrac{2-2^{1-k}}{2}=1-\dfrac{2^{1-k}}{2}=1-2^{1-k-1}=1-2^{-k}\).
This is \(P(k+1)\). \(P(1)\) is true and \(P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\), so \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n\ge1\) by mathematical induction. ∎
Why not the others: B forgets to halve the index (it drops the square root); C only square-roots one factor; D evaluates the base case incorrectly (\(2^{1-1}=2^{0}\), not \(2^{1}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Base \(n=1\); sub \(a_{k}\) into \(\sqrt{2a_{k}}\); halve the index.

questions.stem: Prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}r2^{r}=(n-1)\left(2^{n+1}\right)+2\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: Assume the result for \(n=k\); then the result for \(n=k+1\) is \(k\cdot2^{k+1}+2\)
Check \(n=1,2,3\): all true, so the result is proved
\(\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}r2^{r}=(k+1)2^{k+1}\) by the pattern
questions.hint: MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION: (1) Prove true for \(n=1\). (2) ASSUME true for \(n=k\). (3) Prove true for \(n=k+1\): write the sum to \(k+1\) as (the sum to \(k\)) \(+\) (the \((k+1)\)th term), use the assumption, and simplify to the SAME form with \(n=k+1\): \(k\cdot2^{k+2}+2\).

steps.explain: Step 2: assume \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k}r2^{r}=(k-1)2^{k+1}+2\).
Step 3: the sum to \(k+1\) equals the sum to \(k\) plus the next term \((k+1)2^{k+1}\); use the assumption.

So true for \(n=k+1\) whenever true for \(n=k\); with \(n=1\) true, true for all positive integers \(n\) by induction. Why not the others: B states the result without proving it; C checks examples only; D is a guess.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Induction: add the \((k+1)\)th term to the assumed sum.

questions.stem: Use mathematical induction to prove that for all integers \(n\ge2\), \(\dfrac1{1^{2}}+\dfrac1{2^{2}}+\dfrac1{3^{2}}+\cdots+\dfrac1{n^{2}}<2-\dfrac{1}{n}\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: Assume \(\sum_{r=1}^{k}\dfrac1{r^{2}}<2-\dfrac{1}{k}\). Then \(\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}<2-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}<2-\dfrac1{k+1}\) by part (i), since \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{k+1}<0\)
Assume true for \(n=k\); then true for \(n=k+1\) because \(k+1>k\)
Add \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\) to both sides: \(2-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}>2-\dfrac1{k+1}\)
Check \(n=2,3,4\): all true, so true for all \(n\)
questions.hint: INDUCTION with an inequality: (1) base case \(n=2\); (2) assume \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k}\dfrac1{r^{2}}<2-\dfrac{1}{k}\); (3) ADD the next term \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\) to BOTH sides and use part (i) to show the new right side is LESS than \(2-\dfrac1{k+1}\).

steps.explain: Assume \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k}\dfrac1{r^{2}}<2-\dfrac{1}{k}\) for some \(k\ge2\). Add \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\) to both sides.
Part (i): \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{k+1}<0\), i.e. \(-\dfrac{1}{k}+\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}<-\dfrac1{k+1}\). Add 2 to both sides.
Chain the inequalities: \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}\dfrac1{r^{2}}<2-\dfrac1{k+1}\): true for \(n=k+1\). By induction, true for all \(n\ge2\). ∎
Why not the others: B gives no calculation; C reverses the inequality; D checks examples only.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Add \(\dfrac1{(k+1)^2}\); use (i).

questions.stem: Prove by the method of mathematical induction that for any positive integer \(n>0\), \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{n})=nx^{n-1}\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: Assume \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k})=kx^{k-1}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k+1})=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cdot x^{k})=1\cdot x^{k}+x\cdot kx^{k-1}=x^{k}+kx^{k}=(k+1)x^{k}\) (product rule)
Assume \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k})=kx^{k-1}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k+1})=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x)\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k})=kx^{k-1}\)
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k+1})=(k+1)x^{k}\) because the pattern holds for \(n=1,2,3\)
Assume \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k+1})=(k+1)x^{k}\) and show it for \(n=k\)
questions.hint: INDUCTION: (1) true for \(n=1\); (2) assume true for \(n=k\); (3) prove for \(n=k+1\). Here the trick is to write \(x^{k+1}=x\cdot x^{k}\) and use the PRODUCT rule \((uv)'=u'v+uv'\) together with the assumption for \(\dfrac{d}{dx}x^{k}\).

steps.explain: Step 2: assume \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{k})=kx^{k-1}\) for some \(k\ge1\).
Step 3: write \(x^{k+1}=x\cdot x^{k}\) and use the product rule with \(u=x\) (\(u'=1\)), \(v=x^{k}\) (\(v'=kx^{k-1}\) by the assumption).
Simplify: \(x\cdot x^{k-1}=x^{k}\), so \(kx^{k}\). Add \(x^{k}+kx^{k}=(k+1)x^{k}\).

This is the result with \(n=k+1\). True for \(n=1\) and true for \(k+1\) whenever true for \(k\): true for all positive integers \(n\). ∎ Why not the others: B misuses the product rule (it is NOT the product of derivatives); C is not a proof; D assumes what is to be proved.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(x^{k+1}=x\cdot x^k\); product rule.

questions.stem: Using the result \(k^{2}+k=2m\) (\(m\) an integer) from part (i), prove by mathematical induction that for all positive integers \(n\), \(n^{3}+5n\) is divisible by 6. In the inductive step, assuming \(k^{3}+5k=6p\), the expression \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)\) equals:
questions.hint: Expand \((k+1)^{3}+5(k+1)\), spot the group \(k^{3}+5k\) (use the assumption \(=6p\)) and the group \(3k^{2}+3k=3\left(k^{2}+k\right)\) (use part (i)). Then collect everything as 6 times something.

steps.explain: ASSUMPTION: for some positive integer \(k\), \(k^{3}+5k=6p\) with \(p\) an integer.
Regroup: pull out \(k^{3}+5k\) and combine the constants \(1+5=6\).
Substitute the assumption \(k^{3}+5k=6p\) and part (i) \(k^{2}+k=2m\).
Factor out 6: the result is 6 times an integer.
CONCLUSION: true for \(n=1\), and if true for \(n=k\) then true for \(n=k+1\). By induction \(n^{3}+5n\) is divisible by 6 for all positive integers \(n\).
Why not the others: B treats \(3(2m)\) as \(12m\); C forgets the \(+6\) constant; D treats \(3(2m)\) as \(18m\).
So the correct choice is option A.
