questions.stem: Prove that \(33^{n}-16^{n}-28^{n}+11^{n}\) is divisible by 85 for all positive integers \(n\ge2\). Which argument proves it?
options: Use \(a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+\cdots+b^{n-1}\right)\). Pair \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): each bracket has a factor \(33-16=17=28-11\), so the whole expression is divisible by 17. Pair \(\left(33^{n}-28^{n}\right)-\left(16^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): each has a factor \(33-28=5=16-11\), so divisible by 5. Since \(85=5\times17\) with 5 and 17 coprime, it is divisible by 85.

Use \(a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+\cdots+b^{n-1}\right)\). Pair \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): divisible by 17. Pair \(\left(33^{n}-28^{n}\right)-\left(16^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): divisible by 5. Since \(5+17=22\), the expression is divisible by 22.
Test \(n=2\): \(33^{2}-16^{2}-28^{2}+11^{2}=170=85\times2\). Since it works for \(n=2\), it is divisible by 85 for all \(n\ge2\).
Use \(a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+\cdots+b^{n-1}\right)\). Pair \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): divisible by 17 and also by 5, so it is divisible by \(17+5=85\).
questions.hint: \(85=5\times17\) and 5, 17 are coprime. Show the expression is divisible by 17 and by 5 SEPARATELY using \(a^{n}-b^{n}\) which always has the factor \((a-b)\). Choose the pairing so the differences are 17 (for 17) and 5 (for 5).

steps.explain: Factor fact: for \(n\ge2\), \(a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2}b+\cdots+b^{n-1}\right)\), so \(a^{n}-b^{n}\) is always divisible by \((a-b)\).
Pairing for 17: \(33-16=17\) and \(28-11=17\). Group as \(\left(33^{n}-16^{n}\right)-\left(28^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): the first bracket has factor 17, the second also has factor 17.
Pairing for 5: \(33-28=5\) and \(16-11=5\). Group as \(\left(33^{n}-28^{n}\right)-\left(16^{n}-11^{n}\right)\): both brackets have factor 5.
So \(E=33^{n}-16^{n}-28^{n}+11^{n}\) is divisible by 17 AND by 5.
5 and 17 are PRIME (so they share no common factor), therefore \(E\) is divisible by their product \(5\times17=85\).

Why not the others: C only tests one value, which is not a proof; B adds the divisors (divisible by 17 and 5 means divisible by their PRODUCT, not the sum); D claims divisible by \(17+5\), not by \(17\times5\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(85=5\times17\); pair terms so differences are 17 and 5.

questions.stem: A sequence of polynomials \(T_{k}(x)\) is defined by the recurrence formula \(T_{0}(x)=1\), \(T_{1}(x)=2x\), \(T_{2}(x)=8x^{2}-1\) and \(T_{k}(x)=4xT_{k-1}(x)-T_{k-2}(x)\) for \(k\ge2\) and \(x>1\). Show that \(T_{3}(x)\) and \(T_{4}(x)\) are \(T_{3}(x)=32x^{3}-6x\) and \(T_{4}(x)=128x^{4}-32x^{2}+1\). Which working is correct?
questions.hint: Use the recurrence \(T_{k}=4xT_{k-1}-T_{k-2}\) with \(k=3\) and then \(k=4\). Be careful with the minus sign: subtracting \((8x^{2}-1)\) changes the sign of BOTH terms.

steps.explain: Expand: \(4x\cdot32x^{3}=128x^{4}\), \(4x\cdot(-6x)=-24x^{2}\). The minus bracket gives \(-8x^{2}+1\) (two sign changes).
Why not the others: B has \(+2x\) (the \(-T_{1}\) was added); C forgets that \(-\left(8x^{2}-1\right)=-8x^{2}+1\); D drops the \(x\) in \(4x\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(T_k=4xT_{k-1}-T_{k-2}\); mind the minus signs.

questions.stem: A sequence of polynomials \(T_{k}(x)\) is defined by the recurrence formula \(T_{0}(x)=1\), \(T_{1}(x)=2x\), \(T_{2}(x)=8x^{2}-1\) and \(T_{k}(x)=4xT_{k-1}(x)-T_{k-2}(x)\) for \(k\ge2\) and \(x>1\). Let \(F(Z)=1+2xZ+\left(8x^{2}-1\right)Z^{2}+\cdots+T_{k}(x)Z^{k}+\cdots\) be the power series in \(Z\) whose coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(T_{k}(x)\). Find \(\left(1-4xZ+Z^{2}\right)F(Z)\) and hence show that \(F(Z)=\dfrac{1-2xZ}{1-4xZ+Z^{2}}\). Which result for \(\left(1-4xZ+Z^{2}\right)F(Z)\) is correct?
questions.hint: Multiply out term by term and COLLECT the coefficient of each power \(Z^{k}\). For \(k\ge2\) the coefficient is \(T_{k}-4xT_{k-1}+T_{k-2}\), which is zero by the recurrence, so only the first two terms survive.

steps.explain: The coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) in \(\left(1-4xZ+Z^{2}\right)F(Z)\) is: (1)\(\times T_{k}\) \(+\) \((-4x)\times T_{k-1}\) \(+\) (1)\(\times T_{k-2}\).
For \(k\ge2\), the recurrence says \(T_{k}=4xT_{k-1}-T_{k-2}\), so this coefficient is 0: all terms from \(Z^{2}\) upwards vanish.
Divide both sides by \(1-4xZ+Z^{2}\).
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign (\(T_{1}-4xT_{0}=-2x\), not \(+2x\)); C and D ignore the \(Z\) term.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Coefficient of \(Z^k\): \(T_k-4xT_{k-1}+T_{k-2}=0\).

questions.stem: For \(Z\) sufficiently small, explain why \(\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac{Z}{\alpha}}\) is equal to \(1+\dfrac Z\alpha+\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}+\cdots\). Which explanation is correct?
options: It is the sum of an infinite geometric series with first term 1 and common ratio \(r=\dfrac Z\alpha\). The sum is \(\dfrac{1}{1-r}\) provided \(|r|<1\), i.e. \(|Z|<|\alpha|\), which holds when \(Z\) is small enough.
It is an arithmetic series with first term 1 and common difference \(\dfrac Z\alpha\); the sum is always \(\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac Z\alpha}\).
It is a geometric series with ratio \(\dfrac Z\alpha\) and the sum \(\dfrac{1}{1-r}\) is valid for ALL values of \(Z\).
It is a geometric series with first term \(\dfrac Z\alpha\) and ratio 1, so the formula \(\dfrac{a}{1-r}\) would divide by 0.
questions.hint: Recognise the geometric series \(a+ar+ar^{2}+\cdots=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\), valid ONLY when \(|r|<1\). Identify \(a\) and \(r\) and say why \(|r|<1\) when \(Z\) is small.

steps.explain: The series is \(1+r+r^{2}+r^{3}+\cdots\) with first term \(a=1\) and common ratio \(r=\dfrac Z\alpha\).
Sum of an infinite geometric series: \(S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\), valid when \(|r|<1\).

\(\alpha\) is a fixed non-zero number (for \(x>1\): \(\alpha=2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}>1\)). When \(Z\) is sufficiently small, \(|Z|<|\alpha|\), so \(\left|\dfrac Z\alpha\right|<1\) and the series converges to \(\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac Z\alpha}\).

Why not the others: B calls it an arithmetic series (terms are MULTIPLIED by the same factor, not added); C says it is valid for all \(Z\) (an infinite geometric series only converges for \(|r|<1\)); D uses the wrong first term and ratio.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Geometric series \(\dfrac{a}{1-r}\), valid when \(|r|<1\).

questions.stem: Given \(F(Z)=\dfrac{A}{1-\dfrac Z\alpha}+\dfrac{B}{1-\dfrac Z\beta}\) and that for small \(Z\), \(\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac Z\alpha}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}\) (and similarly for \(\beta\)), show that the coefficient \(T_{k}(x)\) of \(Z^{k}\) in \(F(Z)\) is \(A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}+B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}\). Which statement is correct?
options: Expand both fractions as geometric series: \(F(Z)=A\sum\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}+B\sum\left(\dfrac Z\beta\right)^{k}\). The coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}+B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}\).
Expand both fractions as geometric series. The coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(A\alpha^{k}+B\beta^{k}\).
Expand both fractions as geometric series. The coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}\) only (the \(\beta\) series contributes nothing).
Expand both fractions as geometric series. The coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(\dfrac{A}{\alpha^{k}}\cdot\dfrac{B}{\beta^{k}}\) (the product of the two).
questions.hint: Replace each fraction by its series. In \(\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}=\dfrac{Z^{k}}{\alpha^{k}}=\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}Z^{k}\), the number multiplying \(Z^{k}\) is \(\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}\). Add the two series (do not multiply them).

steps.explain: Substitute the series for each fraction.
The term in \(Z^{k}\) from the first series is \(A\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}=A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}Z^{k}\); from the second series it is \(B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}Z^{k}\).
Add the coefficients of \(Z^{k}\). But \(F(Z)\) was DEFINED so that the coefficient of \(Z^{k}\) is \(T_{k}(x)\).

Why not the others: B misses that \(\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^{k}\) has \(\dfrac1{\alpha^{k}}\), not \(\alpha^{k}\); C leaves out the \(\beta\) series; D multiplies the series (the two parts of \(F\) are ADDED).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(\left(\dfrac Z\alpha\right)^k=\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^kZ^k\); add the two series.

questions.stem: Deduce that the formula for \(T_{k}(x)\) is: using \(A=B=\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\alpha=2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}\) and \(\beta=2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}\), which of the following is \(T_{k}(x)=A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}+B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}\)?
options: \(T_{k}(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}\)
\(T_{k}(x)=\left(\dfrac{1}{2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}+\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}\)
\(T_{k}(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}\)
\(T_{k}(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k-1}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k-1}\)
questions.hint: Substitute the values into \(T_{k}=A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}+B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}\): \(A=B=\dfrac{1}{2}\) (part v), and \(\dfrac1\alpha\), \(\dfrac1\beta\) with \(\alpha,\beta\) from part (iii). Keep the power \(k\) and the plus sign.

steps.explain: From part (vii): \(T_{k}(x)=A\left(\dfrac1\alpha\right)^{k}+B\left(\dfrac1\beta\right)^{k}\).
Substitute \(A=B=\dfrac{1}{2}\) (part v), \(\alpha=2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}\) and \(\beta=2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}\) (part iii).
Check with \(k=1\): \(\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta=\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}=4x\), so \(T_{1}=\dfrac{1}{2}(4x)=2x\) ✓. With \(k=0\): \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=1=T_{0}\) ✓.

Why not the others: B omits the factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (then \(T_{0}=2\), but \(T_{0}=1\)); C has a minus sign (then \(T_{0}=0\)); D has the power \(k-1\) (then \(T_{0}\) would be \(\dfrac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta)\), not 1).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Substitute \(A=B=\dfrac{1}{2}\); check with \(T_0=1\), \(T_1=2x\).

meta.source: James Ruse Agricultural High School 2020 Trial Higher School Certificate Examination Mathematics Extension 2

questions.stem: Using \(T_{k}(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}}\right)^{k}\) for \(x>1\), find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{T_{n+1}(x)}{T_{n}(x)}\).
questions.hint: Since \(\alpha\beta=1\), \(\dfrac1\alpha=\beta\) and \(\dfrac1\beta=\alpha\), so \(T_{k}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\beta^{k}+\alpha^{k}\right)\). For \(x>1\), \(\alpha>1>\beta>0\): the \(\alpha^{k}\) term DOMINATES for large \(k\). Divide the top and bottom by \(\alpha^{n}\).

steps.explain: Use \(\dfrac1\alpha=\beta\) and \(\dfrac1\beta=\alpha\) (they are reciprocals).
Ratio of consecutive terms. The \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) cancels.
Divide the top and bottom by \(\alpha^{n}\) (the dominant term).
For \(x>1\), \(\alpha=2x+\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}>1\) and \(\beta=\dfrac1\alpha\), so \(0<\dfrac\beta\alpha=\beta^{2}<1\). Then \(\left(\dfrac\beta\alpha\right)^{n}\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Take the limit.
Why not the others: B is \(\beta\) (the smaller root, which does not dominate); C would need \(\alpha=\beta\); D is \(\alpha+\beta\) (the sum).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Dominant term \(\alpha^n\): ratio \(\to\alpha\).

questions.stem: Use Mathematical Induction to prove that \(\left(1-\dfrac1{2^{2}}\right)\left(1-\dfrac1{3^{2}}\right)\cdots\left(1-\dfrac1{n^{2}}\right)=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}\) for \(n\ge2\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: Assume true for \(n=k\). Then \(\text{LHS}_{k+1}=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}\right)=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\cdot\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}-1}{(k+1)^{2}}=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\cdot\dfrac{k(k+2)}{(k+1)^{2}}=\dfrac{k+2}{2(k+1)}\), which is the statement for \(n=k+1\).
Assume true for \(n=k\). Then \(\text{LHS}_{k+1}=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{(k+1)^{2}}\right)=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\cdot\dfrac{k^{2}+1}{(k+1)^{2}}=\dfrac{k^{2}+1}{2k(k+1)}\).
Start with \(n=1\): LHS is the empty product \(=1\) and RHS \(=\dfrac{2}{2}=1\); so true for \(n=1\) and the step then follows for \(n\ge2\).
Assume true for \(n=k\). Then \(\text{LHS}_{k+1}=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}+\left(1-\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\right)=\dfrac{k+2}{2(k+1)}\).
questions.hint: Proof by induction: (1) BASE case at the first value, \(n=2\); (2) ASSUME true for \(n=k\); (3) show true for \(n=k+1\) by multiplying the assumed result by the NEW factor \(1-\dfrac1{(k+1)^{2}}\); (4) CONCLUDE.

steps.explain: BASE CASE \(n=2\) (the statement is for \(n\ge2\)): \(\text{LHS}=1-\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}\); \(\text{RHS}=\dfrac{2+1}{2(2)}=\dfrac{3}{4}\) ✓.
ASSUMPTION: for some integer \(k\ge2\), \(\left(1-\dfrac1{2^{2}}\right)\cdots\left(1-\dfrac1{k^{2}}\right)=\dfrac{k+1}{2k}\). To prove: the product up to \((k+1)\) equals \(\dfrac{k+2}{2(k+1)}\).
STEP: the left side is the assumed product TIMES the new factor. Substitute the assumption.
Cancel \(k\) and one factor \((k+1)\).
CONCLUSION: true for \(n=2\), and if true for \(n=k\) then true for \(n=k+1\); by induction it is true for all integers \(n\ge2\).
Why not the others: B has \((k+1)^{2}-1=k^{2}+1\) (it is \(k^{2}+2k\)); C uses the wrong base case (the statement starts at \(n=2\)); D ADDS the new factor instead of MULTIPLYING.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that \(\forall n\in Z^{+}\), \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2n\sqrt n}{3}\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: BASE \(n=1\): LHS \(=1>\dfrac{2}{3}=\) RHS ✓. ASSUME \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}\). Then \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}+\sqrt{k+1}\). It is enough to show \(\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}+\sqrt{k+1}\ge\dfrac{2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}}{3}\), i.e. \(2k\sqrt k\ge(2k-1)\sqrt{k+1}\). Squaring (both sides positive): \(4k^{3}\ge(2k-1)^{2}(k+1)=4k^{3}-3k+1\), i.e. \(3k\ge1\), true for \(k\ge1\).
BASE \(n=1\): LHS \(=1>\dfrac{2}{3}\) ✓. ASSUME true for \(n=k\). Then \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}\cdot\sqrt{k+1}\) (multiply by the new term).
BASE \(n=0\): LHS \(=0\), RHS \(=0\). ASSUME true for \(n=k\); then adding \(\sqrt{k+1}\) to both sides gives the result immediately with no further work.

BASE \(n=1\) ✓. ASSUME true for \(n=k\). Then \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}+\sqrt{k+1}\). It is enough to show \(2k\sqrt k\ge(2k+1)\sqrt{k+1}\), which is true since \(\sqrt k\ge\sqrt{k+1}\).
questions.hint: Induction: (1) BASE case \(n=1\); (2) ASSUME \(n=k\); (3) ADD the new term \(\sqrt{k+1}\) to both sides; (4) show the new right side is at least \(\dfrac{2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}}{3}\) by rearranging and SQUARING (both sides positive).

steps.explain: BASE CASE \(n=1\): LHS \(=\sqrt1=1\); RHS \(=\dfrac{2\cdot1\cdot1}{3}=\dfrac{2}{3}\). \(1>\dfrac{2}{3}\) ✓.
ASSUMPTION: \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}\) for some \(k\ge1\). To prove: \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sqrt i>\dfrac{2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}}{3}\).

It remains to show \(\dfrac{2k\sqrt k}{3}+\sqrt{k+1}\ge\dfrac{2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}}{3}\). Multiply by 3 and collect the \(\sqrt{k+1}\) terms: \(2k\sqrt k\ge2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}-3\sqrt{k+1}=(2k-1)\sqrt{k+1}\).
Both sides are positive (\(k\ge1\)), so square both sides: \(4k^{2}\cdot k=4k^{3}\) and \((2k-1)^{2}(k+1)=\left(4k^{2}-4k+1\right)(k+1)=4k^{3}-3k+1\).
\(3k\ge1\) is true for \(k\ge1\). So the new sum exceeds \(\dfrac{2(k+1)\sqrt{k+1}}{3}\). By induction the statement is true for all positive integers \(n\).

Why not the others: B MULTIPLIES instead of adding; C uses the wrong base case (the statement is for positive integers) and skips the proof; D has \((2k+1)\) and a false justification (\(\sqrt k\ge\sqrt{k+1}\) is false).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Add \(\sqrt{k+1}\); show \(2k\sqrt k\ge(2k-1)\sqrt{k+1}\) by squaring.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction \((2n)!<(n!)^{2}\times4^{n-1}\) for all positive integers \(n\ge5\). Which inductive step is correct?
options: BASE \(n=5\) ✓. ASSUME true for \(k\). Then \((2k+2)!=(2k)!+(2k+2)!\), so the result follows by adding.
questions.hint: Induction: BASE case \(n=5\) (the first value allowed); ASSUME for \(n=k\); for \(n=k+1\) write \((2k+2)!=(2k+2)(2k+1)(2k)!\) and use the assumption to replace \((2k)!\) by the BIGGER expression. Then show the result is at most \(((k+1)!)^{2}4^{k}\).

steps.explain: Use the assumption (multiplying a strict inequality by a positive number keeps it).
CONCLUSION: true for \(n=5\); if true for \(n=k\) then true for \(n=k+1\); so true for all integers \(n\ge5\).
Why not the others: B uses a false base case and a wrong step (\((2k+2)!=(2k+2)(2k+1)(2k)!\), two factors); C writes a nonsense identity; D claims the base case is false (it is true).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.solution: The triangle inequality states that the sum of any two sides of a triangle is strictly greater than the third side: \(a + b > c\).

steps.explain: Recall the triangle inequality.
steps.work: For any triangle with sides \(a\), \(b\), \(c\): \(a + b > c\), \(a + c > b\), and \(b + c > a\).

questions.stem: Using calculus, we can show \(e^x \geq 1 + x\) for all real \(x\). Which approach is correct?
options: Let \(f(x) = e^x - 1 - x\). Show \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f'(x) = e^x - 1\), which is \(\geq 0\) for \(x \geq 0\) and \(\leq 0\) for \(x \leq 0\), so \(f(x) \geq f(0) = 0\)
Substitute \(x = 0\) to verify \(e^0 = 1 + 0 = 1\)
Take the derivative of both sides and compare
Apply the AM-GM inequality directly
questions.solution: Let \(f(x) = e^x - 1 - x\). Then \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f'(x) = e^x - 1\). Since \(e^x \geq 1\) for \(x \geq 0\), \(f\) is increasing for \(x \geq 0\) so \(f(x) \geq f(0) = 0\). Similarly for \(x \leq 0\). Hence \(e^x \geq 1 + x\) for all \(x\).

steps.explain: Define \(f(x) = e^x - 1 - x\) and evaluate at \(x = 0\).
Differentiate.
Analyse the sign of \(f'(x)\).
steps.work: \(f'(x) \geq 0 \iff e^x \geq 1 \iff x \geq 0\). So \(f\) has a global minimum at \(x = 0\). Therefore \(f(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\), i.e. \(e^x \geq 1 + x\). \(\square\)

questions.solution: Sample answer: Let u=a−b≥0 and v=b−c≥0. Then (a+b+c)²−(a²+3b²+5c²)=2(ab+ac+bc−b²−2c²)=2(ub+uc+2cv)≥0. Hence a²+3b²+5c²≤(a+b+c)²≤1.

Each term is nonnegative because b,c,u,v≥0.
Apply the stated upper bound.

questions.stem:
If \(f(x)=\ln x\) is the continuous, strictly increasing function on the interval \([a,b]\), as shown below, which of the following three statements must be true?

I \(\ \int_a^b\ln x\,dx\lt (b-a)\ln b\)
II \(\ \int_a^b\ln x\,dx\gt (b-a)\ln a\)
III there exists a number \(c\) where \(a\lt c\lt b\), such that \(\int_a^b\ln x\,dx=(b-a)\ln c\)
questions.hint: Compare the area with the two rectangles of heights ln a and ln b; for III think of the 'average height'.

steps.explain: The area under the curve from \(a\) to \(b\) lies between two rectangles of width \(b-a\): the short one of height \(\ln a\) and the tall one of height \(\ln b\).

parts.answer: Since \(f'(x)\gt0\) everywhere, f is increasing. f passes through O with gradient f'(0) = 1 (steepest point, a point of inflection, since f' has a maximum there). As \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f'(x)\to0\), so f levels off to horizontal asymptotes above and below. By symmetry of f' (even), f is odd. The sketch is an S-shaped curve through O at 45° with two horizontal asymptotes.

keyPoints.note: The height of f′ is the gradient of f: positive everywhere, largest (= 1) at x = 0, tending to 0.

parts.hint: Use g′(x) = 1 / f′(g(x)).

steps.explain: For inverse functions \(\frac{dy}{dx}=1\Big/\frac{dx}{dy}\). With \(y=g(x)\), i.e. \(x=f(y)\):
At \(x=0\): \(g(0)=0\), so \(g'(0)=\frac{1}{f'(0)}=1\). Since \(0\lt f'\le1\), we get \(g'(x)\ge1\): the minimum value is 1 at \(x=0\).

The domain of \(g\) is the range of \(f\) (between the horizontal asymptotes). Near those values \(g(x)\to\pm\infty\) and \(f'(g(x))\to0\), so \(g'(x)\to\infty\): vertical asymptotes. The graph is U-shaped and even.

parts.answer: Since g is the inverse of f, \(g'(x)=\frac{1}{f'(g(x))}\). g'(0) = 1/f'(0) = 1. f' is at most 1 and positive, so g'(x) ≥ 1, with minimum 1 at x = 0. As x approaches the asymptote values of f, g(x) → ±∞ and f'(g(x)) → 0, so g'(x) → ∞: vertical asymptotes. The graph is a U-shape with minimum (0, 1) between two vertical asymptotes.

questions.stem: Use the trapezoidal rule with \(n-1\) sub-intervals to show that \(\int_1^n\ln x\,dx > \ln n + \dfrac12\ln((n-1)!)\).
questions.answer: The trapezoidal estimate gives \(\dfrac12\ln n+\ln((n-1)!)\), and since \(\ln x\) is concave down the estimate is an underestimate.
questions.hint: Use the trapezoidal rule with the points \(x=1,2,\dots,n\), and remember the curve is concave down.

steps.explain: Trapezoidal rule with \(n-1\) strips of width 1 and points \(x=1,\dots,n\): area \(\approx\dfrac12\left[f(1)+2f(2)+\dots+2f(n-1)+f(n)\right]\), where \(f=\ln x\).
Use \(\ln1=0\) and \(\sum\ln k=\ln\prod k\): the sum becomes \(\dfrac12\left[\ln n+2\ln((n-1)!)\right]=\dfrac12\ln n+\ln((n-1)!)\).
\(\ln x\) is concave down, so each trapezium lies below the curve. The trapezoidal estimate is an underestimate, so the integral is larger.
This is the bound stated in the question, so the proof is complete.

questions.stem: Consider the function \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\) for \(x>0\). Let \(m\) be a positive real number, \(m\ge1\). By integrating \(f(x)\) between \(m\) and \(m+1\), show that \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m<\dfrac{1}{m}\). Which argument is correct?
options: \(\displaystyle\int_{m}^{m+1}\dfrac{dx}{x}=\ln(m+1)-\ln m\). On \([m,m+1]\) the curve \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\) is decreasing, so \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac{1}{m}\). The interval has width 1, so the area is between \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}\times1\) and \(\dfrac{1}{m}\times1\).

\(\displaystyle\int_{m}^{m+1}\dfrac{dx}{x}=\ln(m+1)-\ln m\). Since \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) is decreasing, \(\dfrac{1}{m}<\dfrac{1}{x}<\dfrac1{m+1}\), so the area is between \(\dfrac{1}{m}\) and \(\dfrac1{m+1}\).
\(\displaystyle\int_{m}^{m+1}\dfrac{dx}{x}=\ln(m+1)+\ln m\). Since \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) is decreasing the result follows.
\(\displaystyle\int_{m}^{m+1}\dfrac{dx}{x}=\dfrac{1}{m+1}-\dfrac{1}{m}\). The curve is decreasing so the result follows.
questions.hint: Integrate: \(\int\dfrac{dx}{x}=\ln x\). Then COMPARE the area under the curve with two RECTANGLES of width 1: a smaller rectangle (height at the right end \(\dfrac1{m+1}\)) and a bigger one (height at the left end \(\dfrac{1}{m}\)). The curve \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\) is decreasing.

steps.explain: Integrate \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) between \(m\) and \(m+1\).
On \([m,m+1]\) the function \(y=\dfrac{1}{x}\) is DECREASING, so it is largest at the left end \(x=m\) (height \(\dfrac{1}{m}\)) and smallest at the right end \(x=m+1\) (height \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}\)).
Area under the curve lies between the areas of the small rectangle (height \(\dfrac1{m+1}\), width 1) and the big rectangle (height \(\dfrac{1}{m}\), width 1).
Substitute the integral.

Why not the others: B swaps the bounds (the inequality would be false); C has \(\ln(m+1)+\ln m\) (the integral is a DIFFERENCE of logs); D integrates \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) as if it were \(\dfrac1{x^{2}}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Let \(S_{k}=1+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{k}\). Using \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m<\dfrac{1}{m}\), let \(m\) take on successively the values \(1,2,\dots\) and hence show that \(\ln(k+1)<S_{k}<1+\ln k\). Which argument is correct?
options: Sum \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m\) for \(m=1,\dots,k-1\): the right side telescopes to \(\ln k-\ln1=\ln k\), and the left side is \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{k}=S_{k}-1\). So \(S_{k}<1+\ln k\). Sum \(\ln(m+1)-\ln m<\dfrac{1}{m}\) for \(m=1,\dots,k\): the left side telescopes to \(\ln(k+1)\) and the right side is \(S_{k}\). So \(\ln(k+1)<S_{k}\).
Sum \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m\) for \(m=1,\dots,k\): the left side is \(S_{k}\) and the right side is \(\ln(k+1)\). So \(S_{k}<\ln(k+1)\), and similarly \(\ln k<1+S_{k}\).
Sum \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m\) for \(m=1,\dots,k-1\) only. This gives \(S_{k}<1+\ln k\), and the other inequality follows by the same sum.

Sum \(\ln(m+1)-\ln m<\dfrac{1}{m}\) for \(m=1,\dots,k-1\): the right side is \(S_{k}\) (not \(S_{k-1}\)), and the left side is \(\ln k\). So \(\ln k<S_{k}\), and replacing \(k\) by \(k+1\) gives both inequalities at once.
questions.hint: Add the inequality up for consecutive values of \(m\). \(\ln(m+1)-\ln m\) TELESCOPES (the middle terms cancel). Use the LEFT inequality for the upper bound of \(S_{k}\) and the RIGHT inequality for the lower bound.

steps.explain: LEFT inequality \(\dfrac{1}{m+1}<\ln(m+1)-\ln m\), summed for \(m=1,2,\dots,k-1\). Left side: \(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{k}=S_{k}-1\).
Right side telescopes: \(\left(\ln2-\ln1\right)+\left(\ln3-\ln2\right)+\cdots+\left(\ln k-\ln(k-1)\right)=\ln k-\ln1=\ln k\).
RIGHT inequality \(\ln(m+1)-\ln m<\dfrac{1}{m}\), summed for \(m=1,2,\dots,k\). Left side telescopes to \(\ln(k+1)-\ln1=\ln(k+1)\); right side is \(1+\dfrac{1}{2}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{k}=S_{k}\).
Combine (1) and (2).
Why not the others: B has the inequality direction reversed; C proves only one half; D sums the right inequality to \(k-1\), which gives \(\ln k<S_{k-1}\) (not \(S_{k}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Telescoping sums of both parts of the inequality.

questions.stem: If the functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are such that \(f(x)>g(x)\ge0\) for \(a\le x\le b\), by using a sketch (or otherwise) explain why \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx>\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}g(x)\,dx\). Which explanation is correct?
options: A definite integral of a non-negative function is the AREA between the curve and the \(x\)-axis. Since \(f(x)>g(x)\ge0\), the curve \(y=f(x)\) lies ABOVE \(y=g(x)\), which is above the \(x\)-axis. So the region under \(g\) lies INSIDE the region under \(f\), and the region between the two curves has positive area. Hence the area under \(f\) is strictly bigger.
Since \(f(x)>g(x)\) at \(x=a\) and at \(x=b\), the areas are bigger at the ends, so \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f>\int_{a}^{b}g\).
The derivative of \(f\) is larger than the derivative of \(g\), so \(f\) has the larger integral.
Since \(f(x)>g(x)\), the area under \(g\) is larger because \(g\) is closer to the \(x\)-axis.
questions.hint: Integrals of non-negative functions are AREAS under the curves. Sketch both curves above the \(x\)-axis with \(f\) above \(g\) and compare the two areas.

steps.explain: Because \(f(x)>g(x)\ge0\) on \([a,b]\), both curves are on or above the \(x\)-axis, and \(y=f(x)\) is above \(y=g(x)\) everywhere. Each integral is the area between its curve and the \(x\)-axis.
In the sketch the blue region (under \(g\)) is contained in the larger region under \(f\). The difference is the YELLOW region between the two curves.
The yellow region has POSITIVE area because \(f(x)-g(x)>0\) for every \(x\). In symbols: \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}\left(f-g\right)dx>0\), so \(\displaystyle\int f>\int g\).
Why not the others: B only compares the end values (the integral depends on every \(x\)); C is irrelevant (derivatives do not decide integrals); D reverses the comparison.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: by using a sketch (or otherwise) explain why
keyPoints.note: Integral \(=\) area; area under \(f\) \(=\) area under \(g\) \(+\) positive gap.

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}dt\) for non-negative integers \(n\). Using part (a), or otherwise, show that \(0<I_{n}<I_{n-1}\). Which argument is correct?
options: For \(0<t<1\): \(0<1-t^{2}<1\). A number between 0 and 1 gets SMALLER when raised to a higher power, so \(\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}<\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{2}}\), and both are positive. By part (a), \(0<I_{n}<I_{n-1}\) (the integrand of \(I_{n}\) is positive, so \(I_{n}>0\)).
For \(0<t<1\): \(0<1-t^{2}<1\), so higher powers are LARGER: \(\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}>\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{2}}\). By part (a), \(I_{n}>I_{n-1}\).
\(I_{n}\) and \(I_{n-1}\) are both positive integrals, so \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\).
\(\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\) is the same as \(\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{2}}\) for \(0<t<1\), so \(I_{n}=I_{n-1}\).
questions.hint: Compare the INTEGRANDS \(f(t)=\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{2}}\) (for \(I_{n-1}\)) and \(g(t)=\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\) (for \(I_{n}\)). On \((0,1)\) the base \(1-t^{2}\) is between 0 and 1: bigger exponent means smaller value. Then use part (a).

steps.explain: For \(0<t<1\): \(0<t^{2}<1\), so \(0<1-t^{2}<1\). The exponent for \(I_{n}\) is \(\dfrac{n-1}{2}\), which is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) MORE than \(\dfrac{n-2}{2}\) (for \(I_{n-1}\)).
A number strictly between 0 and 1 gets smaller when the exponent increases, so \(g(t)<f(t)\). Both are positive (a positive base).
Part (a): \(f>g\ge0\) implies \(\int f>\int g\). Here \(\int f=I_{n-1}\) and \(\int g=I_{n}\). Also \(g>0\) so \(I_{n}>0\).
Why not the others: B reverses the effect of the exponent; C only says both are positive (it does not compare them); D is false (the exponents differ).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(0<1-t^2<1\): bigger exponent \(\Rightarrow\) smaller; use part (a).

questions.stem: Using \(J_{n}=nI_{n}I_{n-1}=\dfrac\pi2\) and \(0<I_{n}<I_{n-1}\), hence, or otherwise, prove that \(\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n+2}}<I_{n}<\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n}}\). Which argument is correct?
options: UPPER bound: \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\) so \(\dfrac\pi2=nI_{n}I_{n-1}>nI_{n}^{2}\), giving \(I_{n}^{2}<\dfrac{\pi}{2n}\). LOWER bound: \(J_{n+1}=(n+1)I_{n+1}I_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\) and \(I_{n+1}<I_{n}\), so \(\dfrac\pi2<(n+1)I_{n}^{2}\), giving \(I_{n}^{2}>\dfrac{\pi}{2n+2}\). Take positive square roots.
UPPER bound: \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\) so \(\dfrac\pi2=nI_{n}I_{n-1}<nI_{n-1}^{2}\), giving \(I_{n}<\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n}}\). LOWER bound is the same with \(n+1\).
UPPER bound: \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\) so \(\dfrac\pi2=nI_{n}I_{n-1}>nI_{n}^{2}\), so \(I_{n}^{2}<\dfrac{\pi}{n}\). LOWER bound: \(I_{n}>0\) so \(I_{n}>\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n+2}}\).
UPPER bound: \(J_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\) gives \(I_{n}I_{n-1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2n}\); since \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\), \(I_{n}<\dfrac{\pi}{2n}\). LOWER: similarly \(I_{n}>\dfrac{\pi}{2n+2}\).
questions.hint: Use \(nI_{n}I_{n-1}=\dfrac\pi2\) with the inequality \(I_{n}<I_{n-1}\): replace \(I_{n-1}\) by the smaller \(I_{n}\) to get an inequality in \(I_{n}^{2}\). For the lower bound use \(J_{n+1}=(n+1)I_{n+1}I_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\) and \(I_{n+1}<I_{n}\).

steps.explain: UPPER bound. From \(J_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\): \(nI_{n}I_{n-1}=\dfrac\pi2\). Since \(I_{n-1}>I_{n}>0\), replacing \(I_{n-1}\) by the smaller \(I_{n}\) makes the product SMALLER.
LOWER bound. Use \(J_{n+1}=\dfrac\pi2\): \((n+1)I_{n+1}I_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\). Since \(I_{n+1}<I_{n}\), replacing \(I_{n+1}\) by the larger \(I_{n}\) makes the product LARGER.
Combine: \(\dfrac{\pi}{2n+2}<I_{n}^{2}<\dfrac{\pi}{2n}\). Since \(I_{n}>0\), take positive square roots.

Why not the others: B uses \(I_{n-1}\) on both sides (the direction would be wrong); C gives the weaker \(\dfrac\pi n\) and an invalid lower bound; D forgets the square root (\(I_{n}\) is bounded by the square root).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: By considering the sum to \(n\) terms of the series \(1-t+t^{2}-t^{3}+\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}t^{n-1}\), \(t\ne-1\): Show that \(x-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}+\cdots+(-1)^{n}\dfrac{x^{n}}{n}=\log_{e}(1+x)-(-1)^{n}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}\,dt\) for \(0<t<x\). Which working is correct? (The last term on the left is \((-1)^{n-1}\dfrac{x^{n}}{n}\) in the correct identity.)
options: The series is a GP with first term 1 and ratio \(-t\): \(S_{n}=\dfrac{1-(-t)^{n}}{1+t}=\dfrac{1}{1+t}-\dfrac{(-1)^{n}t^{n}}{1+t}\). Integrate from 0 to \(x\): \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}S_{n}\,dt=x-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}\dfrac{x^{n}}{n}\) (term by term) and \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{dt}{1+t}=\ln(1+x)\). So the sum equals \(\ln(1+x)-(-1)^{n}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt\).
The series is a GP with ratio \(t\): \(S_{n}=\dfrac{1-t^{n}}{1-t}\). Integrating from 0 to \(x\) gives \(-\ln(1-x)\), not \(\ln(1+x)\).
The series is a GP with first term 1 and ratio \(-t\): \(S_{n}=\dfrac{1+(-t)^{n}}{1+t}\). Integrating gives \(\ln(1+x)+(-1)^{n}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt\).
Differentiate the left side term by term to get \(1-x+x^{2}-\cdots\), which equals \(\dfrac{1}{1+x}\) exactly (no remainder), so the integral term is not needed.
questions.hint: The series \(1-t+t^{2}-\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}t^{n-1}\) is a finite GP with first term 1 and common ratio \(-t\), \(n\) terms: \(S_{n}=\dfrac{1-r^{n}}{1-r}\). Write \(S_{n}\) as TWO fractions and integrate from 0 to \(x\). Each term \((-1)^{k-1}t^{k-1}\) integrates to \((-1)^{k-1}\dfrac{x^{k}}{k}\).

steps.explain: GP: first term \(a=1\), ratio \(r=-t\), \(n\) terms. \(S_{n}=\dfrac{a\left(1-r^{n}\right)}{1-r}=\dfrac{1-(-t)^{n}}{1+t}\). Split.
Integrate the LEFT form (the series itself) term by term: \(\int_{0}^{x}(-1)^{k-1}t^{k-1}dt=(-1)^{k-1}\dfrac{x^{k}}{k}\).
Integrate the RIGHT form: \(\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{dt}{1+t}=\ln(1+x)\) and keep the remainder integral.
Equate the two expressions for \(\int_{0}^{x}S_{n}dt\).

Why not the others: B uses ratio \(t\) (the signs alternate, so the ratio is \(-t\)); C has a plus sign in the numerator of \(S_{n}\); D forgets the remainder: a FINITE GP does not equal \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: By considering the sum to \(n\) terms of the series
keyPoints.note: GP ratio \(-t\): \(S_n=\dfrac{1-(-t)^n}{1+t}\); integrate \(0\) to \(x\).

questions.stem: Also, show that \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}\,dt<\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}\,dt\) (for \(x>0\)). Which argument is correct?
options: For \(t>0\): \(1+t>1\), so \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}<1\). Multiplying by \(t^{n}>0\): \(\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}<t^{n}\) for \(0<t\le x\). By the inequality of integrals (as in part 15(a)), \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}dt\).
For \(t>0\): \(1+t>1\), so \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}>1\). Multiplying by \(t^{n}\): \(\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}>t^{n}\); integrating gives the result.
The integrand \(\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}\) and \(t^{n}\) are both positive, so their integrals are equal.

Integrate both: \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt=\dfrac{t^{n+1}}{(n+1)(1+t)}\) and \(\displaystyle\int t^{n}dt=\dfrac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}\); the first is smaller because of the extra factor \(\dfrac{1}{1+t}\).
questions.hint: Compare the INTEGRANDS on \(0<t\le x\): \(\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}\) versus \(t^{n}\). The denominator \(1+t\) is bigger than 1 when \(t>0\), so the fraction is smaller. Then the integral of the smaller function is smaller (like part 15(a)).

steps.explain: For \(t>0\): \(1+t>1\). Taking reciprocals (positive numbers) REVERSES the inequality.
Multiply both sides by \(t^{n}>0\) (the direction stays).
If \(f(t)<g(t)\) on the interval, then \(\int f<\int g\) (area under the smaller curve is smaller).
Why not the others: B reverses the reciprocal inequality; C claims equality (the integrands differ); D uses a false antiderivative.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(1+t>1\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{1+t}<1\); compare integrands.

questions.stem: For \(0<x\le1\), show that \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}\,dt<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). Which argument is correct?
options: From part (ii): \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}dt=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\). Since \(0<x\le1\), \(x^{n+1}\le1\), so \(\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\le\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). Combining: the integral is \(<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).
From part (ii): \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\). Since \(x\le1\), \(x^{n+1}\ge1\), so the integral is bigger than \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).
\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}dt=\dfrac{x^{n}}{n}\), so the integral is less than \(\dfrac{1}{n}\), and \(\dfrac{1}{n}<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).
Put \(x=1\): \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). Hence the result.
questions.hint: Start from the result of (ii) and evaluate \(\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}dt=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\). Then use \(0<x\le1\Rightarrow x^{n+1}\le1\) to bound it by \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). Combine the two inequalities (chain).

steps.explain: By part (ii), \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\int_{0}^{x}t^{n}dt\). Evaluate the right side.
For \(0<x\le1\), raising to the power \(n+1\) keeps a number in \((0,1]\): \(x^{n+1}\le1\). Divide by \(n+1>0\).
Chain the inequalities.
Why not the others: B reverses \(x^{n+1}\le1\); C integrates \(t^{n}\) wrongly (\(\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\)); D wrongly claims equality at \(x=1\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: (ii) \(+\ \int t^n=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\le\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).

questions.stem: Using \(x-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+\cdots\) as the partial sums and \(0<\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\) for \(0<x\le1\), prove that as \(n\to\infty\), \(x-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}+\cdots+(-1)^{n}\dfrac{x^{n}}{n}+\cdots=\log_{e}(1+x)\). Which argument is correct?
options: From the identity: \(\text{partial sum}=\ln(1+x)-(-1)^{n}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt\). Hence \(\left|\ln(1+x)-\text{partial sum}\right|=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\) (and the integral is positive). By the squeeze theorem the integral tends to 0, so the partial sums tend to \(\ln(1+x)\).
As \(n\to\infty\), \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to0\), so the partial sum equals 0.
As \(n\to\infty\), \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to\infty\), so the partial sums diverge.
The integral is positive, so it can never tend to 0; the partial sums therefore do not converge to \(\ln(1+x)\).
questions.hint: The DIFFERENCE between \(\ln(1+x)\) and the partial sum is the remainder \(\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt\), which is positive and less than \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\). Let \(n\to\infty\) and use the SQUEEZE theorem: the remainder goes to 0.

steps.explain: Rearrange the identity from (i): the partial sum \(S\) satisfies \(\ln(1+x)-S=(-1)^{n}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\dfrac{t^{n}}{1+t}dt\).
Apply the bounds from (iii): \(0<\)remainder\(<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).
As \(n\to\infty\), \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to0\). The remainder is squeezed between 0 and a quantity tending to 0 (squeeze theorem), so it tends to 0.
Therefore the partial sums converge to \(\ln(1+x)\): the infinite series equals \(\log_{e}(1+x)\) for \(0<x\le1\).

Why not the others: B confuses the remainder with the partial sum; C says \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to\infty\) (it tends to 0); D says a positive integral cannot tend to 0 (positive numbers can get arbitrarily small).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Remainder \(<\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to0\): squeeze theorem.
